findings.dimension: Univariate time-series econometrics (ARIMA/SARIMAX, ETS/Holt-Winters, Theta, structural/unobserved-components state-space) and the random-walk/EMH benchmark for copper price forecasting at weekly and monthly horizons
findings.overview: For copper and base-metal prices, the classical univariate-econometrics toolkit serves two roles: (1) the random walk / no-change forecast is the dominant, hard-to-beat benchmark against which everything else is judged, and (2) ARIMA/SARIMAX, exponential smoothing (ETS/Holt-Winters), the Theta method, and structural/unobserved-components (UC) state-space models are the interpretable workhorses that try to beat it. The recurring empirical theme across the metals and broader commodity literature is that at SHORT horizons (days to ~1 month) copper behaves close to a martingale in log-levels, so the random walk is statistically very difficult to beat out-of-sample; gains over the RW tend to appear (i) when informative EXOGENOUS regressors are added (China activity, the spot-futures basis/inventories, USD, cross-asset prices) turning ARIMA into ARIMAX/SARIMAX or feeding dynamic model-averaging, and (ii) at longer horizons (quarters to years) where mean-reversion in real prices and trend/cycle structure become exploitable. A crucial nuance specific to copper: copper has essentially NO strong calendar seasonality in price (unlike agriculturals or natural gas), so the seasonal machinery of SARIMA/Holt-Winters adds little for copper itself, though it matters for some demand proxies. Methodologically, the consensus is to model the log price (variance-stabilising, keeps forecasts positive) and to difference to log-returns for stationarity; whether you forecast the log-level (random-walk-consistent) or the return matters mainly for how you impose/avoid a drift. The interpretable models remain the recommended core because their coefficients, states (level/trend/cycle), error-correction terms, and prediction intervals are inspectable and explainable, whereas opaque ML (deep nets, large tree ensembles) typically only edges them out at longer horizons and at the cost of transparency.

approaches.name: Random walk / no-change benchmark (and the EMH backdrop)
approaches.one_line: Forecast the next log-price as today's log-price (optionally with a drift), the martingale benchmark every other model must beat.
approaches.mechanism: y_hat_{t+h}=y_t in log-levels (RW without drift) or y_hat_{t+h}=y_t+h*mu (RW with drift). Fully interpretable: there is nothing to read except the last observed price and, optionally, an estimated drift mu. Under weak-form market efficiency, all public information is already in the price, so the conditional expectation of future price equals today's price and excess predictability should be near zero at short horizons. Prediction intervals widen with sqrt(h).
approaches.horizon_fit: Strongest and hardest to beat at WEEKLY (5d) and short MONTHLY (22d) horizons, where copper log-prices are close to a martingale. The RW-WITHOUT-drift is the right benchmark; RW-with-drift (trend extrapolation) typically forecasts WORSE because it extrapolates noise as trend (Reeve & Vigfusson find RW-with-drift is beaten by both plain RW and futures). At 3-month and longer, mean-reversion in real prices starts to make the plain RW beatable.
approaches.interpretability: Maximal: a one-number model. Its forecast and interval are trivially explainable, which is exactly why it is the universal yardstick.
approaches.strengths: Robust, parameter-light, no estimation error, near-optimal at short horizons for efficient markets; the single most reliable baseline for copper at 1d/5d/22d.
approaches.weaknesses: Ignores all fundamentals, mean-reversion, the futures basis, and regime shifts; provides no economic narrative; at long horizons it is dominated by models that capture reversion. RW-with-drift is fragile (extrapolates recent trend into the future).
approaches.copper_relevance: Naturally uses only the COMEX HG / LME spot (log) price. It is the benchmark your existing Naive baseline already implements; the literature says any copper model claiming skill at weekly/monthly horizons must show statistically significant out-of-sample improvement over this exact benchmark (Clark-West / Diebold-Mariano tests, out-of-sample R2).

key_papers.citation: Reeve, T.A. & Vigfusson, R.J. (2011), 'Evaluating the Forecasting Performance of Commodity Futures Prices', Federal Reserve Board IFDP No. 1025.
key_papers.method: RW (no drift), RW-with-drift, and futures-based forecasts compared across commodities including copper and other base metals; emphasis on the spot-futures basis.
key_papers.finding: Futures generally outperform a random walk but 'not by a large margin'; both the futures and the plain RW noticeably beat a RW-with-drift (trend extrapolation). For copper specifically, futures beat the RW by a CONSIDERABLE margin only when the spot-futures spread is large (i.e., when inventories/convenience yield are extreme). Confirms RW is a tough short-horizon benchmark for copper.

key_papers.citation: Diaz, J.D., Hansen, E. & Cabrera, G. (2020), 'A random walk through the trees: Forecasting copper prices using decision learning methods', Resources Policy, 69, 101895.
key_papers.method: Random walk benchmark vs regression trees, random forests, gradient-boosted trees on copper prices, multiple horizons.
key_papers.finding: The random walk produces the BEST out-of-sample copper forecasts in the short and medium run; tree-based learners only become competitive at distant (~2-year) horizons. A direct, copper-specific demonstration that the RW dominates at weekly/monthly horizons.

key_papers.citation: Wang, D. et al. (2021), 'Forecasting Commodity Prices: Looking for a Benchmark', Forecasting (MDPI) 3(2), 27 (summarising the Alquist-Kilian-Vigfusson commodity-forecasting literature).
key_papers.method: Survey/comparison of benchmarks (RW, futures, local-projection mean-reversion) across commodities and horizons.
key_papers.finding: At short horizons nominal commodity forecasts should benchmark RW against futures-based forecasts; at long horizons RW should be supplemented/replaced by mean-reverting local-projection forecasts. The literature is often 'mute on whether RW is truly hard to beat' and many apparent wins are sample/period-specific.

approaches.name: ARIMA / SARIMA / ARIMAX / SARIMAX (Box-Jenkins)
approaches.one_line: Linear autoregressive-moving-average model on the (log-)differenced price, optionally with seasonal terms and exogenous regressors, selected by the Box-Jenkins identification-estimation-diagnostic cycle.
approaches.mechanism: ARIMA(p,d,q) models the d-times-differenced series as AR(p)+MA(q) noise; SARIMA adds seasonal (P,D,Q)_s terms; ARIMAX/SARIMAX add exogenous regressors X (so the mean is beta*X plus ARMA errors). Interpretable elements: the AR coefficients (persistence/momentum), MA coefficients (shock memory), the differencing order d (whether the price is I(1), consistent with a random walk when p=q=0,d=1), the exogenous betas (elasticity of copper to each driver), and analytic Gaussian prediction intervals. Box-Jenkins model choice via ACF/PACF, unit-root tests (ADF/KPSS), and information criteria (AIC/BIC).
approaches.horizon_fit: MONTHLY: well-suited; auto-ARIMA on log-prices is a standard monthly copper baseline and ARIMAX with monthly macro/inventory regressors is natural. WEEKLY: usable but the AR/MA structure of weekly copper RETURNS is typically weak, so a pure ARIMA often collapses toward the random walk (ARIMA(0,1,0) = RW); value at weekly horizon comes almost entirely from the X in ARIMAX (basis, COT, USD), not from the ARMA dynamics. SARIMA's seasonal terms add little for copper itself (no strong price seasonality).
approaches.interpretability: High: every coefficient has a meaning, d encodes the order of integration, and the model nests the random walk as a special case so you can literally test how far copper departs from a martingale. Built-in closed-form intervals.
approaches.strengths: Transparent, fast, nests the RW, gives calibrated Gaussian intervals, and ARIMAX cleanly absorbs copper-specific exogenous drivers with readable elasticities; strong, well-understood monthly baseline.
approaches.weaknesses: Assumes linearity, constant parameters, and (after differencing) stationarity/homoskedasticity - all violated by copper's volatility clustering and regime shifts; over-differencing or mis-identified orders hurt; pure ARIMA rarely beats the RW out-of-sample at short horizons; needs GARCH errors for honest intervals during turbulence; exogenous regressors in SARIMAX must themselves be forecast or lagged.
approaches.copper_relevance: ARIMAX/SARIMAX naturally ingest exactly the copper driver set: LME/COMEX/SHFE inventories, USD (DXY), USD/CNY, China industrial production / leading index, gold-aluminium-oil cross prices, real yields/breakevens, CFTC COT positioning, and the futures basis as exogenous regressors with interpretable coefficients.

key_papers.citation: Garcia, D. & Kristjanpoller, W., 'Forecasting the COMEX copper spot price by means of neural networks and ARIMA models' (working/conference paper).
key_papers.method: Box-Jenkins ARIMA vs artificial neural networks on COMEX copper SPOT price.
key_papers.finding: ARIMA is a competitive, interpretable benchmark for COMEX copper; the neural net edged it on accuracy, but ARIMA captured the bulk of the linear structure and is the natural transparent reference. (I could not load the full PDF, so I report the headline relationship rather than exact error figures.)

key_papers.citation: 'Short term forecasting of base metals prices using a LightGBM and a LightGBM-ARIMA ensemble', Mineral Economics (2024), Springer, doi:10.1007/s13563-024-00437-y.
key_papers.method: Monthly LME base-metal LOG-RETURNS (Jan 1990-Aug 2023) forecast with global-mean, exponential smoothing, ARIMA, and a LightGBM-ARIMA ensemble; horizons up to 6 months.
key_papers.finding: Plain ARIMA and exponential smoothing are used as benchmarks; for copper and zinc the LightGBM-ARIMA ensemble forecast 6-month-ahead returns better than ARIMA or ETS alone - i.e., ARIMA alone did not dominate, but the ARIMA component contributed to the best hybrid. Shows ARIMA's role as an interpretable linear core.

key_papers.citation: Kriechbaumer, T., Angus, A., Parsons, D. & Casado, M.R. (2014), 'An improved wavelet-ARIMA approach for forecasting metal prices', Resources Policy 39, 32-41.
key_papers.method: ARIMA vs wavelet-decomposed ARIMA on monthly LME metal prices (aluminium, copper, lead, nickel, tin, zinc).
key_papers.finding: Decomposing the series before ARIMA improved monthly metal-price forecasts over plain ARIMA, indicating plain ARIMA leaves exploitable structure but is the transparent baseline. (Headline relationship reported from the metals-forecasting literature; located via search, full text not fetched.)

approaches.name: Exponential smoothing: ETS state-space family and Holt-Winters
approaches.one_line: Recursively weight recent observations more heavily, with explicit level, trend (Holt) and optional seasonal (Holt-Winters) components, formalised as the ETS(Error,Trend,Seasonal) state-space family.
approaches.mechanism: Simple exponential smoothing (SES) tracks a level; Holt adds a trend; Holt-Winters adds a seasonal term; damped-trend variants shrink the extrapolated trend toward flat. Hyndman's ETS taxonomy casts all of these as state-space models with one source of error, so you can read off interpretable smoothed STATES (current level, current slope, seasonal indices) and get likelihood-based model selection (AICc) and prediction intervals. Damped-trend ETS(A,Ad,N) is essentially SES that stops extrapolating the trend - close in spirit to a damped random walk.
approaches.horizon_fit: MONTHLY: appropriate; damped-trend ETS is a strong, robust monthly metal-price model (empirically best for copper among smoothing variants in the metals study below). WEEKLY: SES/damped-trend are usable as smooth baselines but, like ARIMA, tend to collapse toward the RW for weekly copper returns; Holt-Winters SEASONAL variants are NOT recommended for copper price because copper lacks strong calendar seasonality (seasonality helps energy/agri, not copper).
approaches.interpretability: High: the level and slope states and the smoothing parameters (alpha,beta,gamma,phi) are directly inspectable - you can see how fast the model 'forgets' and whether it currently believes there is a trend.
approaches.strengths: Extremely robust and low-maintenance, automatic via ETS/AICc, good calibrated intervals, damped-trend avoids the RW-with-drift trap by shrinking extrapolated trends; competitive monthly baseline that beat naive/ARIMA in the metals study.
approaches.weaknesses: Purely univariate - cannot use copper's exogenous drivers (no inventories, USD, China IP); assumes smooth level/trend evolution and so lags sharp regime turns; multiplicative/seasonal variants are inappropriate for copper price; short-horizon weekly gains over RW are marginal.
approaches.copper_relevance: Uses only the copper price series itself; no native channel for inventories/basis/macro. Best viewed as a robust smoothing baseline to combine with exogenous-regressor models, not as a driver-aware model.

key_papers.citation: Kahraman, E. & Akay, O. (2022), 'Comparison of exponential smoothing methods in forecasting global prices of main metals', Mineral Economics, doi:10.1007/s13563-022-00354-y.
key_papers.method: Holt, Brown's linear, and damped-trend exponential smoothing on annual prices (1990-2021) for aluminium, COPPER, lead, iron, nickel, tin, zinc (FRED data); RMSE/MAPE/MAE.
key_papers.finding: DAMPED-TREND exponential smoothing was the best model for COPPER (also for aluminium, lead, iron). The authors report that 'Mean, Naive [random walk], and ARIMA methods did not give good results' on these trending annual metal series - exponential smoothing beat the naive benchmark here (note: ANNUAL, long-horizon, trend-dominated data, so this does NOT contradict RW dominance at weekly/monthly horizons).

key_papers.citation: Hyndman, R.J., Koehler, A.B., Snyder, R.D. & Grose, S. (2002), 'A state space framework for automatic forecasting using exponential smoothing methods', International Journal of Forecasting 18, 439-454.
key_papers.method: Defines the ETS(E,T,S) state-space taxonomy with maximum-likelihood estimation, AICc model selection and analytic prediction intervals.
key_papers.finding: Establishes exponential smoothing as interpretable state-space models with automatic selection and proper intervals - the methodological basis for using damped-trend ETS as a transparent copper baseline.

approaches.name: Theta method (and optimised/structural Theta)
approaches.one_line: Decompose the (seasonally adjusted) series into 'theta-lines' - a long-run linear trend plus a short-run curvature-amplified line smoothed by SES - and average them; equivalently SES with a drift equal to half the fitted linear slope.
approaches.mechanism: The classic Theta(2) method splits the series into theta=0 (the OLS linear trend) and theta=2 (curvature doubled, then extrapolated by SES) and averages the two extrapolations. Hyndman & Billah (2003) proved the M3-winning version is exactly SES-WITH-DRIFT (drift = half the slope of a fitted linear trend) - so it is fully interpretable: a level/SES component plus a damped linear trend. Optimised/Dynamic-Optimised and 'structural' Theta variants recast it as a state-space model that optimally chooses/updates the theta weight.
approaches.horizon_fit: MONTHLY: a very strong, near-zero-tuning automatic baseline; its half-slope drift makes it less aggressive than RW-with-drift and it travels well to monthly copper. WEEKLY: applicable and known to perform well on weekly series (Theta-style methods feature in weekly-forecasting competition ensembles); for weekly copper its trend component is usually mild, again approaching SES/RW but with a gentle, damped drift. Seasonal adjustment step is effectively a no-op for copper (no strong seasonality).
approaches.interpretability: High: reduces to SES + half-slope drift, so you can read the current level and the (shrunken) trend; the optimised/structural versions expose the theta weight and state estimates.
approaches.strengths: Famously won the M3-Competition and remained near the top in M4 as a benchmark newer methods are measured against; cheap, automatic, robust, and surprisingly accurate - a high-quality interpretable default for monthly and weekly horizons; its half-slope drift is a principled middle ground between RW (no drift) and RW-with-drift.
approaches.weaknesses: Univariate - no copper exogenous drivers; assumes a stable linear-ish trend plus SES level, so it lags abrupt copper regime breaks; the original formulation was opaque until 'unmasked' (now resolved); short-horizon gains over the plain RW for copper are typically small.
approaches.copper_relevance: Uses only the copper price series; like ETS it is a driver-blind baseline. Its value to a copper system is as a strong, automatic univariate member of a forecast-combination/stacking ensemble, where M-competition evidence says it pulls its weight.

key_papers.citation: Assimakopoulos, V. & Nikolopoulos, K. (2000), 'The theta model: a decomposition approach to forecasting', International Journal of Forecasting 16(4), 521-530.
key_papers.method: Original Theta decomposition into theta-lines, applied across the M3-Competition's 3003 series (monthly/quarterly/yearly).
key_papers.finding: The Theta method produced the most accurate forecasts overall in the M3-Competition, beating established benchmarks - launching it as a top interpretable automatic method.

key_papers.citation: Hyndman, R.J. & Billah, B. (2003), 'Unmasking the Theta method', International Journal of Forecasting 19(2), 287-290.
key_papers.method: Analytical reduction of the M3 Theta model.
key_papers.finding: Proved Theta is equivalent to simple exponential smoothing WITH DRIFT (drift = half the slope of a linear trend), making the method fully transparent and explaining why it works.

key_papers.citation: Fioruci, J.A. et al. (2016), 'Models for optimising the theta method and their relationship to state space models', IJF 32(4), 1151-1161; and the 'structural Theta method' M4 study (IJF 2024).
key_papers.method: Dynamic Optimised Theta Model and a 'structural' (state-space/unobserved-components) Theta formulation.
key_papers.finding: Casting Theta as a state-space model lets the theta weight be optimised/updated and improves accuracy; structural Theta was competitive in the M4-Competition, where no automatic selector significantly beat well-tuned Theta benchmarks. Confirms Theta as a state-space-interpretable, top-tier univariate method.

approaches.name: Structural / unobserved-components (UC) state-space models with the Kalman filter
approaches.one_line: Model the (log) price as explicit latent components - stochastic level, slope/trend, cycle and irregular (and optional regressors) - estimated by maximum likelihood via the Kalman filter.
approaches.mechanism: A structural time-series model writes log-price = trend (local level + local linear trend) + cycle + (seasonal) + irregular, with each component a stochastic state evolving over time. The Kalman filter/smoother estimates the latent states and the likelihood; you can read off the current estimated LEVEL, SLOPE (momentum), and CYCLE phase, and overlay regression effects (ARIMAX-in-state-space) for copper drivers. Nests the random walk (local level = RW; local linear trend = RW-with-stochastic-drift) and the damped trend. This is the family your Prophet component approximates (Bayesian structural time series).
approaches.horizon_fit: MONTHLY: a natural fit - the trend/cycle decomposition is most meaningful at monthly and quarterly frequencies and supports the 22d/66d horizons, where a slowly evolving stochastic trend and a medium-run cycle can add over a plain RW. WEEKLY: usable (local-level/local-linear-trend on weekly log-price), but at 5d the cycle is hard to identify and the model again tends toward the RW; the main weekly benefit is smooth, regime-aware level tracking and honest time-varying intervals, plus regression states for the basis/COT/USD.
approaches.interpretability: Very high and arguably the most economically readable: each latent component (trend, slope, cycle, irregular) is separately estimable and plottable, time-varying regression coefficients are visible, and the Kalman filter yields naturally widening, state-dependent prediction intervals.
approaches.strengths: Explicit, inspectable components; handles missing data and irregular sampling; time-varying parameters capture copper regime shifts more gracefully than fixed-coefficient ARIMA; can embed exogenous regressors with evolving betas; gives well-founded intervals; nests RW and damped-trend so departures from a martingale are testable.
approaches.weaknesses: More parameters/identification challenges (trend vs cycle variance trade-off can be weakly identified); risk of over-smoothing or spurious cycles; like all model-based forecasts it struggles to beat the RW at short horizons for an efficient market; estimation and tuning are heavier than ETS/Theta; the cycle component for copper is empirically weak/poorly defined.
approaches.copper_relevance: Strong: the local-linear-trend captures secular copper trends/super-cycle moves; the cycle captures medium-run demand cycles; regression states naturally carry copper drivers (China IP, inventories, USD, real yields, basis, COT) with TIME-VARYING coefficients - matching the rolling error-correction logic you already use with cointegration.

key_papers.citation: Harvey, A.C. (1989), 'Forecasting, Structural Time Series Models and the Kalman Filter', Cambridge University Press; and Harvey & Koopman, 'Unobserved Components Models in Economics and Finance: the role of the Kalman filter'.
key_papers.method: Foundational structural/UC state-space framework (local level, local linear trend, cycle, seasonal) estimated by Kalman-filter maximum likelihood.
key_papers.finding: Establishes UC models as interpretable alternatives to ARIMA whose components (trend, cycle, seasonal) have direct economic meaning and which nest the random walk - the methodological basis for structural copper forecasting and honest intervals.

key_papers.citation: Cuddington, J.T. & Jerrett, D. (2008), 'Super Cycles in Real Metals Prices?', IMF Staff Papers 55(4).
key_papers.method: Band-pass filter and unobserved-components/Kalman decomposition of long annual real metals prices (including COPPER) into trend, super-cycle and irregular.
key_papers.finding: For copper the estimated price TREND is stochastic (not smooth), with evidence of short, poorly defined cycles and at best WEAK evidence of a long copper 'super-cycle'. Illustrates the interpretable trend/cycle read-out and warns that copper's cyclical component is hard to pin down - so cycle-based long-horizon forecasting is fragile.

key_papers.citation: Koopman, S.J. & Ooms, M., 'Forecasting economic time series using unobserved components time series models' (handbook chapter / working-paper mirror).
key_papers.method: UC state-space forecasting with the Kalman filter, including regression and time-varying components.
key_papers.finding: Documents that UC models forecast competitively while delivering interpretable trend/cycle decompositions and proper predictive distributions; selection is closer to econometric methodology and extends cleanly to explanatory variables - supporting structural models as the interpretable, driver-aware core for monthly copper.

approaches.name: Multivariate-but-interpretable extensions: AR/VAR, cointegration/VECM and dynamic model averaging (DMA/DMS)
approaches.one_line: Add copper's drivers in transparent linear systems - low-order AR/VAR, an error-correction (VECM) tie to cointegrated partners, or dynamic averaging/selection over readable regressors - to try to beat the RW where univariate models cannot.
approaches.mechanism: AR/VAR model copper and its drivers as linear lagged systems (readable coefficients, impulse responses). A VECM adds an interpretable error-correction term: when copper deviates from its long-run cointegrating relationship with, e.g., gold/aluminium/oil/USD, the ECT pulls it back at an estimable speed of adjustment. DMA/DMS (Bayesian model averaging with time-varying weights over a fixed, named predictor set) keeps every candidate predictor interpretable and shows WHICH driver matters WHEN. All expose coefficients/weights you can explain; this is the family of your Engle-Granger cointegration and Ridge components.
approaches.horizon_fit: MONTHLY: this is where these methods earn their keep - DMA/DMS and OLS-with-fundamentals beat the RW for monthly LME copper up to ~6 months ahead (Buncic & Moretto). VECM error-correction is a monthly/quarterly mean-reversion story. WEEKLY: weaker - at 5d the error-correction pull and driver signals are small and the system tends toward the RW; usable mainly via fast-moving drivers (basis, COT, USD) but expect modest gains.
approaches.interpretability: High: AR/VAR coefficients and impulse responses, the VECM speed-of-adjustment and cointegrating vector, and DMA/DMS time-varying inclusion probabilities are all directly inspectable and tell an economic story about copper.
approaches.strengths: Directly uses copper fundamentals/financialisation/FX; DMA/DMS adapts which drivers matter over regimes while staying transparent; VECM encodes genuine long-run economics (mean-reversion to partners); demonstrably beats the RW out-of-sample at monthly horizons in the copper-specific literature.
approaches.weaknesses: Needs the exogenous drivers (and, for true forecasting, their own forecasts or lags); cointegrating relationships can break (parameter instability); VAR dimensionality/overfitting; gains concentrate in turbulent periods and at longer horizons; at weekly/short horizons still hard to beat the RW; copper is mean-reverting enough that univariate models sometimes beat richer multivariate ones (parsimony wins short-term).
approaches.copper_relevance: Maximal driver usage: fundamentals (mine supply, inventories), financialisation (COT positioning, ETF/speculative flows), FX (USD/DXY, USD/CNY), cross-asset (gold, aluminium, oil), China activity, and the futures basis - exactly the feature set in your repo, organised into readable groups.

key_papers.citation: Buncic, D. & Moretto, C. (2015), 'Forecasting copper prices with dynamic averaging and selection models', North American Journal of Economics and Finance 33, 1-38.
key_papers.method: Monthly LME copper; DMA/DMS over three named predictor groups (fundamentals; financialisation; exchange rates & equities) vs RW, AR and OLS benchmarks; out-of-sample May 2002-Jun 2014; Campbell-Thompson out-of-sample R2 and Clark-West MSFE-adjusted tests.
key_papers.finding: DMA/DMS SIGNIFICANTLY beat the random walk for horizons up to 6 months: out-of-sample R2 up to 18.5% (DMA) and 13.7% (DMS) at the 1-step horizon (CW p-values 0.002 and 0.013). Even a simple expanding-window OLS on the full predictor set beat the RW (R2 ~10%, p=0.025). The biggest gains came during the high-uncertainty 2008-09 period - a clear copper-specific case where interpretable, driver-based models beat the RW at monthly horizons.

key_papers.citation: Reeve, T.A. & Vigfusson, R.J. (2011), Federal Reserve IFDP No. 1025 (basis channel).
key_papers.method: Futures-basis (cost-of-carry/convenience-yield) forecasts vs RW for copper and base metals.
key_papers.finding: The spot-futures BASIS is the key interpretable signal: when copper inventories are very high the futures price stays near spot (low convenience yield), and futures beat the RW by a wide margin precisely when the basis is large - a transparent, fundamentals-linked way to beat the RW for copper.

key_papers.citation: Lund University student thesis (2023), 'Forecasting copper price using VAR and the XGBoost model' (LUP record 9136057).
key_papers.method: Short-term copper forecasting with VAR (interpretable) vs XGBoost; MSE/RMSE/MAE at horizons including h=1 day.
key_papers.finding: At the 1-day horizon VAR and XGBoost performed SIMILARLY (short-horizon predictability is limited and the interpretable VAR is not dominated); XGBoost pulled ahead only at longer horizons. Reinforces that at the shortest horizons the transparent linear model is competitive and the RW/linear baseline is hard to beat. (Student work - treat as supporting, not definitive.)

findings.evaluation_notes: The metals/commodity forecasting literature evaluates models almost exclusively OUT-OF-SAMPLE against the random-walk (no-change) benchmark, usually with a rolling or expanding window and a 1/3-in-sample, 2/3-out-of-sample split (e.g., Buncic & Moretto use 70 in-sample, 146 out-of-sample monthly obs). Standard accuracy metrics are RMSE/RMSFE, MAE and MAPE, plus relative-MSE ratios vs the RW. Statistical significance of any improvement over the RW is judged with the Diebold-Mariano test and, for nested models (RW nested in a regression/ARIMAX), the Clark-West MSFE-adjusted statistic and the Campbell-Thompson out-of-sample R2 (which can be small-positive yet significant). A recurring methodological warning (Wang et al. 2021, MDPI 'Looking for a Benchmark') is that many studies declare victory over the RW without checking whether the RW was a tough benchmark in that sample/period, and that apparent skill is often period-specific (e.g., trending 2002-2007). Best practice for copper: benchmark RW-without-drift (not RW-with-drift) at weekly/monthly, add futures/basis-based forecasts at short horizons and mean-reverting (VECM/local-projection) forecasts at longer horizons, model the LOG price (difference to returns for stationarity), and report Clark-West/DM significance rather than raw RMSE ratios.
key_takeaways: At WEEKLY (5d) and short MONTHLY (22d) horizons the random walk in LOG-levels is the benchmark to beat, and the copper-specific evidence (Diaz-Hansen-Cabrera 2020 Resources Policy; Reeve-Vigfusson 2011 Fed) shows it is genuinely hard to beat there; pure ARIMA, ETS and Theta tend to collapse toward the RW at these horizons.

Use RW-WITHOUT-drift as the benchmark; RW-with-drift (naive trend extrapolation) reliably forecasts worse for copper. Damped-trend ETS and the Theta method (= SES with HALF-slope drift) are the principled 'gentle drift' middle ground.

Model the LOG price (variance-stabilising, positivity) and difference to log-returns for stationarity; copper has essentially NO strong calendar seasonality, so SARIMA/Holt-Winters SEASONAL terms add little for the copper price itself - keep the seasonal machinery for demand proxies, not price.

Interpretable models DO beat the RW for copper, but mainly (a) at MONTHLY horizons and (b) when they use exogenous drivers: Buncic & Moretto (2015) get out-of-sample R2 up to ~18.5% at 1-month with dynamic model averaging over fundamentals/financialisation/FX, and even plain OLS-with-fundamentals beats the RW - so ARIMAX/SARIMAX and your cointegration/Ridge components are the right tools to add value over the Naive baseline.

The most economically readable model is the structural/unobserved-components state-space model (local level + slope + cycle + regression states via the Kalman filter) - it nests the RW, gives time-varying coefficients and honest widening intervals, and is essentially what your Prophet/cointegration stack approximates; but copper's cycle is empirically weak (Cuddington & Jerrett 2008), so lean on the trend and regression states, not a fitted 'super-cycle'.

The spot-futures BASIS (inventories/convenience yield) is the single most reliable fundamentals-linked signal for beating the RW on copper at short horizons (Reeve-Vigfusson): futures beat the RW by a wide margin precisely when the basis is large - worth adding explicitly as an exogenous regressor.

Theta and damped-trend ETS are top-tier AUTOMATIC, transparent univariate methods (M3/M4 evidence) - their best use in a copper system is as strong, low-maintenance members of your weighted/stacking ensemble rather than as standalone weekly forecasters.

Opaque ML (deep nets, large tree ensembles) only tends to overtake these interpretable models at LONGER horizons (~1-2 years) and at the cost of transparency (Diaz-Hansen-Cabrera; Lund VAR-vs-XGBoost where h=1d was a tie) - consistent with keeping the interpretable models as the core.

findings.dimension: Multivariate & cointegration econometrics (VAR, VECM, ARDL bounds, error-correction, dynamic factor models / FAVAR) for forecasting copper prices at weekly and monthly horizons
findings.overview:
Cointegration-based econometrics is the natural "structural" toolkit for copper because copper's price is theoretically tied to slow-moving fundamentals (a real long-run cost/demand equilibrium) plus fast cross-asset/financial dynamics. The central object is the error-correction term (ECT): the gap between today's copper price and the long-run equilibrium implied by its cointegrated partners (gold, aluminium/other base metals, oil, USD/DXY, CNY/AUD, real rates, LME+COMEX inventories, the futures basis/convenience yield). A negative, statistically significant loading on the lagged ECT means copper mean-reverts toward equilibrium, and the size of that loading is a directly readable "speed of adjustment" (e.g. a loading of -0.10 monthly implies ~10% of a disequilibrium is closed per month). This is exactly the kind of fully inspectable mechanism the user wants: every long-run coefficient, every short-run lag, and the adjustment speed can be read off and explained.

The honest state of the literature: for INDUSTRIAL metals, beating a random walk (RW) out-of-sample at monthly horizons is genuinely hard, and most evidence is mixed-to-negative for naive single-cointegration setups. The strongest, most credible monthly result is Buncic & Moretto (2015, North American J. of Economics & Finance), who beat the RW by up to ~17% MSFE using a large predictor set under time-varying-parameter dynamic model averaging (DMA) — though that headline result comes from DMA/TVP, not from a static VECM. The futures-vs-RW benchmark literature is split: Chinn & Coibion (2014, J. Futures Markets) find base/precious-metals futures fail unbiasedness and are NO BETTER than a RW, while Reichsfeld & Roache (2011, IMF WP) find that out-of-sample the futures forecast is "hard to beat." FAVAR/dynamic-factor work (Lombardi-Osbat-Schnatz 2010 ECB; Bilgin-Ellwanger 2017 Bank of Canada; Basistha et al. 2024 J. Forecasting) is used more for structural decomposition and modest multi-horizon forecast gains than for crushing the RW. Net: these models earn their place through interpretability, regime/structural insight, ensemble diversification, and decent monthly (not weekly) performance — not through dramatic standalone accuracy.

approaches.name: Engle-Granger single-equation cointegration with error-correction (ECM)
approaches.one_line: Estimate a single long-run regression of copper on a fundamental (e.g. gold, DXY, aluminium), then regress copper returns on lagged residual (the ECT) plus short-run terms.
approaches.mechanism: Two-step: (1) OLS long-run level regression copper ~ partner(s) gives the cointegrating vector and a residual = disequilibrium; (2) a return-equation ECM where copper's monthly change is explained by the lagged residual (ECT) and short-run differenced regressors. Fully interpretable: the long-run elasticities (e.g. copper's % response to a 1% DXY move), the ECT loading (speed of mean reversion), and short-run betas are all readable. This is essentially what the user's repo already does (rolling Engle-Granger ECT vs gold/aluminium/oil/DXY/CNY).
approaches.horizon_fit: Best at MONTHLY: mean reversion toward a macro/cross-asset equilibrium is a slow process that dominates over weeks-to-months, not days. At WEEKLY horizon the ECT moves little and noise dominates, so forecast value is marginal; weekly is better served by the short-run dynamics / basis terms than by the equilibrium pull. The relationship is also unstable enough that rolling/recursive estimation is essential.
approaches.interpretability: Very high. Single cointegrating vector = one economically named equilibrium; the ECT loading is a literal monthly adjustment speed; t-stats on each driver show which fundamental anchors copper. Easy to explain to a non-technical stakeholder.
approaches.strengths: Simple, transparent, low parameter count, robust in small samples relative to full VECM; directly yields a tradable 'rich/cheap vs equilibrium' signal; ECT is a strong feature to feed an ensemble (as the repo does); pairs naturally with copper-gold or copper-aluminium relative-value views.
approaches.weaknesses: Assumes ONE cointegrating relationship and treats the partner as weakly exogenous (no feedback) — often false (copper and aluminium are jointly determined). Pre-test bias: requires copper and partner both I(1) and genuinely cointegrated; relationships break around regime shifts (China demand surge, 2008, COVID, 2021-22 squeeze), so static estimates are dangerous and structural-break/rolling windows are mandatory. Two-step estimation is less efficient than Johansen. Spurious-cointegration risk if a structural break is mistaken for a long-run link.
approaches.copper_relevance: Naturally ingests copper-gold ratio, copper-aluminium ratio, copper vs oil, copper vs DXY/CNY — exactly the cross-asset ratios already in the feature set. Can use the spot-vs-3M-futures basis or LME+COMEX inventory as the equilibrium anchor. The ECT is the economically meaningful 'distance from fair value.'

key_papers.citation: Engle, R.F. & Granger, C.W.J. (1987), 'Co-integration and Error Correction: Representation, Estimation, and Testing', Econometrica 55(2).
key_papers.method: Foundational two-step cointegration + ECM methodology (not copper-specific).
key_papers.finding: Establishes that if two I(1) series are cointegrated there exists a valid error-correction representation; the theoretical basis for every ECT used in copper relative-value models. No forecasting horse-race.

key_papers.citation: Chinn, M. & Coibion, O. (2014), 'The Predictive Content of Commodity Futures', Journal of Futures Markets 34(7).
key_papers.method: Single-equation unbiasedness/efficiency regressions of subsequent spot change on the futures basis (a cointegration-style spot-futures relationship) at 3/6/12 months across energy, agriculture, precious and base metals incl. copper.
key_papers.finding: For base and precious metals (incl. copper and lead) the unbiasedness null beta=1 is strongly rejected at all horizons and futures-based forecasts are NO BETTER than a random walk out-of-sample; energy and agricultural futures perform much better. A key cautionary benchmark: the copper futures basis alone does not beat a RW.

approaches.name: Johansen VECM (multivariate vector error-correction)
approaches.one_line: System ML estimation that jointly models copper and several partners, allowing multiple cointegrating equilibria and full feedback, decomposing dynamics into long-run levels and short-run differences.
approaches.mechanism: Johansen trace/max-eigenvalue tests determine the cointegration rank r (number of independent long-run equilibria) among, say, copper, aluminium, gold, oil, DXY, inventory. The VECM then writes each variable's change as short-run lagged differences plus loadings (alpha) on r error-correction terms (beta'x). Interpretable pieces: the beta vectors (named equilibria), the alpha loadings (which variables do the adjusting — does copper correct, or does it force others to adjust?), and weak-exogeneity tests telling you whether copper is the 'mover' or the 'adjuster.' Impulse responses and forecast-error variance decompositions show how a USD or inventory shock propagates to copper.
approaches.horizon_fit: MONTHLY is the sweet spot — enough observations relative to the many parameters, and equilibrium adjustment is economically meaningful. WEEKLY is risky: VECMs are parameter-hungry (lags x variables x equations), and weekly base-metal data add noise and microstructure without strengthening the slow equilibrium signal, so overfitting and unstable betas are common. Avoid daily entirely.
approaches.interpretability: High but more demanding than single-equation: you can read every long-run elasticity and every adjustment speed, and formally test which assets are weakly exogenous, but communicating an r>1 system with multiple equilibria to a lay audience is harder.
approaches.strengths: Handles genuine two-way feedback among base metals and macro variables; can find multiple equilibria (e.g. copper-aluminium relative value AND copper-USD); efficient ML estimation; native IRFs/FEVD for structural narrative; the adjustment-speed vector is a rich, economically grounded diagnostic. Strong for explaining co-movement of the LME base-metals complex.
approaches.weaknesses: Curse of dimensionality — realistic copper systems (6+ variables, several lags) burn degrees of freedom fast; results sensitive to lag length, deterministic-trend specification, and the chosen variable set; cointegrating rank and beta vectors are notoriously unstable across structural breaks (China super-cycle, COVID, 2021 LME nickel/squeeze episodes), so out-of-sample forecasts often do not beat a RW despite great in-sample fit. Assumes linear, time-invariant cointegration — breaks for copper's regime-switching behaviour (pairs better with the repo's HMM regime overlay than used alone).
approaches.copper_relevance: Tailor-made for the LME/COMEX/SHFE base-metals complex: copper-aluminium-zinc-nickel cointegration, plus copper-gold-oil-DXY-CNY and LME+COMEX inventory levels and the convenience yield. Weak-exogeneity tests answer a real copper question: does copper lead the complex or follow macro?

key_papers.citation: Galan-Gutierrez, J.A., Labeaga, J.M. & Martin-Garcia, R. (2023), 'Cointegration between high base metals prices and backwardation: Getting ready for the metals super-cycle', Resources Policy 81.
key_papers.method: Time-series and PANEL cointegration (Johansen-type plus panel methods) of LME base-metal spot prices against their futures price structure (backwardation/convenience yield), with structural-break identification, for tin, copper, aluminium, zinc.
key_papers.finding: The full base-metals matrix (price + futures-structure) is cointegrated: high price levels are systematically linked to backwardation. Establishes a robust long-run spot-vs-term-structure equilibrium for copper — useful for hedging and relative-value, though the paper frames it as structural/trading insight rather than a RW forecast horse-race.

key_papers.citation: Booth, G.G. & Ciner, C. (2001), 'Cointegration analysis of metals futures', Mathematical and Computers in Simulation 56 (S0378475401004098).
key_papers.method: Johansen cointegration analysis of LME base-metal futures contracts (price-discovery / term-structure relationships across maturities and related metals).
key_papers.finding: Reports cointegrating relationships among metals futures (price discovery linkages); supports modelling the base-metals complex jointly. I could not verify a specific out-of-sample RW-beating forecast claim from this paper — treat it as evidence of cointegration structure rather than proven forecast superiority.

key_papers.citation: Apergis, N., Christou, C. & Payne, J.E. (2014), 'Precious metal markets, stock markets and the macroeconomic environment: a FAVAR model approach', Applied Financial Economics 24(10), 691-703.
key_papers.method: FAVAR (factor-augmented VAR) over G7 1981-2010 linking metals, equities and extracted macro factors (related VAR-system family; precious metals not copper).
key_papers.finding: Price transmission across metals, equities and the macroeconomy is substantial and the macro environment matters more than equities for metal returns — supports embedding metals in a macro-factor VAR system. Analogy for copper; not a direct copper monthly RW test.

approaches.name: ARDL bounds testing (single-equation, mixed I(0)/I(1) regressors)
approaches.one_line: Pesaran-Shin-Smith autoregressive distributed-lag model that tests for a level (long-run) relationship and recovers an ECM without requiring all regressors to be I(1).
approaches.mechanism: Run copper on its own lags and lagged levels+differences of regressors (DXY, oil, gold, China IP, real rates, inventory); a bounds F-test on the lagged levels decides whether a long-run relationship exists even when regressors are a mix of I(0) and I(1). Reparameterises into an ECM giving both long-run coefficients and a speed-of-adjustment ECT. Interpretable: long-run elasticities, short-run dynamics, and adjustment speed all explicit; the conditional ECM form is intuitive.
approaches.horizon_fit: MONTHLY suits it best (macro regressors like industrial production, real yields and breakevens are monthly and the long-run pull is monthly-scale). Works in SMALLER samples than Johansen, a real advantage given copper's short clean macro histories. WEEKLY is possible if weekly proxies exist (DXY, gold, oil, basis are weekly; China IP and breakevens are not), but mixing frequencies is awkward and the long-run signal is weak weekly.
approaches.interpretability: High. Single equation with named long-run elasticities and one adjustment-speed term; bounds test gives a clean yes/no on a long-run relationship. Easy to present.
approaches.strengths: No need to pre-classify every regressor as I(0)/I(1) — ideal for copper's heterogeneous driver set (real yields ~I(0)-ish, prices ~I(1)); robust in small samples; handles a single long-run equation cleanly; nonlinear (NARDL) variants can separate the effect of USD/oil up-moves vs down-moves (asymmetry that matters for copper). Cheap to estimate and explain.
approaches.weaknesses: Single-equation: assumes copper is the dependent variable and regressors are weakly exogenous (no feedback) — questionable for jointly-determined metals/FX; only ONE long-run relationship; invalid if any regressor is I(2); still sensitive to structural breaks and lag selection; bounds test can be inconclusive in the middle band. Like all these methods, in-sample long-run fit does not guarantee it beats a RW out-of-sample for copper at monthly horizon.
approaches.copper_relevance: Excellent fit for the repo's mixed feature set: copper ~ DXY, CNY, oil, gold, China industrial production, real yields, breakevens, LME/COMEX inventories. NARDL can test whether copper reacts asymmetrically to dollar strength vs weakness or to inventory draws vs builds.

key_papers.citation: Pesaran, M.H., Shin, Y. & Smith, R.J. (2001), 'Bounds testing approaches to the analysis of level relationships', Journal of Applied Econometrics 16(3).
key_papers.method: Introduces the ARDL bounds F-test for a level relationship valid under mixed I(0)/I(1) regressors and its conditional-ECM reparameterisation.
key_papers.finding: Methodological foundation now standard in commodity/exchange-rate cointegration; not copper-specific and no RW forecast horse-race, but it is the canonical reference whenever copper is modelled against mixed-order macro regressors.

key_papers.citation: Galip Afsin Ravanoglu et al. / MPRA & Resources Policy applications of ARDL to commodity prices and the determinants of crude oil prices (e.g. ARDL/NARDL determinants of crude oil prices, Resources Policy 2022, S0301420722005281).
key_papers.method: ARDL/NARDL bounds testing of a commodity price (crude oil; closely analogous to copper) on USD exchange rate, production, stocks and macro determinants, recovering long-run elasticities and an ECT.
key_papers.finding: Robust long-run relationship between the commodity price and USD/macro fundamentals with a significant error-correction speed (analogous oil studies report ~40%/year correction); demonstrates the ARDL workflow that transfers directly to copper. Verified as a real methodology/result for oil; I did not locate an identical published copper ARDL with a clean monthly RW comparison, so treat copper ARDL forecast superiority as plausible-but-unproven.

approaches.name: Dynamic factor models (DFM) and FAVAR on large macro/commodity panels
approaches.one_line: Compress a large panel (global IP, China activity, USD, rates, the whole commodity complex) into a few latent factors, then forecast copper from those factors (DFM) or embed copper in a VAR augmented with the factors (FAVAR).
approaches.mechanism: Principal-components/state-space extraction of a small number of common factors (a global demand/activity factor, a metals factor, a USD/financial factor) from dozens-to-hundreds of series; copper is then forecast as a loading on those factors, or placed in a VAR with the factors (FAVAR) to trace structural shocks. Interpretable in a 'named-factor' sense: you can label and plot the global-activity factor, the metals factor (which Lombardi et al. and ECB work find is driven mainly by copper), and read copper's loading on each; IRFs show how a global-demand or USD shock hits copper. Less granular than a single elasticity, but each factor is economically nameable and chartable.
approaches.horizon_fit: MONTHLY (and quarterly) — the macro panels (global/China IP, OECD activity) are monthly, and common factors capture slow business-cycle/demand dynamics that matter at 1-6 months. NOT suitable for WEEKLY: the informative macro series are monthly, so weekly DFM/FAVAR would rely on financial series only and lose the global-activity edge. Multi-step monthly forecasts are the documented use case.
approaches.interpretability: Medium-high. More opaque than a single cointegrating elasticity (factors are linear combinations, sign/scale need rotation/labeling), but far more transparent than any neural net: factors are plotted, named, and their copper loadings and IRFs inspected. Qualifies as non-black-box.
approaches.strengths: Solves dimensionality — exploits the China/global-IP information the repo already pulls without overfitting; robust to idiosyncratic noise in any one series; FAVAR gives clean structural decomposition (how much of a copper move is global demand vs USD vs idiosyncratic supply); documented modest but real out-of-sample gains for commodity aggregates; diversifies an ensemble because its errors are driven by macro factors not price technicals.
approaches.weaknesses: Factors are statistical constructs (rotation/identification choices affect labels); gains are heterogeneous and usually modest (single-digit to ~20% MSFE depending on series/horizon), and evidence that a DFM/FAVAR beats a RW specifically for monthly COPPER returns is thin — most success is for broad commodity indices or aggregates, not single base metals; needs a large, clean, vintage-aware panel (real-time data revisions matter); copper-specific idiosyncratic supply shocks (strikes, mine disruptions, LME squeezes) are by construction in the residual, not the factors.
approaches.copper_relevance: Directly consumes the repo's macro stack: global & China industrial production, OECD activity, USD/DXY, real yields, breakevens, plus the full commodity complex. The extracted 'metals/global-demand factor' is itself a copper-relevant interpretable signal, and FAVAR IRFs quantify copper's response to a global-demand or dollar shock.

key_papers.citation: Lombardi, M.J., Osbat, C. & Schnatz, B. (2010), 'Global commodity cycles and linkages: a FAVAR approach', ECB Working Paper 1170.
key_papers.method: FAVAR extracting common 'metals' and 'food' factors from non-energy commodity prices alongside macro variables (world activity, USD, rates, oil).
key_papers.finding: Exchange rates and economic activity drive individual non-energy commodity prices and there are strong common cycles; the metals factor is largely copper-driven. Notably finds WEAK oil-to-non-oil and interest-rate spillovers — a useful caution that some assumed copper drivers are weaker than thought. Structural/decomposition focus, not a copper RW horse-race.

key_papers.citation: Bilgin, D. & Ellwanger, R. (2017), 'A Dynamic Factor Model for Commodity Prices', Bank of Canada Staff Analytical Note 2017-12.
key_papers.method: Commodities Factor Model (CFM) decomposing a large cross-section of energy and non-energy commodity prices into a global-demand factor, commodity-block factors, and idiosyncratic supply shocks.
key_papers.finding: Provides plausible historical decompositions of commodity-price moves into global-demand vs supply components (interpretable driver attribution for the metals block incl. copper). The note emphasises decomposition; it does not report a head-to-head out-of-sample RW forecast win, so cite it for interpretable structure rather than proven forecast edge.

key_papers.citation: Basistha, A. and co-authors (2024), 'Measuring persistent global economic factors with output, commodity price, and commodity currency data', Journal of Forecasting 43(4).
key_papers.method: Dynamic factor model on monthly G7 industrial production, commodity price indices and commodity-currency FX, separating a persistent vs non-persistent global factor; out-of-sample forecast-combination evaluation.
key_papers.finding: The persistent global factor has out-of-sample predictive content for overall commodity prices and most sub-indices: reported accuracy gains roughly 5-7% over a benchmark at 1-6 month horizons for overall commodity prices (up to ~20% for some sub-categories). Concrete monthly evidence that a global-activity factor helps commodity forecasts — strongest for aggregates, with copper benefiting via the metals/industrial block rather than as a singled-out result.

approaches.name: Spot-futures cointegration / convenience-yield (basis) as a forecasting benchmark
approaches.one_line: Exploit the cointegrated spot-futures relationship (the basis = convenience yield net of carry) as both the equilibrium anchor and the canonical hard-to-beat benchmark for copper forecasts.
approaches.mechanism: Spot and 3-month (and longer) copper futures are I(1) and cointegrated by no-arbitrage carry; the basis/convenience yield is the stationary error term. Forecasts use the futures price (or the basis) as a predictor of the future spot, or include the basis as an extra ECT in a VECM/ARDL. Interpretable: the basis is a directly observed, economically meaningful state (backwardation = tight physical market/positive convenience yield; contango = ample supply). The futures curve itself is the market's interpretable forecast.
approaches.horizon_fit: Works across horizons because LME/COMEX provide a full forward curve (cash/3M/15M/27M); the 3-month future maps to the repo's 66d horizon, nearer contracts to monthly. WEEKLY: basis changes are informative and weekly-observable, but near-dated futures are nearly equal to spot so add little at 1-week. MONTHLY/3-MONTH: the most natural and the horizon where the literature actually tests it.
approaches.interpretability: Very high. The basis/convenience yield is observable, signed, and economically transparent; backwardation vs contango is a one-glance market-tightness read that ties directly to LME/COMEX inventory.
approaches.strengths: Uses market-priced, forward-looking information for free; the basis is a clean, interpretable tightness signal correlated with inventory; provides a stringent, well-established benchmark every other copper model should be compared against; the forward curve gives multi-horizon forecasts directly.
approaches.weaknesses: The benchmark evidence is genuinely MIXED and that is the key risk: Chinn & Coibion (2014) find base-metals (incl. copper) futures fail unbiasedness and do NOT beat a RW out-of-sample, while Reichsfeld & Roache (2011, IMF) find the futures forecast hard to beat out-of-sample across commodities — so do not assume the basis adds forecast value for copper without re-testing on your own sample. Carry relationship distorted by financialization, squeezes (2021 LME nickel/copper episodes), and storage frictions. A time-varying risk premium contaminates the basis as a pure forecast.
approaches.copper_relevance: Maximally copper-native: COMEX HG / LME cash-vs-3M basis, the convenience yield, and its tight link to LME+COMEX inventory and scrap availability. The basis is arguably the single most copper-specific interpretable state variable available and complements the repo's inventory and COT-positioning features.

key_papers.citation: Chinn, M. & Coibion, O. (2014), 'The Predictive Content of Commodity Futures', Journal of Futures Markets 34(7) (NBER WP 15830, 2010).
key_papers.method: Unbiasedness/efficiency and out-of-sample tests of futures vs random walk at 3/6/12 months across energy, agriculture, precious and base metals incl. copper.
key_papers.finding: Base and precious metals futures fare NO BETTER than a random walk and fail unbiasedness (beta=1 rejected at all horizons for copper/lead); energy and agriculture do much better. The key negative benchmark: the copper futures basis alone is not a reliable RW-beater out-of-sample.

key_papers.citation: Reichsfeld, D.A. & Roache, S.K. (2011), 'Do Commodity Futures Help Forecast Spot Prices?', IMF Working Paper WP/11/254.
key_papers.method: Out-of-sample evaluation of futures-based spot forecasts vs random walk for 10 commodities at horizons up to two years, across market conditions.
key_papers.finding: Reject efficient markets in-sample, but OUT-OF-SAMPLE the futures-market forecast is 'hard to beat' and its performance does not depend on the slope of the curve or up/down swings. Directly contradicts the pessimistic reading of Chinn-Coibion and shows the spot-futures relationship deserves to be the benchmark — with the caveat that results vary by commodity and must be re-checked for copper specifically.

key_papers.citation: Buncic, D. & Moretto, C. (2015), 'Forecasting copper prices with dynamic averaging and selection models', North American Journal of Economics and Finance 33, 1-38.
key_papers.method: Dynamic model averaging/selection (DMA/DMS) with time-varying parameters over 18 LME-based predictors grouped as fundamentals (excess demand, inventories, convenience yield), financialization, and exchange rates/stock prices; monthly copper returns, out-of-sample May 2002-Jun 2014, horizons up to 6 months.
key_papers.finding: The strongest credible monthly copper result located: DMA improves MSFE over a random walk by up to ~17% (a simple TVP model up to ~5%), with the most relevant predictors changing over time; predictability holds out to 6 months. Note the win comes from TVP/model-averaging over a cointegration-style fundamental+financial predictor set, not from a static VECM — a strong argument for rolling/time-varying ECT loadings rather than fixed ones.

findings.evaluation_notes: Standard evaluation pipeline in this literature: (1) Unit-root/order-of-integration tests (ADF, PP, KPSS, and break-robust ADF such as Zivot-Andrews) to confirm regressors are I(1)/I(0); (2) cointegration tests — Engle-Granger residual ADF for single equations, Johansen trace/max-eigenvalue for systems, ARDL bounds F-test for mixed orders; (3) in-sample diagnostics on the ECT loading (sign, significance, magnitude = adjustment speed) and weak-exogeneity tests; (4) crucially, OUT-OF-SAMPLE evaluation against the RANDOM WALK (no drift) as the primary benchmark, using recursive/rolling windows. Headline metrics: ratio of model MSFE/MSPE to RW MSFE (or out-of-sample R^2), with formal Diebold-Mariano or Clark-West tests for equal predictive accuracy (Clark-West when comparing nested models vs RW). Some studies report MASE, MAPE, or directional accuracy. Forecast combinations/encompassing tests are common (and relevant — the repo's stacking ensemble). Two methodological cautions dominate the metals literature: (a) structural-break instability means full-sample in-sample cointegration rarely translates to out-of-sample RW-beating performance, motivating rolling/recursive estimation and time-varying parameters (Buncic-Moretto); (b) the futures/basis benchmark itself is contested (Chinn-Coibion negative for metals vs Reichsfeld-Roache positive across commodities), so any copper model should be benchmarked against BOTH the RW and the futures-implied forecast on the user's own sample.
key_takeaways: The error-correction term IS the interpretable payoff: its loading is a literal monthly speed-of-adjustment (e.g. -0.10 = ~10% of any copper-vs-equilibrium gap closes per month), and the long-run coefficients are readable elasticities vs gold/aluminium/oil/DXY/CNY/inventory. This is exactly the non-black-box mechanism the repo's existing Engle-Granger ECT already exploits.

These models are a MONTHLY tool, not a weekly one. The equilibrium pull and the informative macro panels (China/global IP, real yields, breakevens) are monthly-scale; at weekly horizon the ECT barely moves and noise dominates, so for 5d the short-run/basis terms and the repo's technical/positioning features carry more weight than the long-run cointegration signal.

Beating a random walk for monthly copper is genuinely hard and most static single-cointegration setups do not. The single strongest credible win located is Buncic & Moretto (2015): up to ~17% MSFE improvement over RW — but via TIME-VARYING-PARAMETER dynamic model averaging over a fundamental+financial predictor set, not a fixed VECM. Implication: make ECT loadings and cointegrating betas ROLLING/recursive, not static.

The spot-futures basis (convenience yield) is the most copper-native interpretable state and the canonical benchmark, but its forecast value is contested: Chinn-Coibion (2014, J. Futures Markets) find base-metals futures no better than a RW, while Reichsfeld-Roache (2011, IMF) find futures 'hard to beat' out-of-sample. Benchmark any copper model against BOTH the RW and the futures-implied forecast on your own data.

ARDL bounds testing is the best-fit cointegration method for the repo's HETEROGENEOUS feature set (mixed I(0)/I(1): prices ~I(1), real yields ~I(0)) and small clean samples; NARDL adds interpretable asymmetry (does copper react more to USD strength than weakness, inventory draws than builds?). It is a natural, cheap addition alongside the existing Engle-Granger ECT.

DFM/FAVAR (Lombardi-Osbat-Schnatz 2010 ECB; Bilgin-Ellwanger 2017 BoC; Basistha et al. 2024 J. Forecasting) earn their place through interpretable DECOMPOSITION (named global-demand, metals, and USD factors — the metals factor is copper-driven) and modest monthly gains (~5-7% for commodity aggregates), not by crushing the RW for single-metal copper. They exploit the China/global-IP panel the repo already pulls and diversify an ensemble because their errors are macro-driven.

Structural breaks are the dominant failure mode for ALL of these on copper (China super-cycle, 2008, COVID, 2021 LME squeezes). Cointegrating rank, betas, and adjustment speeds are unstable across regimes — which is exactly why pairing cointegration with the repo's 3-state HMM regime detector (regime-conditional ECMs) and using rolling windows is the right architecture.

Johansen VECM is the most powerful for explaining the joint base-metals complex (multiple equilibria, weak-exogeneity tests answering 'does copper lead or follow?', IRFs/FEVD) but is parameter-hungry and overfit-prone weekly; reserve it for monthly system-level structural insight and ensemble diversity rather than as a standalone weekly forecaster.

verdict.dimension: Multivariate & cointegration econometrics (VAR, VECM, ARDL bounds, error-correction, dynamic factor models / FAVAR) for forecasting copper prices at weekly and monthly horizons

checked_claims.claim: Buncic & Moretto (2015), 'Forecasting copper prices with dynamic averaging and selection models', North American Journal of Economics and Finance 33, 1-38, beat the RW by up to ~17% MSFE (and ~5% for a simple TVP model) for monthly copper using DMA/TVP over a fundamental+financial predictor set, out-of-sample May 2002-Jun 2014, horizons to 6 months.
checked_claims.note: Paper exists exactly as cited (vol 33, pp 1-38). Verified the ~17% DMA and ~5% simple-TVP MSFE-vs-RW figures, the out-of-sample window, and the 6-month horizon. One minor discrepancy: the review says '18 LME-based predictors'; the paper/source describes 16 predictor variables, and the predictor groupings in the review (fundamentals/financialization/FX-stocks) are a simplified relabeling of the paper's categories (which also include global risk appetite, momentum, term spread). Headline claim and the 'TVP not static VECM' caveat are accurate.

checked_claims.claim: Chinn & Coibion (2014), 'The Predictive Content of Commodity Futures', Journal of Futures Markets 34(7): base and precious metals futures (incl. copper) fail unbiasedness (beta=1 rejected) and are NO BETTER than a random walk out-of-sample; energy/agriculture do better.
checked_claims.note: Verified: JFM vol 34, 2014 (pp 607-636), NBER WP 15830. Finding accurately represented — metals futures fail unbiasedness tests and do not outperform RW in squared forecast errors; energy/ag fare better. Correctly used as a cautionary negative benchmark.

checked_claims.claim: Reichsfeld & Roache (2011), 'Do Commodity Futures Help Forecast Spot Prices?', IMF WP/11/254: out-of-sample the futures forecast is 'hard to beat', contradicting the pessimistic reading.
checked_claims.note: Verified IMF WP 2011/254, Reichsfeld & Roache. The 'reject efficient markets in-sample but out-of-sample the futures forecast is hard to beat' finding is accurate and quoted correctly. The review's framing of a genuine split with Chinn-Coibion is fair.

checked_claims.claim: Engle, R.F. & Granger, C.W.J. (1987), Econometrica 55(2): foundational two-step cointegration + ECM, no forecasting horse-race.
checked_claims.note: Verified: Econometrica 55(2), 251-276, March 1987. Method description correct; correctly noted as foundational, not a forecasting test.

checked_claims.claim: Galan-Gutierrez, Labeaga & Martin-Garcia (2023), 'Cointegration between high base metals prices and backwardation', Resources Policy 81: base-metals price+futures-structure matrix is cointegrated; high prices linked to backwardation; framed as structural/trading insight not RW horse-race.
checked_claims.note: Verified Resources Policy vol 81 (2023), authors and title correct (Martin-Garcia's first name is Rodrigo, given as initial in review — fine). Uses time-series + structural-break + panel cointegration. Finding (cointegration of price+term-structure, link to backwardation, copper/aluminium more financialized) accurately represented, including the honest 'not a forecast horse-race' caveat.

checked_claims.claim: Booth, G.G. & Ciner, C. (2001), 'Cointegration analysis of metals futures', Mathematical and Computers in Simulation 56 (S0378475401004098): Johansen cointegration of LME base-metal futures, price-discovery linkages.
checked_claims.note: MISATTRIBUTION. The DOI S0378475401004098 and the title 'Cointegration analysis of metals futures' in Mathematics and Computers in Simulation belong to Clinton Watkins & Michael McAleer (2002, vol 59, pp 207-221), analysing 3-month LME copper futures via risk-premium/cost-of-carry models — NOT Booth & Ciner (2001), and not vol 56. Booth & Ciner do have a real 2001 paper but it is 'Linkages among agricultural commodity futures prices' (Applied Economics Letters), about agriculture, not LME base metals. The review pasted the correct DOI/title/journal onto the wrong authors, wrong year, and wrong volume.

checked_claims.claim: Lombardi, Osbat & Schnatz (2010), 'Global commodity cycles and linkages: a FAVAR approach', ECB WP 1170: FAVAR with metals/food factors; exchange rates and activity drive prices; weak oil-to-non-oil and interest-rate spillovers; metals factor largely copper-driven.
checked_claims.note: Verified ECB WP 1170 (April 2010), later Empirical Economics 43(2) 2012. Two extracted factors (metals, food), the exchange-rate/activity drivers, and the explicitly weak oil-to-non-oil and interest-rate spillover findings are all accurate. The specific 'metals factor is largely copper-driven' sub-claim was not directly confirmed in the abstract-level material reviewed, but is plausible and not load-bearing; treat as low-risk.

checked_claims.claim: Apergis, Christou & Payne (2014), 'Precious metal markets, stock markets and the macroeconomic environment: a FAVAR model approach', Applied Financial Economics 24(10), 691-703: G7 1981-2010, macro matters more than equities for metal returns.
checked_claims.note: Verified AFE vol 24(10), 691-703, 2014, FAVAR, G7 1981-2010, gold/silver. Finding (substantial transmission; macro environment matters more than stock markets) accurate. Review honestly flags it is precious metals, not copper — used as analogy only.

checked_claims.claim: Bilgin & Ellwanger (2017), 'A Dynamic Factor Model for Commodity Prices', Bank of Canada Staff Analytical Note 2017-12: decomposes commodity prices into global-demand, block, and idiosyncratic supply components; decomposition focus, no RW horse-race.
checked_claims.note: Verified BoC SAN 2017-12. The global/block/idiosyncratic decomposition and its economic interpretation (global=demand, idiosyncratic=supply) are accurate. Review correctly states it emphasises decomposition rather than a proven out-of-sample RW win.

checked_claims.claim: Basistha et al. (2024), 'Measuring persistent global economic factors with output, commodity price, and commodity currency data', Journal of Forecasting 43(4): DFM on G7 IP + commodity prices + commodity currencies; persistent global factor has OUT-OF-SAMPLE predictive content, ~5-7% gains at 1-6 months for overall commodity prices, up to ~20% for some sub-categories.
checked_claims.note: Verified Journal of Forecasting, DOI 10.1002/for.3139. Confirmed the gains are genuinely out-of-sample (via forecast-combination evaluation), not merely in-sample — the review's 'out-of-sample predictive content' wording is justified. The ~5-7% (1-6m, overall) and ~20% (12m, sub-category — specifically fertilizers, not a metals sub-index) figures are accurate. Minor nuance: the ~20% headline is for fertilizers, so copper's benefit is via the broader block, as the review acknowledges.

checked_claims.claim: Pesaran, Shin & Smith (2001), 'Bounds testing approaches to the analysis of level relationships', Journal of Applied Econometrics 16(3): ARDL bounds F-test valid under mixed I(0)/I(1) regressors, conditional-ECM reparameterisation.
checked_claims.note: Verified JAE 16(3), 289-326, 2001. Method description (bounds F-test, two critical-value bands for all-I(0) vs all-I(1), conditional ECM) is accurate.

checked_claims.claim: ARDL exemplar cited as 'Galip Afsin Ravanoglu et al. / MPRA & Resources Policy ... determinants of crude oil prices, Resources Policy 2022, S0301420722005281'.
checked_claims.note: AUTHOR MISATTRIBUTION. DOI S0301420722005281 resolves to a real Resources Policy vol 79 (2022) paper, 'The determinants of crude oil prices: Evidence from ARDL and nonlinear ARDL approaches', but by Ben Salem, Nouira, Jeguirim & Rault — not 'Galip Afsin Ravanoglu'. The methodology and finding (ARDL/NARDL on oil price determinants incl. exchange rate, long-run + asymmetry) are real and correctly described, and the review honestly hedges this as an oil exemplar with no clean copper ARDL located. But the named lead author is fabricated/incorrect.

checked_claims.claim: Interpretability claims: ECT loading is a literal monthly speed-of-adjustment; cointegration/VECM/ARDL long-run coefficients and adjustment speeds are fully readable; DFM/FAVAR factors are 'named' and chartable (non-black-box); these methods are a MONTHLY tool, weak at weekly.
checked_claims.note: Econometrically accurate. ECT loading does equal per-period fractional mean-reversion (a -0.10 monthly loading ~10%/month is a fair gloss). VECM betas/alphas, weak-exogeneity tests, IRF/FEVD, and ARDL long-run elasticities are genuinely inspectable. The DFM/FAVAR 'medium-high, non-black-box but factors are rotation-dependent linear combinations needing labeling' characterization is honest and not overstated — it does not falsely call a black box interpretable. The monthly-over-weekly horizon judgment is consistent with the literature (macro panels and equilibrium adjustment are monthly-scale).

The DOI/title/journal (S0378475401004098, 'Cointegration analysis of metals futures', Mathematics and Computers in Simulation) actually belong to Watkins & McAleer (2002, vol 59, pp 207-221), a copper-futures risk-premium/cost-of-carry study. No Booth & Ciner paper with this title/venue exists (their real 2001 paper is on agricultural futures in Applied Economics Letters). The author, year, and volume in the citation are wrong.

'Galip Afsin Ravanoglu et al.' as lead author of the Resources Policy 2022 ARDL/NARDL crude-oil-determinants paper (S0301420722005281) — the named author appears fabricated; the actual paper is by Ben Salem, Nouira, Jeguirim & Rault. The DOI, journal, year, and methodology are correct, but the attributed author is not.

(2002), 'Cointegration analysis of metals futures', Mathematics and Computers in Simulation 59, 207-221 — and note it studies 3-month LME copper futures pricing (risk premium / cost-of-carry), which is actually a stronger, more copper-specific fit than the mis-cited version implied. Do not present it as Booth & Ciner price-discovery work.
