Keep the honest caveat that no clean copper-specific ARDL with a monthly RW comparison was located.

Correct the Buncic & Moretto predictor count: the paper uses ~16 predictor variables (grouped including fundamentals, financialization, global risk appetite, momentum, term spread, FX/stock prices), not '18'. Immaterial to the headline but should be accurate.

Clarify the Basistha et al. (2024) ~20% figure: the ~20% out-of-sample gain is for fertilizers at the 12-month horizon, not a metals/copper sub-index. The review already implies copper benefits only via the broader industrial/metals block; make explicit that the ~20% headline is fertilizer-specific so it is not read as a copper result.

Soften the unverified sub-claim that the Lombardi-Osbat-Schnatz metals factor is 'largely copper-driven' to 'metals factor (to which copper contributes heavily)' unless a direct quote from the paper supports the stronger wording — this specific attribution was not confirmable at abstract level.

findings.dimension: Volatility & density forecasting (GARCH family, GARCH-MIDAS, HAR-RV, MIDAS mixed-frequency, quantile regression) for weekly/monthly copper
findings.overview: This dimension covers interpretable models that forecast the *distribution* of copper returns (volatility, quantiles, intervals, densities) rather than just a point. For a copper repo already producing point forecasts at 1d/5d/22d/66d, these methods are the natural way to attach *calibrated* prediction intervals and risk measures (VaR/ES) and to let copper-specific macro drivers (China IP, USD, real rates, PPI, inventories, EPU) move the long-run risk level transparently. The literature has a clear hierarchy. (1) Univariate GARCH-family models (GARCH, EGARCH, GJR-TGARCH, APARCH, FIGARCH) are the workhorse for return volatility; for copper specifically the leverage/asymmetry effect is real but weaker and sometimes inverted versus equities (industrial metals can show *positive* asymmetry around demand shocks). (2) HAR / HAR-RV (Corsi 2009) exploits high-frequency intraday data to build realized volatility and is repeatedly the model to beat at daily-to-weekly horizons; in the only dedicated COMEX-copper realized-volatility horse-race located (Wang & Lu 2024), HAR beat LSTM/GRU/RNN deep nets on daily QLIKE. (3) GARCH-MIDAS / component-GARCH (Engle-Lee, Spline-GARCH, Engle-Ghysels-Sohn) decomposes volatility into a fast mean-reverting piece and a slow macro-driven long-run piece, and is the most copper-relevant family because it lets monthly macro (IP, PPI, interest rates, EPU) drive the long-run risk of daily/weekly copper in an explicitly readable way — and it tends to win at the 1-3 month horizon. (4) MIDAS regressions mix daily/weekly predictors into monthly targets without ad-hoc aggregation. (5) Quantile / mixed-frequency quantile regression delivers VaR/ES and full predictive intervals directly. Standing: GARCH/HAR/GARCH-MIDAS are mature, peer-reviewed and standard at central banks and on commodity desks; copper-specific evidence is thinner than for oil and equities, so much of the strongest evidence is from analogous commodities (oil, gold, base-metal panels) that the user should treat as transferable but verify on HG=F/LME data.

approaches.name: Univariate GARCH family with asymmetry/long-memory (GARCH, EGARCH, GJR-TGARCH, APARCH, FIGARCH)
approaches.one_line: Models the conditional variance of copper returns as a function of past squared shocks and past variance, with extensions for leverage/asymmetry (EGARCH, GJR, APARCH) and long memory (FIGARCH).
approaches.mechanism: Conditional variance h_t is an explicit, low-dimensional recursion. In GARCH(1,1) h_t = omega + alpha*eps_{t-1}^2 + beta*h_{t-1}: alpha is the reaction to the last shock, beta the persistence, alpha+beta the volatility half-life. EGARCH models log-variance (guarantees positivity, allows a leverage coefficient gamma whose sign tells you whether negative or positive shocks raise vol more); GJR-TGARCH adds a gamma*I(eps<0)*eps^2 term so you can read off extra variance from down-moves; APARCH estimates the power delta of the volatility process; FIGARCH replaces (1-L) with a fractional difference d in (0,1) to capture slow-decaying long memory. Every coefficient is inspectable and economically nameable. Combined with an assumed (Student-t / skew-t) innovation, it yields a full one-step conditional density and hence quantile-based prediction intervals.
approaches.horizon_fit: Strongest at DAILY and WEEKLY copper, where volatility clustering is sharp and the recursion is informative. At MONTHLY horizon a pure daily-GARCH forecast mean-reverts to the unconditional variance and adds little over a constant, which is exactly why the component/MIDAS variants below exist. FIGARCH's long-memory term helps push usable persistence out toward the monthly horizon. For the repo's 1d and 5d interval generation this is the most direct upgrade.
approaches.interpretability: Fully transparent: persistence (alpha+beta), shock reaction, leverage sign/size, tail thickness (t degrees of freedom), and long-memory parameter d are all readable single numbers with clear meaning.
approaches.strengths: Tiny parameter count, fast to estimate, well-understood diagnostics, directly produces conditional densities and VaR; asymmetric variants capture that copper sell-offs (demand scares) often spike vol; t/skew-t innovations give calibrated fat-tailed intervals out of the box.
approaches.weaknesses: Uses only the return's own history — ignores copper fundamentals unless extended; the daily-frequency version has almost no useful signal at 22d/66d (forecasts collapse to unconditional vol); leverage sign for industrial metals is unstable and can flip versus equities (must be estimated, not assumed); structural breaks (2008, 2011 super-cycle peak, 2020, 2021-22) break stationarity and inflate persistence toward a spurious unit root (IGARCH); does not forecast the price level, only its dispersion.
approaches.copper_relevance: Native inputs are HG=F / LME 3-month copper returns; the chosen innovation distribution calibrates tails. Extends naturally to GARCH-X by adding exogenous variance regressors the repo already has (DXY moves, real-yield shocks, CFTC positioning extremes, inventory draws) as drivers of h_t, keeping interpretability.

key_papers.citation: Wang & Lu (2024), 'COMEX Copper Futures Volatility Forecasting: Econometric Models and Deep Learning', arXiv:2409.08356
key_papers.method: GARCH(1,1) and Realized GARCH vs HAR vs RNN/LSTM/GRU on COMEX copper, daily and hourly realized volatility, 2000-2023, MSE & QLIKE loss
key_papers.finding: On daily realized vol GARCH (QLIKE 5.99E-08) and the deep nets (6.70-6.73E-08) were all beaten by HAR (2.39E-09); plain GARCH lagged HAR by ~an order of magnitude but matched/beat the neural nets, and deep nets only closed the gap with GARCH as the horizon lengthened. Confirms simple GARCH is a serious, interpretable benchmark for copper, not dominated by deep learning.

key_papers.citation: Li & Li (2015), 'Forecasting copper futures volatility under model uncertainty', Resources Policy 46(P2):167-176
key_papers.method: Multiple GARCH-family specifications combined via time-varying / OLS model-averaging on copper futures, evaluated under several loss functions out-of-sample
key_papers.finding: No single GARCH spec was reliably best; OLS time-varying weighted *averaging* of GARCH models achieved the smallest forecast error and significantly reduced the over-prediction percentage. Direct support for combining GARCH variants rather than picking one — analogous to the repo's existing ensemble philosophy applied to volatility.

key_papers.citation: Reference standard: Bollerslev (1986) GARCH; Nelson (1991) EGARCH; Glosten-Jagannathan-Runkle (1993) GJR; Ding-Granger-Engle (1993) APARCH; Baillie-Bollerslev-Mikkelsen (1996) FIGARCH
key_papers.method: Foundational econometric specifications (cited here as method definitions, located via the survey/secondary literature above, not the primary papers)
key_papers.finding: Define the asymmetry (EGARCH/GJR/APARCH) and long-memory (FIGARCH) machinery used throughout the commodity-volatility literature; included as method anchors, not as copper empirical evidence.

approaches.name: HAR / HAR-RV (Heterogeneous Autoregressive realized-volatility models)
approaches.one_line: Forecasts realized volatility of copper as a simple linear regression on yesterday's, last week's and last month's realized volatility, optionally adding jumps and leverage.
approaches.mechanism: RV_{t+1} = c + beta_d*RV_d + beta_w*RV_w(5-day avg) + beta_m*RV_m(22-day avg) + error, where RV is built from high-frequency (e.g. 5-minute) intraday squared returns. It is an OLS regression — coefficients beta_d/beta_w/beta_m are directly interpretable as the weight of daily/weekly/monthly traders' horizons (the 'heterogeneous market' cascade). Extensions: HAR-RV-J adds a separately-estimated jump component (so you can read how much next-period vol comes from discontinuous price jumps vs continuous variation), HAR-RV-CJ splits continuous and jump variation, and leverage/semivariance terms let down-moves load differently. Because it's linear in observed RV, it is estimated by OLS and every term is transparent.
approaches.horizon_fit: Built for multi-horizon by construction: the weekly (5d) and monthly (22d) RV terms map almost exactly onto the repo's 5d and 22d targets, and the cascade gives genuine persistence out to ~monthly, so HAR is well suited to WEEKLY and the lower end of MONTHLY. The main practical constraint is needing intraday data to compute RV; HG=F intraday is available, LME less granular.
approaches.interpretability: Very high — an OLS regression whose three (or five) coefficients have a direct 'trader-horizon' reading; jump and leverage terms quantify discrete-move and asymmetry contributions explicitly.
approaches.strengths: Repeatedly the best or near-best volatility forecaster across assets despite simplicity; captures long-memory-like persistence without fractional integration; trivial to estimate and combine; jump/leverage extensions add interpretable structure; in the copper-specific test it beat LSTM/GRU/RNN on daily QLIKE.
approaches.weaknesses: Requires reliable high-frequency intraday copper data to construct RV (microstructure noise, overnight gaps, low-liquidity LME sessions degrade it); forecasts realized variance, not the price level or its sign; is purely backward-looking on its own (no macro/fundamental input unless augmented, e.g. HAR-X with implied vol or COT); performance edge shrinks at higher sampling frequencies where deep nets catch up.
approaches.copper_relevance: Inputs are intraday HG=F (COMEX) returns aggregated to daily/weekly/monthly RV; naturally augmentable with copper implied volatility, overnight-return and CFTC-positioning terms, giving an interpretable HAR-X that ties realized risk to copper-specific flow.

key_papers.citation: Corsi (2009), 'A Simple Approximate Long-Memory Model of Realized Volatility', Journal of Financial Econometrics 7(2):174-196
key_papers.method: Original HAR-RV: cascade of daily/weekly/monthly realized-volatility components estimated by OLS
key_papers.finding: Reproduces long memory, fat tails and self-similarity of returns with remarkably good, parsimonious forecasting performance — the foundational reference establishing HAR as a benchmark-beating yet fully interpretable RV model.

key_papers.citation: Wang & Lu (2024), 'COMEX Copper Futures Volatility Forecasting: Econometric Models and Deep Learning', arXiv:2409.08356
key_papers.method: HAR vs GARCH/Realized-GARCH vs RNN/LSTM/GRU on COMEX copper realized vol, daily & hourly, 2000-2023, QLIKE/MSE/RMSE
key_papers.finding: HAR was the single best model for DAILY copper realized volatility (QLIKE 2.39E-09, ~one order of magnitude below GARCH and the deep nets; RMSE 0.0001 vs 0.0003-0.0004). Deep nets only matched HAR at the hourly frequency. Strongest direct evidence that an interpretable HAR is the model to beat for copper realized vol.

key_papers.citation: Fang, Zhao & Zhong (2022), 'Volatility Forecasting of Copper Futures Based on HAR-RV Model', BCP Business & Management
key_papers.method: HAR-RV augmented with investor sentiment and day-of-week effects on copper futures, 5-minute high-frequency data
key_papers.finding: HAR-RV gave relatively stable and more accurate LONG-term (weekly/monthly) volatility forecasts for copper, with investor sentiment and weekend effects entering negatively at medium/long horizons. Abstract did not report head-to-head RMSE versus a random walk, so treat the magnitude of the edge as unverified.

approaches.name: GARCH-MIDAS & multiplicative component GARCH (Engle-Lee, Spline-GARCH, GARCH-MIDAS, MF2-GARCH)
approaches.one_line: Splits copper volatility into a short-run daily GARCH component times a slow long-run component driven by monthly macro variables via a MIDAS weighting scheme.
approaches.mechanism: Variance = tau_t (long-run) x g_t (short-run unit-GARCH). The long-run tau_t is a MIDAS-weighted sum of low-frequency macro variables: log tau_t = m + theta * sum_k phi_k(w) * X_{t-k}, where X is monthly macro (IP, PPI, interest rate, EPU, or realized vol), the Beta/Exp-Almon weights phi_k decay over lags, and crucially the single slope theta tells you the *sign and strength* with which that macro driver moves copper's long-run risk. The short-run g_t mean-reverts daily. Engle-Lee (1999) is the additive two-component analogue; Spline-GARCH (Engle-Rangel 2008) uses an exponential spline for the slow component; MF2-GARCH (Conrad 2025) models volatility cycles. So you can literally read 'a one-unit rise in monthly PPI raises copper's long-run variance by theta' — exactly the interpretable macro-to-risk link the repo's cointegration/HMM components aim at, but for the second moment.
approaches.horizon_fit: This is the standout family for MONTHLY (22d) and 3-MONTH (66d) copper risk: the macro-driven long-run component is precisely what carries forecast power at 1-3 month horizons where pure daily GARCH decays to a constant. Conrad-Kleen show only GARCH-MIDAS models survive in the Model Confidence Set at 2-3 months. It also improves weekly forecasts via a more accurate variance level. Needs a span of monthly macro history to estimate the MIDAS weights.
approaches.interpretability: High and *the most macro-readable* of all these families: one theta per driver gives a signed elasticity of long-run copper volatility to each macro factor; the MIDAS weight curve shows which lags matter; the short/long decomposition separates transient noise from fundamentals-driven risk.
approaches.strengths: Directly answers 'which macro drivers raise copper's risk and by how much'; wins at monthly/quarterly horizons; mixes daily copper with monthly macro without aggregation loss; produces calibrated long-horizon densities; mature R tooling (mfGARCH).
approaches.weaknesses: More parameters and a non-trivial likelihood (identification of theta vs the weight shape can be fragile in short samples); requires choosing macro regressors and a MIDAS weight form; vulnerable to macro structural breaks and to look-ahead bias if vintages aren't respected (China IP/PPI are revised); copper-specific published evidence is still thin and partly in working-paper form, so out-of-sample superiority should be re-validated on HG=F/LME.
approaches.copper_relevance: Tailor-made for copper's macro story: documented drivers of the long-run component include interest rates, industrial production, PPI, the dollar index, term spread and EPU — all series the repo already pulls from FRED. China IP, real yields and breakevens slot straight in as MIDAS regressors; COT or inventory series can proxy the long-run state.

key_papers.citation: Engle, Ghysels & Sohn (2013), 'Stock Market Volatility and Macroeconomic Fundamentals', Review of Economics and Statistics 95(3):776-797
key_papers.method: Introduces GARCH-MIDAS: daily unit-GARCH short run x MIDAS-weighted monthly macro (inflation, industrial-production growth) long run
key_papers.finding: Long-run component driven by inflation and IP growth performs at par with or *outperforms* traditional volatility models at longer horizons; macro fundamentals matter even at short horizons. The methodological anchor for macro-to-long-run-vol modelling.

key_papers.citation: Conrad & Kleen (2020), 'Two are better than one: Volatility forecasting using multiplicative component GARCH-MIDAS models', Journal of Applied Econometrics 35(1):19-45
key_papers.method: GARCH-MIDAS vs HAR, Realized GARCH, HEAVY, MS-GARCH on S&P 500; Model Confidence Set with QLIKE
key_papers.finding: At 2- and 3-month horizons ONLY GARCH-MIDAS models remained in the Model Confidence Set, with a housing-starts-driven GARCH-MIDAS achieving the lowest QLIKE. Strong (equity) evidence that the component-MIDAS structure is the interpretable winner at the monthly/quarterly horizon the repo cares about.

key_papers.citation: Wang & Li (2024), 'On the macroeconomic fundamentals of long-term volatilities and dynamic correlations in COMEX copper futures', arXiv:2409.08355
key_papers.method: GARCH-MIDAS, GJR-GARCH(1,1) short run, DCC-GARCH and DCC-MIDAS on daily COMEX copper + monthly macro, 2002-2022
key_papers.finding: PPI was the most efficient macro driver of copper's long-run volatility (positive effect), with interest rates and industrial production entering negatively; DCC-MIDAS with PPI beat realized-vol specifications for the long-run copper-equity correlation. Direct copper evidence that interpretable macro-MIDAS components carry the long-run risk signal.

approaches.name: MIDAS mixed-frequency regression for the conditional mean/level (and mixed-frequency density)
approaches.one_line: Forecasts a monthly copper target directly from current and lagged daily/weekly predictors using a parsimonious MIDAS lag polynomial instead of pre-aggregating the high-frequency data.
approaches.mechanism: y_{t+h} (monthly copper return/level) = beta0 + beta1 * sum_k phi_k(w) * X_high_{t-k} + error, where X_high is a daily/weekly predictor (e.g. daily DXY, real yields, copper futures basis, COT) and phi_k(w) is a tightly parameterised Beta or Exp-Almon weight that compresses many high-frequency lags into 1-2 parameters. The estimated weight curve is directly plottable and interpretable (which recent days matter, how fast their influence decays), and a single slope gives the predictor's signed effect. It is a *direct* h-step forecaster, so a separate model is fit per horizon (5d, 22d, 66d), avoiding iterated-forecast error accumulation.
approaches.horizon_fit: Designed exactly for the WEEKLY-to-MONTHLY mismatch: it lets fast-moving daily copper drivers inform the 22d/66d target without throwing away within-month information by averaging. Best when high-frequency predictors genuinely lead the monthly move (USD, rates, positioning); less useful at 1d.
approaches.interpretability: High: a handful of slope coefficients plus an explicit, plottable lag-weight curve; far more transparent than feeding lagged daily features into a tree ensemble.
approaches.strengths: Avoids ad-hoc temporal aggregation and the parameter proliferation of unrestricted lag models; nowcasting evidence shows it can beat random-walk and AR benchmarks for monthly targets; integrates cleanly with the repo's daily FRED/Alpha Vantage/COT feeds; pairs with quantile loss to give mixed-frequency density forecasts.
approaches.weaknesses: The restricted weight shape can be mis-specified (bias if the true lag pattern isn't Beta/Exp-Almon); a linear conditional-mean MIDAS captures level, not volatility, so you still need GARCH-MIDAS or quantile-MIDAS for intervals; predictor selection and real-time vintage discipline matter; copper-specific point-forecast MIDAS evidence is sparse (most evidence is for inflation/IP/exchange rates and oil), so transfer with care.
approaches.copper_relevance: Naturally consumes the repo's daily cross-asset and macro features (DXY, gold/aluminium/oil ratios, real yields, breakevens, futures basis, CFTC COT) as high-frequency predictors of monthly/3-month copper; a copper-price-index-style MIDAS could also feed the macro side.

key_papers.citation: Ghysels, Santa-Clara & Valkanov (2004/2007), 'The MIDAS Touch: Mixed Data Sampling Regression Models' (working paper / subsequent JoE outlets)
key_papers.method: Introduces MIDAS regression with Beta/Exp-Almon weighting to relate low-frequency targets to high-frequency predictors
key_papers.finding: Establishes that a parsimonious MIDAS lag polynomial extracts predictive content from high-frequency data better than aggregating to the low frequency — the methodological foundation; cited as method anchor rather than copper evidence.

key_papers.citation: World Bank Policy Research WP 10611 (2023), Arroyo Marioli, Khadan, Ohnsorge & Yamazaki, 'Forecasting Industrial Commodity Prices'
key_papers.method: Model suite (futures-based, bivariate correlations, consensus, BVAR, large-scale macroeconometric model) for oil + six LME metals incl. copper, multiple horizons
key_papers.finding: Futures prices and bivariate (cross-asset) correlations performed well at SHORT horizons; consensus forecasts and a large macroeconometric model performed well at LONG horizons; the suite emphasised sizeable forecast-error bands (density/interval thinking). Supports horizon-dependent, fundamentals-aware copper forecasting and interval reporting; it did not crown a single random-walk-beating point model for copper.

approaches.name: Quantile regression & mixed-frequency quantile regression for VaR / ES / prediction intervals
approaches.one_line: Directly models chosen quantiles of the copper return distribution (e.g. 5%, 50%, 95%) as functions of predictors, giving calibrated intervals and Value-at-Risk without assuming a parametric error distribution.
approaches.mechanism: For quantile level q, minimise the pinball (check) loss of (return - X*beta_q); the fitted X*beta_q is the conditional q-quantile, so stacking several q's traces the whole predictive density and the gap between, say, the 5% and 95% fits *is* the prediction interval / VaR. Each beta_q is an interpretable sensitivity of that tail to the predictor (e.g. how much the 5% copper return worsens when realized vol or EPU rises). Mixed-frequency quantile regression (MIDAS-QR) puts high-frequency predictors behind a MIDAS weight inside the quantile regression, so daily volatility/uncertainty drives monthly VaR. Žikeš-Baruník-style VaR regresses returns on ex-post realized volatility to get a quantile directly. No Gaussian assumption is needed, and asymmetry/fat tails are captured non-parametrically.
approaches.horizon_fit: Flexible across WEEKLY and MONTHLY: a direct per-horizon, per-quantile fit (like MIDAS) avoids iteration error, and the mixed-frequency version is explicitly built to forecast monthly VaR/ES from daily inputs. Already used in the repo at the point level — the upgrade is feeding it volatility/realized-vol and mixed-frequency macro predictors for sharper, better-calibrated tails.
approaches.interpretability: High: each coefficient is the marginal effect of a driver on a specific quantile, so you can say which factors widen the downside vs upside tail of copper; no opaque distributional assumption.
approaches.strengths: Distribution-free, robust to fat tails and asymmetry, directly yields calibrated intervals/VaR/ES that can be formally backtested (Kupiec/Christoffersen); naturally combined with MIDAS for mixed frequency; complements GARCH by not requiring a parametric innovation; pairs with the repo's existing quantile component and forecast-combination layer.
approaches.weaknesses: Quantile crossing (fitted quantiles can cross and need rearrangement); each quantile is a separate model so the full density needs several fits and can be noisy in the tails with limited data; less efficient than a correctly-specified parametric model when that model is right; predictor and weight choice still required; pure cross-sectional QR ignores volatility dynamics unless realized-vol/GARCH terms are added as regressors.
approaches.copper_relevance: Predictors are exactly the repo's stack — realized/implied vol, DXY, real yields, breakevens, futures basis, inventories, CFTC COT, cross-asset ratios — entered linearly per quantile; mixed-frequency QR lets daily copper risk drive monthly/3-month VaR for the user's 22d/66d horizons.

key_papers.citation: Čech & Baruník (2019), 'Panel quantile regressions for estimating and predicting the Value-at-Risk of commodities', Journal of Futures Markets
key_papers.method: Panel quantile regression of commodity returns on ex-post and ex-ante volatility measures across energy and metals, controlling for unobserved heterogeneity; out-of-sample VaR/ES with rolling re-estimation (backtested from Jan 2017)
key_papers.finding: Future conditional quantiles of commodity returns depend on common, time-varying volatility factors; the panel-quantile framework produced and backtested out-of-sample VaR and ES forecasts across commodity sectors including metals. Demonstrates interpretable quantile-based tail forecasting on the commodity cross-section relevant to copper (verify copper-specific accuracy directly).

key_papers.citation: Mixed-frequency quantile regression literature, e.g. 'Mixed-frequency quantile regressions to forecast value-at-risk and expected shortfall', Annals of Operations Research (2023)
key_papers.method: MIDAS-weighted high-frequency predictors inside quantile regression to forecast VaR and ES at lower frequency
key_papers.finding: Mixing high-frequency information into quantile regression improves out-of-sample VaR/ES forecasts versus standard low-frequency quantile and parametric benchmarks. Establishes the MIDAS-QR route to monthly copper VaR from daily inputs (located via search; copper application not yet published, so treat as a transferable method).

key_papers.citation: Nature Scientific Reports (2025), hybrid quantile interval framework for copper price prediction (cited as a contrast point)
key_papers.method: Quantile *deep learning* with multi-objective optimisation and kernel density estimation for copper price interval prediction
key_papers.finding: Builds copper prediction intervals and recovers a thin-tailed copper price density via quantile regression + KDE. Noted only as a contrast: the interval/quantile idea is sound and copper-applicable, but the deep-learning engine is the opaque variant the user wants to AVOID — the takeaway is to use the same quantile/KDE interval machinery on transparent (linear/MIDAS) quantile models.

findings.evaluation_notes: Evaluation in this literature centres on volatility-specific loss functions that are robust to the latent-target problem: QLIKE (the field's preferred, asymmetric, robust loss) and MSE/RMSE against a realized-volatility proxy, plus MAE/MAPE. The Wang & Lu (2024) copper study ranks models by QLIKE/MSE against 5-minute realized volatility. Model selection increasingly uses the Model Confidence Set (Hansen-Lunde-Nason) — Conrad-Kleen (2020) use it to show only GARCH-MIDAS survives at 2-3 month horizons — and pairwise Diebold-Mariano tests. For interval/density/VaR work, evaluation shifts to coverage backtests: Kupiec unconditional-coverage and Christoffersen conditional-coverage/independence tests, the pinball/quantile (check) loss, and ES backtests, typically with rolling/expanding re-estimation windows (Čech-Baruník backtest VaR/ES out-of-sample from 2017). The pervasive benchmark for the *level* is the driftless random walk / no-change forecast (and futures-implied prices for commodities); for *volatility* the benchmarks are GARCH(1,1), HAR and realized GARCH. Two integrity caveats: (1) several copper-specific results (Fang-Zhao-Zhong 2022; the copper GARCH-MIDAS working paper) report a model 'winning' without a clean random-walk/DM comparison in the accessible text, so their edge magnitude is unverified here; (2) much of the strongest random-walk-beating, MCS-based evidence is on equities, oil and gold rather than copper, and should be re-validated on HG=F/LME before relying on it.
key_takeaways: For copper realized-volatility at the DAILY-to-WEEKLY horizon, HAR/HAR-RV is the interpretable model to beat — in the only dedicated COMEX-copper horse-race located (Wang & Lu 2024) HAR beat GARCH and LSTM/GRU/RNN on daily QLIKE by roughly an order of magnitude; it needs intraday HG=F data to build realized volatility.

For the user's MONTHLY (22d) and 3-MONTH (66d) risk horizons, GARCH-MIDAS / multiplicative component-GARCH is the best-fit interpretable family: it makes monthly macro (PPI, IP, interest rates, EPU) drive copper's long-run volatility through a single readable slope theta, and the equity evidence (Conrad-Kleen 2020) shows only GARCH-MIDAS survives the Model Confidence Set at 2-3 months. Copper-specific work (Wang & Li 2024) finds PPI the most efficient long-run driver.

Plain GARCH-family models (with skew-t innovations and a GJR/EGARCH/APARCH asymmetry term) remain the fastest route to attach calibrated fat-tailed prediction intervals to the repo's 1d/5d forecasts; but assume nothing about the leverage sign — for industrial metals it must be estimated, and Li-Li (2015) show *averaging* several GARCH specs beats picking one, mirroring the repo's ensemble approach.

MIDAS conditional-mean regression is the clean way to push the repo's existing daily features (DXY, real yields, futures basis, COT, cross-asset ratios) into monthly/3-month copper without ad-hoc aggregation, with a plottable lag-weight curve; combine with quantile loss (mixed-frequency quantile regression / Čech-Baruník-style VaR) to upgrade the repo's existing quantile-interval component into backtestable monthly VaR/ES.

Evaluate with QLIKE + Model Confidence Set for volatility and Kupiec/Christoffersen coverage + pinball loss for intervals, always against a random-walk (level) and GARCH(1,1)/HAR (vol) benchmark. Treat copper-specific 'wins' lacking a clean DM/random-walk comparison as unverified, and re-validate equity/oil/gold evidence on HG=F/LME data. Use the copper quantile-*deep-learning* papers only as a contrast — keep the quantile/KDE interval machinery but on transparent linear/MIDAS engines.

findings.dimension: Regime-switching & interpretable nonlinear models (Markov-switching, TAR/SETAR, STAR/LSTAR, time-varying-parameter) for copper price forecasting at weekly and monthly horizons
findings.overview: This family of models extends linear AR/ARIMAX by letting the data-generating process change across discrete or smoothly-varying "regimes." For copper specifically — a metal whose price alternates between demand-driven trending phases, sharp inventory-/risk-driven sell-offs, and quiet range-bound periods — the appeal is twofold: (1) the models naturally encode the well-documented nonlinearity and asymmetry of industrial-metal prices (faster, larger moves in stress/high-vol regimes; mean-reversion to a cost-of-production or cointegration anchor in calm regimes), and (2) every component is human-readable: you can read off the regime label, its mean/vol, the smoothed probability that you are in it today, the threshold level that triggers a switch, or the time path of a coefficient. The standing of these methods in the literature is nuanced and important for a practitioner to internalize. They almost universally improve IN-SAMPLE fit and density/volatility forecasting (clearly capturing fat tails, asymmetry and clustering). Their OUT-OF-SAMPLE point-forecast edge over a random walk is far less reliable, horizon- and regime-dependent, and for some specifications (notably STAR for commodity price levels) essentially absent. The strongest copper-specific positive result is for time-varying-parameter / dynamic-model-averaging regressions at the monthly horizon (Buncic & Moretto 2015), where the gain is concentrated in the 2008 crisis regime — i.e., the nonlinearity pays off precisely when it is supposed to. The honest consensus is: use these as regime-conditioning and density/interval tools and as economically-interpretable diagnostic overlays, and be skeptical of claims that any of them durably beats a no-change forecast for the conditional mean at short horizons.

approaches.name: Markov-switching autoregression (MS-AR / Hamilton model) and Markov-switching VAR (MSVAR)
approaches.one_line: An AR (or VAR) whose intercept, slopes and/or variance jump between a small number of hidden states governed by a Markov chain, so the model infers (probabilistically) which regime — e.g. bull/bear or low-vol/high-vol — copper is in today.
approaches.mechanism: The latent state s_t follows a first-order Markov chain with a fixed transition matrix P. Conditional on s_t, copper returns follow a Gaussian AR. Estimation is by maximum likelihood with the Hamilton filter, which delivers filtered and smoothed regime probabilities. Interpretable outputs you can read off directly: (i) regime-specific mean and variance (e.g. a 'contraction/high-vol' state with negative drift and large sigma vs an 'expansion/low-vol' state), (ii) the transition matrix P, from which you compute expected regime durations 1/(1-p_ii) and the staying probabilities, and (iii) the smoothed probability series P(s_t = k | data), a 0-1 'which-regime-are-we-in' signal you can chart against copper price. This is the direct generalization of your existing 3-state Gaussian HMM — an HMM on returns IS a Markov-switching model; adding autoregressive terms and exogenous regressors (MS-ARX) is the natural upgrade.
approaches.horizon_fit: Better suited to MONTHLY than weekly for point forecasts: the regime structure of metals maps onto business-cycle and inventory-cycle frequencies, and monthly data give cleaner regime identification with fewer spurious one-off switches. At WEEKLY frequency the main payoff is volatility/regime tagging (risk-on/risk-off, high-vol clustering) rather than mean prediction; weekly copper returns are close to unforecastable in mean, so the MS layer is best read as a state classifier feeding intervals and position sizing. For multi-step forecasts the conditional mean is a probability-weighted average over regimes, which mechanically shrinks toward the unconditional mean as horizon grows — i.e. it tends back toward a random-walk-like forecast at longer horizons.
approaches.interpretability: High. You can name each regime by its estimated mean/vol and verify it against known copper episodes (2008 collapse, 2011 peak, 2020 COVID crash, 2021-22 squeeze). Transition probabilities and expected durations are economically meaningful. The smoothed regime-probability path is directly explainable to a non-technical stakeholder ('85% probability we are in the high-volatility regime'). Opaque parts: the number of regimes is a modelling choice, and the latent state is inferred, not observed.
approaches.strengths: Captures asymmetry and volatility clustering that linear ARIMAX misses; gives a probabilistic regime signal usable for risk management, interval widening, and ensemble weighting; well-developed inference (filtered/smoothed probabilities, ergodic probabilities); integrates exogenous copper drivers via MS-ARX or MSVAR (e.g. inventories, DXY, China IP) and lets their effect differ by regime.
approaches.weaknesses: Regime identification can be unstable / produce spurious short-lived regimes, especially at weekly frequency or with too many states; transition matrix is assumed time-invariant (real copper regimes are driven by changing fundamentals, so constant P is a strong assumption); likelihood is multi-modal and sensitive to starting values; the 'which regime tomorrow' forecast still relies on persistence (p_ii near 1), so at the switch points — exactly when you need it — it is least reliable; out-of-sample mean-forecast gains over a random walk are not robustly demonstrated for metal returns (the documented edge is mostly in-sample fit and volatility/density, not point MSFE).
approaches.copper_relevance: Natural home for high-vol vs low-vol and bull/bear copper regimes. MSVAR variants let copper interact with its drivers regime-dependently — e.g. copper futures vs spot, USD, and macro demand — and several published copper-futures studies use exactly this. Inventories (LME/COMEX/SHFE), the futures basis/convenience yield, DXY and China activity are the standard regime-relevant inputs. Directly complements your existing 3-state HMM by adding AR dynamics and exogenous regressors.

key_papers.method: Foundational Markov-switching AR; mean-switching model of US GNP growth with Hamilton filter; NBER-dated expansions/contractions recovered as regimes.
key_papers.citation: Hamilton, J.D. (1989), 'A New Approach to the Economic Analysis of Nonstationary Time Series and the Business Cycle,' Econometrica 57(2), 357-384.
key_papers.finding: Seminal paper: shows the parameters of an AR can be modelled as the outcome of a discrete Markov process, and that the smoothed regime probabilities line up with NBER business-cycle turning points (quarterly US GNP, 1952-1984). Not a forecasting horse-race vs random walk; establishes the interpretable two-regime framework that all later copper/metal applications inherit.

approaches.name: Threshold autoregression (TAR / SETAR) and momentum-threshold error-correction (M-TAR, Enders-Siklos)
approaches.one_line: A piecewise-linear AR (or error-correction model) that switches abruptly between regimes when an observable threshold variable — a lagged price/return, or the size/direction of the deviation from a cointegration anchor — crosses an estimated boundary, capturing asymmetric adjustment.
approaches.mechanism: SETAR: y_t follows AR coefficients in regime 1 if the threshold variable (e.g. y_{t-d}) is below a threshold c, and different coefficients above it; c and the delay d are estimated (often by grid search minimizing SSR). TAR/M-TAR error-correction (Enders-Siklos): the speed of mean-reversion to a long-run cointegrating relationship is allowed to differ depending on whether the disequilibrium (error-correction term) is positive vs negative (TAR), or whether it is RISING vs FALLING (M-TAR / momentum). Interpretable outputs: the estimated threshold value c (an economically meaningful trigger level), the regime-specific AR/adjustment coefficients (e.g. 'reverts at rate 0.3 when above its gold/aluminium-implied fair value but only 0.05 when below'), and a clear hypothesis test for asymmetric adjustment (F-test that the two adjustment speeds are equal). This is the asymmetric/nonlinear generalization of your existing Engle-Granger rolling error-correction setup.
approaches.horizon_fit: Most natural at WEEKLY and MONTHLY where the threshold variable (a deviation from a cointegration anchor vs gold/aluminium/oil/DXY/CNY, or a momentum/basis signal) is meaningfully persistent. M-TAR error-correction in particular fits the monthly horizon and is a direct asymmetric upgrade to your cointegration component. SETAR on raw returns is less compelling at weekly frequency because the threshold on noisy short-horizon returns is hard to pin down.
approaches.interpretability: Very high and arguably the most transparent of the family: the regime boundary is an observable number you can plot and interpret ('when copper is more than X% rich to its DXY/aluminium-implied level, adjustment is fast'); the two adjustment speeds and their formal asymmetry test are directly reportable. No latent state to infer — the regime is a deterministic function of observed data.
approaches.strengths: Encodes asymmetric mean-reversion (copper often falls faster than it rises, or corrects overvaluation faster than undervaluation) that symmetric ECM/ARIMAX cannot; threshold is observable and testable; M-TAR test has good power vs the standard Engle-Granger no-cointegration test; integrates cleanly with cross-asset cointegration you already compute; supports formal nonlinearity/asymmetry hypothesis tests.
approaches.weaknesses: Abrupt switching can be unrealistic and over-fit a single in-sample threshold; threshold and delay estimates can be unstable out-of-sample; needs enough observations in EACH regime, so weekly data spread thin across regimes weaken estimates; assumes the cointegrating relationship itself is stable (copper's cross-asset relationships drift — e.g. the copper-gold and copper-oil links change with the energy transition); like all these models, in-sample asymmetry does not guarantee out-of-sample point-forecast gains.
approaches.copper_relevance: Ideal for asymmetric error-correction of copper against gold/aluminium/oil/DXY/CNY (your existing cointegration pairs), and for futures-spot or cash-3M basis adjustment. Momentum-threshold (M-TAR) is the canonical tool for testing whether copper futures lead spot asymmetrically, especially under high volatility. Threshold variables that fit copper economics: the error-correction term vs a fair-value anchor, the futures basis/convenience yield, inventory change, or a momentum signal.

key_papers.method: Threshold cointegration: TAR and momentum-TAR (M-TAR) error-correction with asymmetric adjustment; introduces the now-standard asymmetric-cointegration test.
key_papers.citation: Enders, W. & Siklos, P.L. (2001), 'Cointegration and Threshold Adjustment,' Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 19(2), 166-176.
key_papers.finding: Foundational methodology paper. Shows the M-TAR specification (adjustment depends on whether the disequilibrium is rising or falling) has good power relative to the standard Engle-Granger test and provides a formal test for asymmetric error-correction. This is the template that copper/metal basis and cross-asset studies apply; not itself a copper forecasting horse-race.

key_papers.method: Hybrid M-TAR-GARCH (momentum-threshold autoregression in the error-correction term, with GARCH errors) on LME copper futures-vs-spot.
key_papers.citation: Goo & Chen (2020), 'Asymmetric Momentum Threshold Effect of Copper Futures Returns on Spot Returns Volatility in the London Metals Exchange under High Volatility,' Modern Economy 11(1) (SciRP).
key_papers.finding: Finds statistically significant asymmetric momentum-threshold effects: when the lagged error-correction term is below its threshold during high-volatility regimes, LME copper futures returns exert a larger impact on spot-return volatility, and the M-TAR (momentum) effect dominates the plain TAR effect. Headline is asymmetric adjustment under high volatility (an in-sample structural result), not an out-of-sample point forecast beating a random walk.

key_papers.method: Survey/positioning evidence on SETAR/TAR forecasting performance vs linear models.
key_papers.citation: General SETAR/TAR forecasting literature (e.g. Tong's threshold framework; comparative finance studies surveyed in the 'Forecasting: theory and practice' review, arXiv 2012.03854).
key_papers.finding: SETAR/TAR can improve in-sample and sometimes out-of-sample accuracy over ARIMA in specific financial series, but the broad survey view is that threshold models' out-of-sample edge is application-specific and often modest; they were historically the dominant nonlinear tool before being partly displaced by ML. Use as an asymmetry-capturing ECM, not a guaranteed RW-beater.

approaches.name: Smooth-transition autoregression (STAR / LSTAR / ESTAR) and smooth-transition VECM
approaches.one_line: A nonlinear AR in which the regime change is GRADUAL — coefficients move smoothly between two extremes as a transition variable passes through a threshold, governed by a logistic (LSTAR) or exponential (ESTAR) transition function.
approaches.mechanism: y_t = (linear AR part) + G(z_t; gamma, c) x (second AR part), where G is a transition function bounded in [0,1]. In LSTAR, G is logistic in the transition variable z_t (e.g. lagged return, oil price, inflation, ENSO index), giving asymmetric high/low regimes; in ESTAR, G is exponential and symmetric (same behaviour for large positive and large negative deviations, distinct behaviour near equilibrium) — popular for mean-reversion-to-equilibrium stories. Interpretable outputs: the location parameter c (where the transition centres), the smoothness/speed parameter gamma (how abruptly the regime flips — large gamma approaches a TAR/SETAR step), the transition variable choice (an economic narrative for WHAT drives the regime), and the fitted transition weight G(z_t) over time, which you can plot as a continuous 0-1 'regime intensity.' STAR nests linear AR (gamma -> 0) and TAR (gamma -> infinity), so it is testable against both.
approaches.horizon_fit: Most explored at MONTHLY frequency for commodity price levels and for mean-reversion stories. Crucially, the commodity evidence is mixed-to-negative for point forecasting at multistep horizons (see Ubilava 2022 below), so for copper this is better viewed as a flexible diagnostic / density tool than a weekly or monthly mean-forecast workhorse. Weekly STAR on copper returns is rarely compelling.
approaches.interpretability: High in principle: you read off where the transition centres (c), how sharp it is (gamma), and which economic variable drives it (z_t). The continuous transition weight is intuitive ('we are 70% into the high-inflation regime'). Caveat: gamma is notoriously hard to estimate precisely (the likelihood is flat in gamma), so its point estimate is often not reliable even though the regime shape is.
approaches.strengths: Avoids the unrealistic abruptness of TAR by modelling gradual regime change; nests and is testable against both linear AR and TAR; the transition variable can be an exogenous economic driver, giving a clear causal narrative (e.g. regime depends on the USD, inflation, or a demand index); strong fit to nonlinear/asymmetric in-sample dynamics.
approaches.weaknesses: Documented to offer LITTLE or NO out-of-sample point-forecast advantage over plain AR for commodity prices, and sometimes does worse (Ubilava 2022) — a critical honest caveat; gamma is poorly identified; many parameters relative to data (over-fitting risk), worsened at weekly frequency; multi-step forecasting requires simulation/bootstrap (iterated) or many horizon-specific models (direct), adding complexity for little payoff; sensitive to the choice of transition variable.
approaches.copper_relevance: Could let copper's dynamics depend smoothly on an exogenous driver (USD index, real rates, a China activity index, inflation/breakevens, or the futures basis) — e.g. faster mean-reversion when the USD is strong. Smooth-transition VECM is the natural smooth analogue of your cointegration component. But the commodity-forecasting track record means it should be positioned as an interpretability/robustness check rather than a core forecaster.

key_papers.method: Direct vs iterated multistep forecasting with STAR (LSTAR/ESTAR) across many commodity prices.
key_papers.citation: Ubilava, D. (2022), 'A comparison of multistep commodity price forecasts using direct and iterated smooth transition autoregressive methods,' Agricultural Economics 53(5), 687-701.
key_papers.finding: Key honest counter-evidence: across 25 agricultural and non-agricultural commodity prices, even when STAR models appear to fit the nonlinear dynamics well IN-SAMPLE, they offer little advantage and are in most cases INFERIOR to a simple linear AR for multistep out-of-sample forecasting. Strong caution against treating STAR as a default copper forecaster.

key_papers.method: Time-varying STAR with an exogenous transition variable (ENSO sea-surface-temperature anomaly) for commodity price predictability.
key_papers.citation: Ubilava, D. (2018), 'The Role of El Nino Southern Oscillation in Commodity Price Movement and Predictability,' American Journal of Agricultural Economics 100(1), 239-263.
key_papers.finding: Positive but selective: a STAR model with ENSO as the smooth transition variable yields statistically significant out-of-sample predictive gains for tropical AGRICULTURAL commodities (amplified price responses during El Nino), but explicitly NO predictive power for non-agricultural goods such as METALS and timber. Implication for copper: an exogenous-transition STAR works only when there is a genuine nonlinear exogenous driver, which is not established for copper.

key_papers.method: STAR vs linear AR for ENSO dynamics (methodological evidence that STAR can win when nonlinearity is real).
key_papers.citation: Ubilava, D. & Helmers, C.G. (2013), 'Forecasting ENSO with a smooth transition autoregressive model,' Environmental Modelling & Software 40, 181-190 (MPRA 36890).
key_papers.finding: STAR-type nonlinearity in sea-surface-temperature anomalies produces superior out-of-sample forecasts vs linear AR, especially at short-to-intermediate horizons. Establishes that STAR pays off when the underlying process is genuinely smoothly-nonlinear — a condition met for ENSO but, per Ubilava 2018/2022, not clearly met for metal prices.

approaches.name: Time-varying-parameter regression / dynamic model averaging & selection (TVP, DMA/DMS) and structural breaks
approaches.one_line: A regression of copper returns on economic predictors whose coefficients EVOLVE over time (random-walk state-space coefficients), optionally combined with dynamic model averaging that lets both the coefficients and the set of active predictors change adaptively — capturing structural breaks and changing driver relevance.
approaches.mechanism: Coefficients beta_t follow a state-space law of motion (typically a random walk) estimated by the Kalman filter; the conditional forecast is x_t' beta_{t|t-1}. Dynamic Model Averaging (DMA) runs many such TVP regressions over different predictor subsets and forms a time-varying probability weight on each model via a forgetting factor, so the ensemble can 'turn on' inventories in one period and the USD or VIX in another. Dynamic Model Selection (DMS) just picks the highest-probability model each period. Interpretable outputs you can read off: the time path of each coefficient (e.g. industrial production's effect on copper changing sign around 2008), the posterior inclusion probability of each predictor over time (which drivers matter when), and the implied structural breaks. This is the rigorous, probabilistic generalization of your Ridge/ARIMAX-with-exogenous-regressors and a natural complement to your stacking ensemble.
approaches.horizon_fit: Best-evidenced at the MONTHLY horizon for copper (the strongest positive copper result in this whole dimension is monthly TVP/DMA — Buncic & Moretto 2015). Predictability decays but persists to ~6 months. At WEEKLY frequency TVP can still adapt coefficients but the signal-to-noise is lower and the documented copper gains are monthly; weekly use is reasonable for slowly-evolving driver loadings (e.g. COT positioning sensitivity) rather than fast mean prediction.
approaches.interpretability: High and economically rich: you get an explicit, plottable history of how each driver's coefficient and inclusion probability changes — directly answering 'what is driving copper now and how has that shifted.' Structural breaks are visible as coefficient shifts. The main subjective knobs (forgetting factors, state-noise variance) control how fast coefficients move and are themselves interpretable as 'memory length.'
approaches.strengths: Handles structural instability head-on (copper's driver relationships demonstrably change across cycles and with the energy transition); DMA elegantly solves model uncertainty by time-varying averaging instead of committing to one specification; produces built-in time-varying intervals/density forecasts; integrates ALL your copper drivers (inventories, convenience yield/basis, DXY, term spread, VIX/TED risk appetite, IP, COT) and tells you when each matters; has the best documented out-of-sample copper record in the interpretable class.
approaches.weaknesses: Gains are concentrated in turbulent/break periods (e.g. 2008) and can be small or absent in calm markets — so average out-of-sample improvement may look modest; sensitive to forgetting-factor / prior choices; random-walk coefficients can drift spuriously with noisy weekly data; many tuning choices create researcher degrees of freedom; density-forecast gains are typically larger and more robust than point-forecast gains (true across the TVP commodity literature).
approaches.copper_relevance: Arguably the best-fit interpretable nonlinear upgrade for this repo: it directly ingests copper's full driver set and produces an explainable, adaptive picture of which drivers are active. Buncic & Moretto's predictors map almost one-to-one onto your feature set (excess demand, inventories, convenience yield, SP500, VIX, term/TED spreads, industrial production, momentum, FX).

key_papers.method: Dynamic Model Averaging/Selection (DMA/DMS) and simple TVP regression of monthly LME copper returns on 18 economic predictors.
key_papers.citation: Buncic, D. & Moretto, C. (2015), 'Forecasting copper prices with dynamic averaging and selection models,' The North American Journal of Economics and Finance 33, 1-38.
key_papers.finding: Strongest copper-specific positive result in this dimension. Out-of-sample May 2002-June 2014, monthly horizon: DMA improves mean-squared-forecast-error over a random walk by up to ~17% (reported out-of-sample R^2 as high as ~18.5%), and even a simple TVP model gives up to ~5% MSFE improvement. Predictability extends (weaker) to ~6 months. A large part of the gain is realized during the 2008 financial-crisis peak — i.e. concentrated in the high-stress regime. Interpretable mechanism: coefficients on SP500, VIX, the yield spread, the TED spread, industrial production and the convenience yield shift with structural change, with IP and the convenience yield even CHANGING SIGN over the period.

key_papers.method: Time-varying-parameter / comovement model with parameter instability for point and density forecasting of major commodity indices.
key_papers.citation: Allayioti, A. & Venditti, F. (2024), 'The Role of Comovement and Time-Varying Dynamics in Forecasting Commodity Prices,' ECB Working Paper No. 2901.
key_papers.finding: Across ten major commodity indices, exploiting time-varying comovement and parameter instability yields only SMALL point-forecast improvements (varying by horizon and index) but LARGE and statistically significant gains in DENSITY forecasting, and higher portfolio returns/utility for investors. Reinforces the cross-cutting lesson: the value of TVP/regime methods for commodities is mainly in the distribution/intervals and risk, not the conditional mean.

key_papers.method: TVP-SVAR with stochastic volatility decomposing copper price shocks (supply, aggregate demand, copper-specific demand) and their time-varying effects.
key_papers.citation: Time-varying effects of international copper price shocks on China's PPI, Resources Policy (2019), vol. 62, pp. 507-514 (TVP-SVAR-SV).
key_papers.finding: Shows the impact of copper price shocks is genuinely time-varying, with the aggregate-demand shock dominating, and effects strongest at short-to-medium horizons. Establishes (in-sample, structural) that copper's driver relationships are unstable over time — the empirical justification for using TVP rather than constant-coefficient regressions. Not a point-forecast horse-race vs random walk.

findings.evaluation_notes: Standard practice in this literature: (1) Benchmark is almost always the random walk / no-change forecast (RW with or without drift), sometimes also a linear AR(p) or ARIMAX; for copper the RW is a notoriously strong benchmark at short horizons. (2) Point-forecast metrics are out-of-sample MSFE/RMSE and out-of-sample R^2 (1 - MSFE_model/MSFE_RW), often with the Diebold-Mariano or Clark-West test for significance, and rolling/recursive (expanding) windows. (3) Density/interval evaluation (increasingly emphasized) uses log predictive scores, CRPS, and PIT/coverage tests, and tends to show MUCH larger gains for regime/TVP models than point metrics do. (4) Volatility-regime studies use HMSE/QLIKE and the Hansen Model Confidence Set. (5) Recurrent caveat across studies: in-sample nonlinearity tests (LR for MS, threshold tests, STAR linearity tests) are frequently significant even where out-of-sample point forecasts do NOT beat the RW — so in-sample evidence of regimes must not be conflated with forecasting value. Best-practice for the user's repo: evaluate any added regime/TVP model with rolling-origin out-of-sample R^2 vs the existing Naive/RW baseline plus Diebold-Mariano, and separately score interval/density quality (coverage, CRPS) where these models are expected to add the most.
key_takeaways: Interpretable regime/nonlinear models reliably improve IN-SAMPLE fit, volatility, and DENSITY/interval forecasts for copper and base metals, but their OUT-OF-SAMPLE point-forecast edge over a random walk is horizon- and regime-dependent and often small or absent at weekly frequency.

The strongest copper-specific positive result in this class is monthly time-varying-parameter / dynamic-model-averaging regression: Buncic & Moretto (2015) report up to ~17% MSFE improvement (DMA) and ~5% (simple TVP) over a random walk on LME copper, with the gain concentrated in the 2008 crisis regime and interpretable sign-changing coefficients on industrial production and the convenience yield. This maps almost one-to-one onto the repo's existing driver set and is the most promising addition.

Markov-switching AR/VAR is the natural upgrade to the repo's existing 3-state Gaussian HMM: add autoregressive terms and exogenous copper drivers (MS-ARX/MSVAR) so regimes carry mean dynamics and driver effects, and read off named high-vol/low-vol or bull/bear states, transition probabilities, expected durations, and a smoothed 'which-regime-now' probability for risk/ensemble weighting.

Momentum-threshold error-correction (M-TAR, Enders-Siklos 2001) is the most transparent and copper-relevant asymmetric upgrade to the repo's existing Engle-Granger cointegration component: it lets copper mean-revert to its gold/aluminium/oil/DXY/CNY anchor at DIFFERENT speeds depending on the sign or momentum of the deviation, with an observable threshold and a formal asymmetry test. Goo & Chen (2020) document exactly such asymmetric momentum-threshold effects in LME copper futures-vs-spot under high volatility.

STAR/LSTAR/ESTAR is the weakest forecasting bet for copper despite high interpretability: Ubilava (2022) shows STAR is mostly INFERIOR to a simple AR for multistep commodity point forecasts, and Ubilava (2018) finds exogenous-transition STAR helps tropical agricultural commodities but explicitly NOT metals. Treat STAR as a diagnostic/robustness overlay, not a core forecaster.

Evaluate any new regime/TVP component against the repo's Naive/RW baseline with rolling-origin out-of-sample R^2 + Diebold-Mariano for the mean, AND separately with coverage/CRPS for intervals/density — because these models tend to win on the distribution and on risk-regime tagging more than on the conditional mean, especially at the 5d weekly horizon.

Black-box contrast only: tree ensembles (random forests, gradient boosting) have been shown to beat regression trees and sometimes the RW for copper, but they sacrifice the regime/coefficient interpretability that is the entire value proposition here; keep them as complements (as the repo already does with XGBoost/LightGBM), not as the explainable core.

findings.dimension: Bayesian & model-averaging methods (BVAR, Bayesian Model Averaging, Dynamic Model Averaging/Selection, forecast combination, BSTS/Prophet) for forecasting copper and analogous commodity prices at weekly and monthly horizons
findings.overview: This family sits squarely in the "interpretable" camp the user cares about: every method here exposes something a human can read — shrunk VAR coefficients and impulse responses (BVAR), posterior inclusion probabilities (BMA, BSTS), time-varying model/predictor weights (DMA/DMS), or transparent combination weights (forecast combination). The central empirical fact across the commodity-forecasting literature is that beating a random walk (RW) out-of-sample is genuinely hard, and the methods that do so most reliably are the ones that pool information and let importance shift over time rather than committing to a single fixed specification. The strongest copper-specific result is Buncic & Moretto (2015, N. Am. J. Econ. & Finance), who forecast MONTHLY LME copper returns with Dynamic Model Averaging/Selection over 18 economically-motivated predictors and report out-of-sample R-squared vs RW as high as ~18.5% (their working-paper framing also cites up to ~17% MSFE improvement), with predictability persisting to 6 months. For copper VOLATILITY (a different target), Diaz, Hansen & Cabrera (2021, Resources Policy) use Bayesian Model Averaging and find several economic variables beat an AR benchmark, with predictability varying over the business cycle; Li & Li (2015, Resources Policy) reach a similar conclusion for copper futures volatility under model uncertainty via OLS time-varying model averaging. For the broader system view, the World Bank's model suite (Arroyo Marioli, Khadan, Ohnsorge & Yamazaki, 2023, PRWP 10611) explicitly includes a Bayesian VAR among six approaches for oil and six industrial metals including copper, and concludes futures/bivariate correlations win at short horizons while consensus and large macro-models win long, with BVAR's value lying in scenario generation and uncertainty bands. The forecast-combination literature (Stock-Watson's "forecast combination puzzle"; Genre et al. ECB) is the crucial cautionary backdrop: sophisticated optimal weighting rarely and not durably beats the simple equal-weighted average once you account for estimation error and multiple-comparison bias — directly relevant to how the user should weight an ensemble. Most of this work is MONTHLY; genuine WEEKLY copper studies with these exact methods are thin, so weekly conclusions are largely extrapolated from monthly evidence and from the general principle that macro/fundamental predictors carry little signal at weekly frequency.

approaches.name: Dynamic Model Averaging / Dynamic Model Selection (DMA/DMS)
approaches.one_line: Runs many small time-varying-parameter regressions in parallel and recursively reweights them by recent predictive performance, so both the coefficients AND the set of active predictors drift over time.
approaches.mechanism: Built on the Koop-Korobilis (2012) framework: each candidate model is a TVP regression updated by a Kalman filter; two 'forgetting factors' (lambda for state evolution, alpha for model weights) let coefficients and model probabilities decay toward recent data instead of being re-estimated by MCMC, making it fast. DMA averages forecasts across models weighted by their recursively-updated posterior model probabilities; DMS just picks the single highest-probability model each period. What is directly interpretable: (1) the time path of each predictor's posterior inclusion probability — you can literally plot when 'inventories' or 'the convenience yield' mattered and when they stopped; (2) the time-varying regression coefficients themselves; (3) which model DMS selects at each date. This is the method whose interpretability matches the user's HMM regime story most naturally.
approaches.horizon_fit: Designed for and validated at MONTHLY frequency, which is its best fit for copper — the predictor importance shifting around the 2008 crisis is exactly the structural-break behaviour it captures. For WEEKLY copper it is usable mechanically but weaker in spirit: most of its informative predictors (industrial production, excess demand, term spread) are monthly/lower-frequency, so at 5d horizon you'd be averaging mostly financial/momentum predictors and the edge over RW shrinks. No strong weekly-copper DMA study was located, so weekly use is an extrapolation.
approaches.interpretability: Very high and uniquely dynamic: posterior inclusion probabilities as a time series, time-varying coefficients, and the selected model path are all human-readable. You can answer 'what is the model paying attention to right now and why' — something neither XGBoost nor a static regression gives you.
approaches.strengths: Handles structural breaks and parameter instability natively; reduces overfitting vs throwing all predictors into one regression; unifies model averaging + time-varying parameters in one fast (non-MCMC) recursion; documented to beat RW out-of-sample on monthly copper. Naturally produces a predictive density, not just a point.
approaches.weaknesses: Sensitive to the choice of forgetting factors (alpha, lambda) — these are tuning knobs that can be over-fit; model space grows as 2^k so predictor sets must be kept modest; assumes linear-Gaussian state space so it won't capture sharp nonlinear squeeze/backwardation dynamics; gains are concentrated in turbulent periods (crisis) and can be thin in calm regimes; relies on RW being the benchmark, and the edge can be modest in MSFE terms even when statistically present.
approaches.copper_relevance: Excellent fit. Buncic & Moretto explicitly use LME copper data with copper-fundamental predictors — excess demand, LME inventories, convenience yield — alongside global risk appetite (VIX), S&P 500, TED spread, yield/term spread, industrial production, and momentum. This maps almost one-to-one onto the user's existing feature set (CFTC COT positioning, real yields, cross-asset ratios, China IP proxy). The SHFE/COMEX/LME inventory and futures-basis (convenience yield) inputs the user can source are precisely the fundamentals DMA found informative.

Demonstrates the DMA edge transfers across commodities, though exact RW margins are not stated in the abstract.

approaches.name: Bayesian Model Averaging (BMA) over predictor sets
approaches.one_line: Averages forecasts across all (or many) subsets of candidate predictors, weighting each model by its posterior probability, so no single predictor set is trusted and each variable gets a posterior inclusion probability.
approaches.mechanism: Treats the choice of which predictors enter the regression as itself uncertain. Each model = one subset of regressors; BMA computes posterior model probabilities (via marginal likelihoods, often with Zellner g-priors) and forms a weighted-average prediction. The headline interpretable output is the Posterior Inclusion Probability (PIP) per variable — the total posterior weight of all models containing it — plus posterior means/SDs of coefficients averaged over model uncertainty. Unlike DMA the weights are static over the estimation window (no time-varying state), making it simpler but less able to track regime shifts.
approaches.horizon_fit: Used at MONTHLY frequency in the copper studies (both copper applications target monthly copper VOLATILITY, not price level). For monthly copper price/return forecasting it is a reasonable, more conservative cousin of DMA. For WEEKLY copper it is less compelling because its fundamental predictors are low-frequency and its static weights can't exploit the fast regime turnover that dominates weekly moves.
approaches.interpretability: High but static: PIPs tell you which predictors robustly matter on average over the sample, and posterior coefficient densities give signs/magnitudes with proper model-uncertainty-inflated error bars. You lose the 'when did it matter' time dimension that DMA provides.
approaches.strengths: Principled handling of model uncertainty and 'which features matter' — directly answers a question the user's XGBoost importance scores answer only opaquely; robust to including many weak predictors; produces honest predictive intervals; combination forecasts shown to beat single-model and AR benchmarks for copper volatility.
approaches.weaknesses: Static weights miss structural breaks (the copper studies themselves note predictability varies across the business cycle, which static BMA captures only as an average); sensitive to the g-prior / model-prior choice; assumes linear regression; for the price LEVEL (vs volatility) the documented copper evidence is thinner than for DMA; can be computationally heavy if the predictor set is large and you enumerate all subsets.
approaches.copper_relevance: Strong and well-evidenced for copper. Diaz, Hansen & Cabrera (2021) sort 23 predictors into copper-industry fundamentals, economic-uncertainty, and financial groups — the same three buckets the user already has (COT positioning, breakevens/real yields, cross-asset). PIPs would tell the user which of their FRED/EIA/Alpha-Vantage/COT features are doing real work.
