key_papers.method: Bayesian Model Averaging over 23 predictors (copper fundamentals, uncertainty, financial) for MONTHLY copper price volatility; benchmark = autoregressive model.
key_papers.finding: Several economic variables have significant out-of-sample forecasting power and BMA combination forecasts conclusively outperform the AR benchmark while reducing forecast uncertainty; predictability varies across the business cycle. (Target is volatility, not the price level — relevant for the user's interval/quantile components.)

key_papers.citation: Li, G. & Li, Y. (2015), 'Forecasting copper futures volatility under model uncertainty', Resources Policy, 46(P2), 167-176.
key_papers.method: Model averaging (incl. OLS time-varying weighted averaging) across GARCH-class models for copper futures volatility; multiple loss functions.
key_papers.finding: OLS time-varying weighted model averaging achieves the smallest forecasting error and significantly reduces over-prediction versus individual GARCH-type models — a model-averaging win for copper volatility under uncertainty. Not a price-level result.

approaches.name: Bayesian VAR with Minnesota / shrinkage priors (BVAR)
approaches.one_line: A multivariate VAR linking copper to its macro/cross-asset system, where a Minnesota-style prior shrinks coefficients toward a random walk to tame the parameter explosion, yielding stable forecasts, impulse responses and scenario fans.
approaches.mechanism: Litterman/Sims Minnesota prior centres each equation on a random walk and shrinks longer lags and cross-variable coefficients harder, with one or two hyperparameters controlling overall shrinkage. The estimable, interpretable objects are the (shrunk) coefficient matrices, impulse-response functions (how a USD or China-IP shock propagates to copper), forecast-error variance decompositions, and — crucially for a metals desk — coherent multi-variable scenario forecasts with credible bands. Banbura, Giannone & Reichlin (2010) showed large BVARs can forecast well precisely because the prior prevents overfitting.
approaches.horizon_fit: Best at MONTHLY (and quarterly) frequency where the macro system it models actually moves; this is how the World Bank suite deploys it for copper and other metals. At WEEKLY frequency a macro BVAR is poorly suited — IP, inventories and real rates barely move week to week — though a smaller financial-only weekly VAR (copper, DXY, gold, oil, equities) is conceivable but not well-documented for copper specifically.
approaches.interpretability: High in the structural-economics sense: signed, shrunk coefficients; IRFs and variance decompositions you can narrate ('most copper forecast variance at 12m is own-price + global activity'); and explicit scenario fans. Less 'feature-importance' oriented than BMA/DMA but far more transparent than any ML model.
approaches.strengths: Captures the joint dynamics and feedback among copper and its drivers rather than treating them as static exogenous features; shrinkage gives stable, well-calibrated density forecasts; excellent for conditional/scenario forecasting ('if DXY rises 5% and China IP slows, where does copper go'); handles many variables without blowing up. In oil, Bayesian shrinkage VARs have produced sizeable RW-beating gains at short horizons (e.g. ~30% MSPE reduction at 1 month, ~20% at 3 months in real-oil-price VARs), with gains fading past ~12 months.
approaches.weaknesses: Linear and (in basic form) constant-parameter — misses the regime shifts the user's HMM targets unless extended to TVP/stochastic-volatility BVAR; forecast edge over RW for metals is horizon-dependent and contested (recent replications find oil VAR gains over RW are fragile in real time); requires clean, aligned, vintage-aware macro data (revisions matter); choice of variables and shrinkage hyperparameters drives results; for copper specifically the published RW-beating evidence is weaker than the DMA result, with the World Bank suite positioning BVAR more for scenarios/uncertainty than for point-forecast superiority.
approaches.copper_relevance: Natural home for the user's cross-asset and macro block: copper, gold, aluminium, oil, DXY, CNY, real yields, breakevens, China IP all become endogenous variables, and LME/SHFE inventories or the futures basis can enter as well. This is the one method here that directly models the cointegration-style cross-asset relationships the user currently handles with Engle-Granger ECM — a BVAR (or BVECM) is the multivariate Bayesian generalisation of that component.

key_papers.citation: Arroyo Marioli, F., Khadan, J., Ohnsorge, F. & Yamazaki, T. (2023), 'Forecasting Industrial Commodity Prices: Literature Review and a Model Suite', World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 10611.
key_papers.method: Six-approach model suite (incl. a Bayesian VAR, futures-based, bivariate correlations, consensus forecasts, a large macroeconometric model) for oil and six industrial metals including COPPER; benchmark includes random walk/futures.
key_papers.finding: No single model dominates: futures prices and bivariate correlations forecast best at short horizons, consensus and the large macro-model best at long horizons; the BVAR's distinctive value is generating coherent forecast scenarios and the wide error bands underscore deep price uncertainty. Tempers any claim that a BVAR cleanly beats RW for copper.

key_papers.citation: Banbura, M., Giannone, D. & Reichlin, L. (2010), 'Large Bayesian vector auto regressions', Journal of Applied Econometrics, 25(1), 71-92.
key_papers.method: Large BVARs with Minnesota-type shrinkage; macro forecasting (methodological benchmark for shrinkage priors).
key_papers.finding: With appropriate prior shrinkage, large BVARs forecast at least as well as, and often better than, small VARs and factor models — establishing why Minnesota-prior shrinkage is the workhorse for many-variable commodity systems. Not a copper paper; cited for the prior mechanism.

key_papers.citation: Baumeister, C. & Kilian, L. (and subsequent real-time reappraisals, e.g. Benyo et al. 2026, Economic Inquiry), real-price-of-oil VAR forecasting literature.
key_papers.method: Reduced-form / Bayesian VARs for the real price of oil with global activity, production and inventory variables; benchmark = random walk and futures.
key_papers.finding: Original work reported VARs beating the RW at short horizons (MSPE reductions ~32% at 1m, ~22% at 3m) with gains dissipating beyond a year; later real-time replications find these RW improvements are not consistently significant — a key caution that headline VAR gains can be fragile out of sample. Oil, not copper, but the canonical cautionary evidence for commodity VARs.

approaches.name: Forecast combination (Bates-Granger, Granger-Ramanathan, and the 'forecast combination puzzle')
approaches.one_line: Combine the user's existing model forecasts into one, where the robust empirical lesson is that a simple equal-weighted average is very hard to beat out-of-sample — the directly relevant guidance for the repo's ensemble layer.
approaches.mechanism: Bates-Granger (1969) derive variance-minimising weights from the forecast error covariance; Granger-Ramanathan recast combination as a regression of the realised target on the component forecasts (optimal least-squares weights, possibly with intercept/unconstrained). The interpretable object is the weight vector itself — you can read off how much each model (Ridge, ARIMAX, Prophet, cointegration, HMM, quantile, XGBoost) contributes. The 'puzzle', named by Stock & Watson, is that these theoretically-optimal estimated weights routinely fail to beat the naive 1/N average once estimation error in the weights is accounted for.
approaches.horizon_fit: Horizon-agnostic and directly applicable at WEEKLY and MONTHLY copper alike — it operates on whatever component forecasts the repo already produces, so it inherits each component's horizon. This is the single most immediately actionable item for the user's existing 'weighted + stacking' ensemble.
approaches.interpretability: Maximal and model-level: the weights are the explanation. Equal weights are trivially transparent; regression-based weights show each model's marginal contribution and can flag redundant or harmful components (negative weights). This is strictly more interpretable than stacking with a black-box meta-learner.
approaches.strengths: Cheap, robust, and consistently competitive; diversifies away individual-model error and structural-break risk; equal-weighting needs no estimation so it can't overfit the weights; well-suited to combining the user's heterogeneous interpretable models. Strong theory + decades of forecasting-competition evidence behind it.
approaches.weaknesses: Estimated optimal weights (Granger-Ramanathan, performance-based, Bayesian-shrinkage weights) are prone to overfitting and multiple-comparison bias — Genre et al. show apparent gains over the simple average often don't survive a reality check; combination can't help if all components share the same blind spot; equal weighting ignores genuine, persistent skill differences. The user's STACKING ensemble is exactly the kind of estimated-weight scheme the puzzle warns may not beat a plain average out-of-sample.
approaches.copper_relevance: Indirect but high-leverage: it is the meta-layer over the copper-specific components. It doesn't add new copper data itself, but it governs how the repo blends its copper RW baseline, ARIMAX-with-exog, cointegration-ECM, Prophet, HMM and ML forecasts — and the literature says benchmark any fancy weighting against simple averaging and trimmed means.

key_papers.citation: Stock, J. H. & Watson, M. W. (2004), 'Combination forecasts of output growth in a seven-country data set', Journal of Forecasting, 23(6), 405-430.
key_papers.method: Combination of many predictor-based forecasts (simple average, discounted, shrinkage) for output growth; AR benchmark.
key_papers.finding: Individual predictor forecasts are unstable and on average beat by an AR benchmark, yet combinations — especially the simple mean — improve on the AR benchmark and are the least sensitive to recent performance. Coined the 'forecast combination puzzle' that simple averages are not systematically beaten by sophisticated weighting.

key_papers.citation: Genre, V., Kenny, G., Meyler, A. & Timmermann, A. (2013), 'Combining expert forecasts: Can anything beat the simple average?', International Journal of Forecasting, 29(1), 108-121 (ECB WP 1277, 2010).
key_papers.method: Principal-components, trimmed means, performance-weighting, least-squares optimal weights and Bayesian shrinkage applied to the ECB Survey of Professional Forecasters; benchmark = equal-weighted average.
key_papers.finding: Only a few schemes beat the simple average for GDP and unemployment (stronger for inflation), and after White's reality-check correction for multiple comparisons the apparent improvements are not reliable going forward — i.e. don't assume estimated weights will beat 1/N. Directly cautions the user's stacking layer.

key_papers.citation: Bates, J. M. & Granger, C. W. J. (1969), 'The combination of forecasts', Operational Research Quarterly, 20(4), 451-468 (foundational; located via the combination literature, not separately fetched).
key_papers.method: Variance-minimising linear combination of two forecasts using their error covariance.
key_papers.finding: Establishes that combining forecasts can yield lower error variance than either component — the theoretical origin of forecast combination. Cited as the mechanism; specific empirical numbers not re-verified here.

approaches.name: Bayesian Structural Time Series (BSTS) and Prophet
approaches.one_line: Decompose the series into interpretable additive components (local level/trend + seasonality + a regression block), with BSTS adding a spike-and-slab prior that does Bayesian variable selection on regressors and yields full predictive densities; Prophet is a faster, simpler curve-fitting cousin.
approaches.mechanism: BSTS (Scott & Varian) is a state-space model: a structural part (local linear trend, seasonal dummies/harmonics) plus a regression component whose coefficients carry a spike-and-slab prior, which both selects predictors (posterior inclusion probabilities) and shrinks the rest to exactly zero, all sampled by MCMC to give genuine posterior predictive intervals. Prophet (Facebook) is a related but non-MCMC additive model — piecewise-linear/logistic trend with automatic changepoints + Fourier seasonality + holiday effects, fit by MAP — marketed as a 'Bayesian structural time series'-style decomposition. Interpretable outputs: the trend and changepoint locations, the seasonal shape, and (BSTS) the regressor PIPs.
approaches.horizon_fit: Prophet/BSTS shine where trend+seasonality+calendar structure dominate; copper has weak, unstable seasonality, so the seasonal block adds little. At MONTHLY horizon BSTS's regression+spike-slab block (driven by copper fundamentals/macro) is the useful part and is interpretable; at WEEKLY horizon the trend/changepoint machinery can track momentum but the literature consensus is that Prophet is quick and easy but considerably less accurate than ARIMA/ML on volatile financial series like copper. The user already runs Prophet, so this row is mostly about realistic expectations and the BSTS upgrade path.
approaches.interpretability: High and component-wise: you can plot the estimated trend, the changepoints, and the seasonality separately, and (BSTS) read regressor inclusion probabilities — the same PIP transparency as BMA but inside a structural-time-series wrapper with built-in intervals.
approaches.strengths: Clean component decomposition; automatic, robust handling of changepoints/holidays (Prophet) with minimal tuning; BSTS gives principled posterior predictive intervals and spike-and-slab variable selection in one model; both are easy to deploy and explain to non-specialists. BSTS subsumes much of what Prophet does but with proper Bayesian uncertainty.
approaches.weaknesses: On volatile, weakly-seasonal commodity prices both tend to underperform ARIMAX/ML on point accuracy (documented for copper-type series); Prophet's intervals are often poorly calibrated and it can overfit changepoints; the additive structural assumption misses nonlinear regime/volatility dynamics; without an informative regression block they reduce to a fancy trend-follower that a random walk can match at short horizons. BSTS MCMC is slower and needs care at weekly frequency.
approaches.copper_relevance: Moderate. The structural/seasonal block is weak for copper, but the BSTS regression-with-spike-and-slab block can ingest the same copper drivers (inventories, USD, real yields, China IP, COT positioning, futures basis) and report which ones the model includes — giving the user PIP-style interpretability inside their existing Prophet slot. Best viewed as an interpretable upgrade from Prophet to BSTS rather than a new data source.

key_papers.citation: Scott, S. L. & Varian, H. R. (2014), 'Predicting the present with Bayesian structural time series', International Journal of Mathematical Modelling and Numerical Optimisation, 5(1/2), 4-23.
key_papers.method: Structural time series (local trend + seasonal) plus a regression component with a spike-and-slab prior for Bayesian variable selection; MCMC; applied to nowcasting initial unemployment claims and retail sales with search-query predictors.
key_papers.finding: The spike-and-slab prior induces sparsity (many coefficients exactly zero) and the ensemble averages over predictor combinations, improving short-term nowcasts while exposing which predictors are included via posterior inclusion probabilities. Establishes BSTS's interpretable variable-selection mechanism; not a copper study.

key_papers.citation: Taylor, S. J. & Letham, B. (2018), 'Forecasting at scale' (Prophet), The American Statistician, 72(1), 37-45 (method reference; corroborated via comparative studies below).
key_papers.method: Additive decomposable model: piecewise trend with automatic changepoints + Fourier seasonality + holidays, fit by MAP.
key_papers.finding: Provides fast, analyst-friendly, decomposable forecasts; comparative studies on financial/commodity series (e.g. ARIMA-vs-Prophet-vs-LSTM reviews and copper-focused hybrids) find Prophet quick and easy but considerably less accurate than ARIMA/LSTM on volatile series like copper, so it is typically used as a component or wrapped in hybrids rather than a standalone copper forecaster.

findings.evaluation_notes: The standard yardstick throughout is out-of-sample point accuracy against a no-change RANDOM WALK (for price levels) or an AR/GARCH benchmark (for volatility), measured by MSFE/MSPE ratios, out-of-sample R-squared (1 minus MSFE-ratio), and Theil's U; statistical significance via Diebold-Mariano / Clark-West tests, and — importantly in the combination literature — White's Reality Check / SPA tests to guard against data-snooping when many schemes are compared (Genre et al.). Best practice in these papers is a rolling/recursive (pseudo-real-time) out-of-sample window, and the oil literature stresses vintage/real-time data because retrospective gains over RW often shrink or vanish in genuine real time (Baumeister-Kilian reappraisals). Bayesian methods are additionally judged on density-forecast calibration (log predictive scores, CRPS, PITs), not just point error — a relevant criterion given the user's interval/quantile components. Horizon reporting is almost always MONTHLY (1, 3, 6, 12 months); credible WEEKLY copper evaluations with these exact methods are scarce, so weekly claims should be treated as extrapolations and validated in-repo.
key_takeaways: The single most directly relevant copper result is Buncic & Moretto (2015): Dynamic Model Averaging/Selection on MONTHLY LME copper returns beat a random walk out-of-sample with R-squared up to ~18.5% (and gains to 6 months), using exactly the kind of fundamental + financial predictors the repo already has. This is the strongest evidence-backed interpretable add for the monthly horizon.

DMA/DMS is the best interpretability-for-copper match because its posterior inclusion probabilities and time-varying weights are a TIME SERIES — you can show when inventories vs the dollar vs positioning drove copper — complementing the existing HMM regime detector rather than duplicating it.

Bayesian Model Averaging is well-validated for copper but in the published work it targets VOLATILITY (Diaz-Hansen-Cabrera 2021; Li-Li 2015), not the price level; deploy it for the repo's interval/quantile block and for feature-importance transparency (PIPs), not as the primary point forecaster.

A Bayesian VAR (Minnesota prior) is the natural multivariate generalisation of the repo's Engle-Granger cointegration component: make copper/gold/aluminium/oil/DXY/CNY/real-yields endogenous and read off impulse responses and scenario fans. But the World Bank suite and oil-VAR reappraisals caution that BVAR's edge over RW for metals is horizon-dependent and fragile in real time — its surest value is scenarios and well-calibrated uncertainty bands, not guaranteed point-forecast wins.

The forecast-combination puzzle (Stock-Watson; Genre et al.) is the most actionable governance lesson: benchmark the repo's STACKING ensemble against a simple equal-weighted (and trimmed-mean) average, because estimated 'optimal' weights frequently fail to beat 1/N out-of-sample once estimation error and multiple-comparison bias are accounted for.

All these methods are macro/fundamental in spirit and were validated MONTHLY; at the WEEKLY horizon their fundamental predictors carry little signal, so expect the random walk to be much harder to beat and lean on financial/momentum/positioning predictors and on robust combination at 5d.

BSTS is the principled, interpretable upgrade path from the repo's existing Prophet slot: same component decomposition plus spike-and-slab variable selection (PIPs) and proper posterior predictive intervals; but on volatile copper both are weak standalone point forecasters and are best used as components or for the trend/seasonality/changepoint decomposition.

Deep nets / opaque tree ensembles only sometimes edge out these reduced-form models and only at the very shortest horizons (World Bank review), at the cost of all interpretability — reinforcing that the Bayesian/averaging family is the right backbone when explanation matters.

checked_claims.claim: Buncic & Moretto (2015), 'Forecasting copper prices with dynamic averaging and selection models', North American Journal of Economics and Finance, 33, 1-38 — uses DMA/DMS over 18 predictors for monthly LME copper returns, OOS R2 vs random walk as high as ~18.5%, predictability up to 6 months, gains concentrated in the 2008 crisis.
checked_claims.note: Fully verified against the St. Gallen WP abstract (ideas.repec.org/p/usg/econwp/201430.html) and the SSRN/published record. Abstract states 'a total of 18 predictor variables', OOS period 'May 2002 to June 2014', 'out-of-sample R2 (relative to a random walk benchmark) can be as high as 18.5 percent for the DMA framework', predictability 'up to 6 months ahead' (weaker than 1-month), and 'a large part of the improvement... is realised during the peak of the financial crisis period at the end of 2008'. Venue, vol 33, pp 1-38 all correct. The finding's parenthetical that the working paper 'also cites up to ~17% MSFE improvement' is consistent — a search summary reported a 17% MSFE figure alongside the 18.5% R2; both framings trace to the same paper. The '~5% for a simple TVP model' figure was not visible in the abstract but is plausible and not contradicted.

checked_claims.claim: Diaz, Hansen & Cabrera (2021), 'Economic drivers of commodity volatility: The case of copper', Resources Policy, 73, 102134 — BMA over predictors for MONTHLY copper VOLATILITY (not price level); several economic variables beat an AR benchmark; predictability varies over the business cycle.
checked_claims.note: Verified via RePEc/ScienceDirect. Authors Juan D. Diaz, Erwin Hansen, Gabriel Cabrera; Resources Policy vol 73 (2021); uses Bayesian Model Averaging for monthly copper price VOLATILITY; finds several economic variables have significant out-of-sample forecasting power vs an AR benchmark and predictability varies across the business cycle. The finding correctly flags that the target is volatility, not price level. The specific count of '23 predictors' was not confirmed in the abstract text seen but is consistent with the paper's framing; treat as plausible/unverified-exact.

Model averaging across GARCH-class models for copper futures volatility, OLS time-varying weighting most effective. Accurately represented; correctly flagged as a volatility (not price-level) result.

checked_claims.note: Verified via Inderscience/Google Research. Correct venue (Int. J. Mathematical Modelling and Numerical Optimisation), vol 5, issue 1/2, pp 4-23, 2014. checked_claims.note: Verified via RePEc/Taylor & Francis. Correct venue, vol 72(1), pp 37-45, 2018, DOI 10.1080/00031305.2017.1380080. Decomposable model with interpretable parameters confirmed. Minor over-precision in the finding: Prophet is implemented in Stan and supports MAP or full MCMC; describing fitting strictly 'by MAP' is the default but not the only mode, and 'marketed as a Bayesian-structural-time-series-style decomposition' is loose — the authors describe it as a decomposable/GAM model, not as BSTS. Does not affect the substantive comparison.

checked_claims.claim: Naser (2016), 'Estimating and forecasting the real prices of crude oil: A data rich model using a dynamic model averaging (DMA) approach', Energy Economics, 56, 75-87 — DMA outperforms alternatives and beats futures as a proxy for expected spot; data favour model variation over parameter variation.
checked_claims.note: Verified via RePEc/ScienceDirect. Correct venue, vol 56, pp 75-87, 2016. WTI real oil, monthly Mar 1983-Dec 2011; DMA outperforms alternatives, better than futures, 'model but not parameter variation' — exactly as the finding states. The finding's caveat that exact RW margins are not in the abstract is honest and correct.

checked_claims.claim: Drachal (2017), 'Forecasting Spot Oil Price Using Google Probabilities', PMLR — DMA/DMS with Google-search and macro predictors; superior out-of-sample performance vs random walk/futures; value in readable PIP/weight paths.
checked_claims.note: Verified via PMLR (proceedings.mlr.press/v58/drachal17a). Monthly WTI 2004-2015; even unmodified DMA beats futures and naive forecasts; adding Google searches gives slightly better forecasts with small weight. Accurately represented. Venue framing ('PMLR / J. of Forecasting-adjacent') is slightly loose but the cited PMLR paper is real and correctly described.

checked_claims.claim: Baumeister & Kilian real-oil-price VAR: original work reported VARs beating the RW at short horizons with 'MSPE reductions ~32% at 1m, ~22% at 3m', gains dissipating beyond a year; later real-time replications (e.g. Benyo et al. 2026, Economic Inquiry) find these RW improvements are not consistently significant.
checked_claims.note: PARTIALLY WRONG ON THE NUMBERS. Baumeister & Kilian (2012, 'Real-Time Forecasts of the Real Price of Oil', Bank of Canada WP 11-16 / IJF) report real-time MSPE reductions vs the no-change forecast of 'as high as 25 percent' at 1 month and '24 percent' at 3 months — NOT 32% and 22%. Verified directly from the abstract. The 32%/22% pair appears to be a misremembered/misattributed figure (it does not match this canonical source). The qualitative claims are correct and verified: short-horizon VAR gains over the RW that fade beyond ~1 year, and the Benyo (2026) Economic Inquiry reappraisal does exist and questions the real-time robustness of these gains. So the citation and the cautionary narrative are sound; only the specific percentages are wrong.

checked_claims.claim: Overview/mechanism: DMA is 'built on the Koop-Korobilis (2012) framework' with two forgetting factors (lambda for states, alpha for model weights), Kalman-filter TVP regressions, non-MCMC.
checked_claims.note: Mechanism description is accurate. Minor attribution nuance: DMA originates with Raftery, Karny & Ettler (2010) in engineering and was brought into econometrics by Koop & Korobilis (2012, International Economic Review, 'Forecasting inflation using dynamic model averaging'); the Nonejad (2021, J. Economic Surveys 35(2), 566-614) survey cited in sources confirms the Koop-Korobilis lineage. Calling it 'the Koop-Korobilis framework' is conventional shorthand and acceptable.

checked_claims.claim: Interpretability claims: DMA/DMS expose posterior inclusion probabilities as a time series and time-varying coefficients (human-readable); BMA gives static PIPs; BVAR gives IRFs/variance decompositions; combination weights are the explanation; BSTS gives spike-and-slab PIPs. These are described as genuinely interpretable vs black-box ML.
checked_claims.note: These interpretability characterisations are technically correct and not overstated. PIPs, time-varying coefficients, IRFs, FEVDs and combination weights are all genuinely human-readable objects, materially more transparent than tree-ensemble/NN feature attributions. No misleading 'interpretable-but-actually-black-box' claims detected in this dimension. The Prophet/BSTS component decomposition is correctly described as interpretable.

checked_claims.claim: Weekly-horizon claims are extrapolations: genuine weekly copper studies with these exact methods are thin, fundamental predictors carry little signal weekly, so the random walk is harder to beat at 5d.
checked_claims.note: This is an appropriately hedged, honest characterisation. The verified copper studies (Buncic-Moretto, Diaz-Hansen-Cabrera, Li-Li) are all MONTHLY, and the World Bank suite is monthly+; no weekly-copper DMA/BMA/BVAR study surfaced in searches. The finding explicitly labels weekly conclusions as extrapolations to be validated in-repo, which is the correct epistemic stance.

It is plausible as a synthesis of the broader literature but should not be attributed specifically to the World Bank review without checking the full text; treat as weakly supported.

findings.dimension: Commodity-finance theory & futures-based forecasting (theory of storage, convenience yield, term structure/basis, hedging pressure, risk premium, structural supply-demand models) for forecasting COPPER (COMEX HG / LME) at weekly and monthly horizons — interpretable models only
findings.overview: This dimension is the part of the commodity-forecasting literature where economic theory is most explicit and most interpretable, and it is also where the benchmarks are most humbling. Two foundational frameworks anchor it. (1) The theory of storage (Working 1949; Kaldor; Brennan; formalised empirically by Fama-French 1987, 1988) links the futures-spot basis to the cost of carry minus a convenience yield, and predicts that the convenience yield is a decreasing, convex function of inventories — so the basis (contango vs backwardation) is a readable state variable for scarcity. (2) The theory of normal backwardation / hedging-pressure (Keynes 1930; Cootner; Hirshleifer; Bessembinder; Basu-Miffre 2013) treats futures as a risk-transfer market in which speculators earn a premium for absorbing hedgers' price risk, making the sign/size of net positioning (CFTC COT) a predictor of the futures risk premium. Gorton-Hayashi-Rouwenhorst (2007) unify the two: inventories drive both the basis and the risk premium, and price-based proxies (basis, momentum, prior returns) carry the same information when inventory data are missing. For COPPER specifically, the most important empirical fact is that the futures curve and the random walk (no-change) forecast are very strong benchmarks that most models fail to beat out-of-sample at short horizons. The Reeve-Vigfusson (Fed, 2011) and World Bank (Arroyo-Marioli, Khadan, Ohnsorge, Yamazaki 2023) studies find copper futures roughly tie or modestly underperform a random walk for level forecasts at 3-12 months, though futures help conditionally when the basis is large and add directional/scenario value. The strongest credible copper-specific OOS result for an interpretable model is Buncic-Moretto (2015), whose dynamic model averaging over fundamental + financial predictors (including convenience yield and inventories) beats the random walk at monthly horizons (OOS R^2 up to ~18.5% one-step-ahead). Factor models (carry/basis, momentum, basis-momentum; Koijen et al. 2018; Boons-Prado 2019) are cross-sectional and interpretable but are designed to rank a basket of commodities for relative-value returns, not to produce a copper level/return forecast — useful as a feature source rather than a standalone copper forecaster. Structural supply-demand balance models (mine supply, scrap, China consumption, inventories; IMF/World Bank/ICSG-style) are the most economically transparent but are data-lagged, hard to estimate at weekly/monthly frequency, and better at 1-3+ year horizons than at the user's weekly/monthly cadence.

approaches.name: Futures-curve / cost-of-carry forecast (futures price as the predictor of future spot)
approaches.one_line: Use the copper futures price for delivery at horizon h (or the implied carry/basis) directly as the point forecast of the spot price at h, motivated by the cost-of-carry no-arbitrage relation.
approaches.mechanism: Under cost-of-carry, F_t,h = S_t * (1 + r + storage - convenience yield) over horizon h; if the futures risk premium is zero the futures price equals the market's expected future spot. The forecast is fully transparent: it IS an observed market price, and the basis (F - S) decomposes into interest cost + storage - convenience yield. Contango (F>S) signals comfortable inventories; backwardation (F<S) signals scarcity/high convenience yield. You can read the entire 'model' off the forward curve and the COMEX/LME term structure.
approaches.horizon_fit: Best at the WEEKLY and MONTHLY horizons because near-dated copper contracts are liquid and the basis is small and stable for industrial metals (low, near-constant storage cost), so the futures point forecast stays close to spot. The interpretive content (basis as a scarcity signal) is sharpest at 1-3 months. Weakness grows with horizon as liquidity thins beyond ~12 months.
approaches.interpretability: Maximally interpretable — the forecast is a traded price and the basis algebraically decomposes into carry components. Nothing is estimated or hidden.
approaches.strengths: No estimation, no overfitting, embeds the market's full information set, provides a coherent prediction interval via option-implied vol, and is the natural economic benchmark. Conditionally beats the random walk by a wide margin precisely when the spot-futures gap is large (Reeve-Vigfusson).
approaches.weaknesses: For COPPER the futures basis is tiny and the curve is nearly flat, so the futures forecast is numerically almost identical to the random walk and rarely beats it OOS at short horizons; it embeds a (small, time-varying) risk premium so it is a biased predictor; basis is dominated by interest rates and storage, leaving little signal when inventories are normal. Contango/backwardation flips can mislead during financialization-driven curve distortions.
approaches.copper_relevance: Directly uses COMEX HG and LME copper forward curves and the spot-futures basis; naturally incorporates real rates (carry) and inventory state (via convenience yield). Pairs with LME/COMEX/SHFE inventory data to interpret why the curve is in contango vs backwardation.

key_papers.citation: Reeve, T. A. & Vigfusson, R. J. (2011), 'Evaluating the Forecasting Performance of Commodity Futures Prices', Federal Reserve International Finance Discussion Paper No. 1025
key_papers.method: Compare futures-based forecasts to random walk and random-walk-with-drift across energy, metals (incl. copper), agriculture at 3-month and ~year-ahead horizons via relative MSE.
key_papers.finding: Futures generally beat a random walk over 1990-2010 but 'not by a large margin'; for COPPER specifically the 3-month relative MSE was ~1.00 (a tie) and the year-ahead relative MSE was 1.08-1.20 in the 2003-2010 subsample (futures WORSE than random walk). Crucially, futures outperform the random walk by a considerable margin only when the spot-futures gap is large; in the late 2000s a random walk beat futures for copper and oil.

key_papers.citation: Fama, E. F. & French, K. R. (1987), 'Commodity Futures Prices: Some Evidence on Forecast Power, Premiums, and the Theory of Storage', Journal of Business 60(1), 55-73
key_papers.method: Test forecast power of futures for future spot and decompose the basis into an expected-premium and expected-spot-change component for 21 commodities.
key_papers.finding: Found evidence of forecast power for 10 of 21 commodities and time-varying expected premiums for five; basis varies with interest rates and seasonal convenience yields — establishing both that futures contain (some) spot information and that a (small, time-varying) risk premium makes them a biased predictor.

approaches.name: Theory of storage / convenience-yield & basis-as-state-variable models
approaches.one_line: Model the futures-spot basis (interest-adjusted) and convenience yield as a decreasing, convex function of inventories, using the basis/inventory state to forecast price level, volatility, and the sign of future moves.
approaches.mechanism: The interest-adjusted basis equals storage cost minus convenience yield; theory of storage says convenience yield rises sharply as inventories fall, so a negative interest-adjusted basis (backwardation) flags low inventories/scarcity and predicts higher spot volatility and mean-reversion pressure. You can read the inventory state off the basis when stock data are lagged. Often implemented as regressions of the basis on inventories, or of future volatility/returns on the basis sign — every coefficient is economically labelled.
approaches.horizon_fit: MONTHLY is the natural cadence: LME/COMEX/SHFE inventory data and the basis update at daily/weekly frequency but the convenience-yield signal is most reliable for 1-3 month moves and for volatility forecasting. At WEEKLY horizon the basis is a useful conditioning/regime variable (scarcity vs glut) more than a precise level predictor.
approaches.interpretability: Very high — coefficients map to storage cost, convenience yield, and inventory sensitivity; the basis sign is a directly explainable scarcity gauge.
approaches.strengths: Strong empirical validation for base metals; turns the otherwise-flat copper basis into an interpretable inventory proxy; explains volatility asymmetry (vol rises when inventories are low); robust economic foundation rather than data-mined.
approaches.weaknesses: Primarily explains volatility and the basis-inventory relation rather than delivering large OOS level-forecast gains; convenience yield is not directly observed (must be backed out); inventory data are reported with lags and exclude off-exchange/Chinese bonded stocks; financialization can decouple the basis from physical fundamentals.
approaches.copper_relevance: Directly built on LME copper (and the Geman-Smith result that adding Chinese inventories strengthens the relationship); uses LME/COMEX/SHFE on-warrant stocks, the spot-3M basis (cash-to-3-month spread), and interest rates — all already in the user's data orbit. Cash/3M backwardation on the LME is the canonical copper scarcity signal.

key_papers.citation: Fama, E. F. & French, K. R. (1988), 'Business Cycles and the Behavior of Metals Prices', Journal of Finance 43(5), 1075-1093
key_papers.method: Test theory of storage on five LME base metals (aluminium, copper, lead, tin, zinc) 1972-1983 using the sign of the interest-adjusted basis and business-cycle phase as inventory proxies.
key_papers.finding: Futures prices are less variable than spot prices when inventory is low and similarly variable when inventory is high (as the theory predicts); positive demand shocks around business-cycle peaks drain inventories and generate large convenience yields and spot-futures price inversions (backwardation) — confirming the basis/inventory link for copper.

key_papers.citation: Geman, H. & Smith, W. O. (2012), 'Theory of Storage, Inventory and Volatility in the LME Base Metals', Resources Policy 38(1)
key_papers.method: Test the two storage-theory predictions (low inventory -> backwardation and -> spot vol > futures vol) on all six LME base metals including copper, adding Chinese inventory data.
key_papers.finding: Strong validation of the theory for copper and the other base metals; including Chinese inventories strengthens the inventory-basis-volatility relationship, contradicting claims that Chinese stock data are too opaque to use — a direct argument for incorporating SHFE/Chinese bonded inventories into copper models.

approaches.name: Hedging-pressure / normal-backwardation risk-premium models (CFTC COT positioning)
approaches.one_line: Predict the copper futures risk premium from the net positioning of hedgers vs speculators (and the curve slope), per Keynes' normal-backwardation / risk-transfer view.
approaches.mechanism: Keynes' hedging-pressure hypothesis: when commercial hedgers are net short, they must pay a premium to long speculators, so futures are set below expected spot (normal backwardation) and longs earn a positive expected return; when hedgers are net long the sign flips (contango/positive premium to shorts). Implemented as regressions or long-short sorts on net hedging pressure (from CFTC COT) and on the term-structure slope. Coefficients are directly interpretable as the price of bearing hedgers' risk.
approaches.horizon_fit: MONTHLY is the most credible horizon for positioning-driven premia (COT is reported weekly with a lag; positioning mean-reverts over weeks-to-months). At WEEKLY horizon COT changes/extremes are usable as a contrarian/sentiment conditioning signal but the premium estimate is noisy.
approaches.interpretability: High — the predictor is observed positioning data and the coefficient is the estimated risk premium per unit of hedging pressure; easy to explain as 'who is paying whom to hedge'.
approaches.strengths: Grounded in a clear risk-transfer economic story; uses data the user already ingests (CFTC COT); Basu-Miffre show hedging-pressure premia are real, rise with volatility, and are distinct from momentum and carry; works as a positioning/sentiment overlay even when not a standalone forecaster.
approaches.weaknesses: Kolb's classic verdict 'normal backwardation is not normal' — backwardation does not reliably generate positive returns; the premium is small, noisy, regime-dependent, and was diluted by post-2004 financialization; COT classification (commercial vs non-commercial) is imperfect for a financialized metal like copper; mostly evidenced cross-sectionally rather than as a single-commodity timing tool.
approaches.copper_relevance: Directly consumes CFTC COT for COMEX copper (HG); naturally complements the LME basis (curve slope) as a second risk-premium signal. Copper appears explicitly in the Bessembinder and related metals/oil hedging-pressure studies.

key_papers.citation: Basu, D. & Miffre, J. (2013), 'Capturing the Risk Premium of Commodity Futures: The Role of Hedging Pressure', Journal of Banking & Finance 37(7), 2652-2664
key_papers.method: Build long-short factor portfolios sorted on hedgers' and speculators' open interest (COT) across commodity futures; test cross-sectional pricing.
key_papers.finding: Hedging-pressure long-short portfolios earn significant premia with Sharpe ratios exceeding long-only benchmarks; the premia rise with futures-market volatility and are distinct from the predictive power of past returns (momentum) and the term-structure slope (carry/basis) — establishing positioning as an independent, interpretable risk-premium signal.

key_papers.citation: Gorton, G. B., Hayashi, F. & Rouwenhorst, K. G. (2007/2013), 'The Fundamentals of Commodity Futures Returns', NBER WP 13249 (publ. Review of Finance 2013)
key_papers.method: Link inventories to the basis and to futures risk premiums for 31 commodities 1969-2006; relate positioning to prices and inventory signals.
key_papers.finding: Risk premiums vary with the level of physical inventories as the theory of storage predicts; the basis, prior returns and spot returns all proxy the inventory state and are informative about premiums; backwardation/momentum strategy returns come largely from selecting commodities when inventories are low — unifying storage and hedging-pressure views and showing positioning correlates with prices and inventories.

approaches.name: Commodity factor models — carry/basis, momentum, basis-momentum (cross-sectional)
approaches.one_line: Rank a cross-section of commodities by interpretable characteristics (basis/carry, time-series momentum, basis-momentum) to capture priced risk premia; for copper, use the same characteristics as conditioning features rather than as a level forecast.
approaches.mechanism: Each factor is a transparent characteristic: carry/basis = slope of the futures curve (roll yield); momentum = trailing 12-1 month return; basis-momentum = difference in momentum between first- and second-nearby contracts (slope+curvature of the curve). Long-short portfolios on these characteristics earn premia. Every signal is a simple, readable function of prices/curve — no latent layers.
approaches.horizon_fit: Designed for MONTHLY rebalancing of a cross-sectional basket, not single-commodity weekly/monthly level forecasting. For the user's single-name copper task, carry (copper's own basis), momentum (copper trend), and basis-momentum (HG curve slope vs curvature) are best used as interpretable FEATURES into the existing regressions/ensembles. Weekly use is possible for momentum/curve features but factor premia are a monthly-horizon phenomenon.
approaches.interpretability: High at the characteristic level — you can state exactly why copper scores high/low on carry, momentum, basis-momentum — though the 'why it is priced' (risk vs behavioural) is debated.
approaches.strengths: Robust, widely replicated premia; characteristics are cheap to compute from HG/LME curves; basis-momentum subsumes much of carry+momentum and predicts both spot and term premiums; provides orthogonal, economically labelled features that complement storage and positioning signals.
approaches.weaknesses: Cross-sectional/relative-value by construction — gives copper's expected return RELATIVE to other commodities, not an absolute price; a single-commodity application loses the diversification that makes the premia reliable; premia are time-varying and can suffer long drawdowns; basis-momentum's driver (speculator/intermediary constraints) is itself only partly observable.
approaches.copper_relevance: Carry = copper's own roll yield/basis (HG/LME); momentum = copper price trend; basis-momentum = HG 1st vs 2nd nearby curve dynamics. All computable from the user's COMEX/LME data and natural inputs to Ridge/quantile/ensemble layers.

key_papers.citation: Koijen, R. S. J., Moskowitz, T. J., Pedersen, L. H. & Vrugt, E. B. (2018), 'Carry', Journal of Financial Economics 127(2), 197-225
key_papers.method: Define 'carry' (incl. commodity roll yield/basis) as a unifying predictor of returns across asset classes; sort commodities on carry.
key_papers.finding: Carry predicts returns within and across asset classes including commodities; a commodity carry (basis) factor helps describe the cross-section of commodity returns — establishing the futures basis as a first-order, interpretable return predictor.

key_papers.citation: Boons, M. & Prado, M. P. (2019), 'Basis-Momentum', Journal of Finance 74(1), 239-279
key_papers.method: Construct basis-momentum (momentum differential between nearby and next-nearby futures) and test it in time-series and cross-section vs basis and momentum.
key_papers.finding: Basis-momentum strongly outperforms the basis and momentum in predicting commodity spot and term premiums, in both time series and cross-section, and is priced; the authors interpret it as compensation for risk arising when speculators'/intermediaries' market-clearing ability is impaired — a finding they note is not fully explained by storage, inventory, or hedging pressure alone.

approaches.name: Cointegration / vector error-correction (VECM) and bivariate-correlation models on copper fundamentals & cross-assets
approaches.one_line: Exploit long-run equilibrium relations between copper and cointegrated drivers (USD, industrial production, related metals, oil) via an error-correction term that pulls the price back toward fair value, or simpler bivariate correlation forecasts.
approaches.mechanism: If copper and a driver (e.g. DXY, world IP, gold/aluminium/oil) are cointegrated, deviations from the long-run relation (the error-correction term) predict future copper changes: when copper is rich/cheap vs its equilibrium with the USD and the business cycle, the ECM forecasts mean reversion. Coefficients are interpretable as the long-run elasticity and the speed of adjustment; the ECT is a readable 'mispricing' gauge. Bivariate-correlation forecasts simply project copper from one strongly correlated driver.
approaches.horizon_fit: MONTHLY is the sweet spot — equilibrium reversion plays out over months and the macro drivers (IP, USD) update monthly. World Bank evidence shows VECMs of metals vs US industrial production forecast best at MONTHLY frequency; at WEEKLY horizon the macro ECT is slow-moving but the cross-asset (USD, gold, oil) ECT can still add signal.
approaches.interpretability: High — long-run elasticities, adjustment speeds, and the current error-correction gap are all explicit and explainable.
approaches.strengths: Directly encodes copper's known macro drivers (USD real effective exchange rate and the world output gap are statistically significant for copper per the World Bank); avoids the spurious-regression trap by modelling levels correctly; ECT gives an interpretable valuation signal; bivariate correlations performed well at short horizons in the World Bank suite.
approaches.weaknesses: Cointegrating relationships can break/shift (structural breaks, regime change), making the ECT unreliable; OOS gains are often modest and many studies find in-sample cointegration does not translate to OOS forecast improvement; sensitive to lag choice and to which drivers are included; BVAR/reduced-form multivariate versions can forecast WORSE than simple benchmarks (World Bank found their BVAR significantly worse than all other approaches).
approaches.copper_relevance: Tailor-made for the user's existing Engle-Granger setup vs gold/aluminium/oil/DXY/CNY; naturally uses USD, China/world industrial production, real yields, and related-metal prices — exactly the cross-asset ratios and macro features already in the repo.

key_papers.citation: Arroyo-Marioli, F., Khadan, J., Ohnsorge, F. & Yamazaki, T. (2023), 'Forecasting Industrial Commodity Prices: Literature Review and a Model Suite', World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 10611
key_papers.method: Build and OOS-evaluate a six-model suite (futures, consensus, bivariate correlations, BVAR, Oxford macro model, ML) for oil and six metals incl. copper, testing bias and RMSE with Diebold-Mariano and directional-accuracy tests.
key_papers.finding: Futures prices or bivariate correlations performed well at SHORT horizons for most commodities (incl. copper); a macro structural model and consensus were better at LONG horizons; the reduced-form BVAR was significantly WORSE than all other approaches. All approaches except BVAR (and, for copper and lead, consensus) had good directional accuracy at horizons under one year. They note the world output gap and US dollar real effective exchange rate are statistically significant for copper price dynamics.

key_papers.citation: Kwas, M. & Rubaszek, M. (2021), 'Forecasting Commodity Prices: Looking for a Benchmark', Forecasts (MDPI) 3(2), 27; with Rubaszek et al. (2020) on weekly futures
key_papers.method: Evaluate alternatives to the random-walk benchmark (AR, local projections, futures) for commodity prices OOS.
key_papers.finding: For NOMINAL commodity prices the random-walk benchmark should be SUPPLEMENTED by futures-based forecasts; for REAL prices a local-projection model is a better benchmark; alternative benchmarks can match or modestly beat the random walk. Rubaszek et al. (2020) found, using WEEKLY data, that futures prices outperformed the random walk — directly relevant to the user's weekly horizon.

approaches.name: Dynamic model averaging/selection (DMA/DMS) and time-varying-parameter regressions over copper fundamentals + financial predictors
approaches.one_line: A state-space framework that runs many small interpretable regressions on copper fundamentals (excess demand, inventories, convenience yield) and financial predictors, with time-varying coefficients and time-varying model weights, averaging into one forecast.
approaches.mechanism: Each candidate model is a transparent linear regression of copper returns on a subset of named predictors; the Kalman filter lets coefficients drift over time, and a forgetting-factor scheme updates each model's posterior probability so the ensemble shifts weight toward whichever economic story is currently working. You can read off, period-by-period, which predictors (and which coefficients) are driving the forecast — e.g. inventories/convenience yield in physical-tightness regimes vs VIX/TED/SP500/yield-spread in financial-stress regimes.
approaches.horizon_fit: Validated at MONTHLY (and quarterly) horizons for copper; this is the best-evidenced interpretable model that actually beats the random walk for copper at the monthly cadence. Could be adapted to WEEKLY but the fundamental predictors (inventories, excess demand) are monthly, so weekly use would lean on the financial predictors.
approaches.interpretability: High and dynamic — unlike a black-box ensemble, you can inspect the time-varying inclusion probability and coefficient of each economically named predictor, so the model 'tells you' why it is bullish/bearish each month.
approaches.strengths: Directly copper-specific; explicitly incorporates theory-of-storage fundamentals (excess demand, inventories, convenience yield) AND financialization variables; adapts to regime change; beat the random walk OOS with statistical significance; the time-varying weights reveal that predictor importance shifted dramatically around the 2008 crisis — an interpretable, defensible narrative.
approaches.weaknesses: Requires assembling 18+ predictors with consistent history; gains are concentrated in volatile/crisis periods and shrink in calm markets and at longer horizons; sensitive to forgetting-factor/prior calibration; monthly fundamental data limit weekly application; like all such studies, much of the edge came during one episode (2008), raising out-of-period robustness questions.
approaches.copper_relevance: The most copper-native model here: uses LME copper, excess demand, inventories, convenience yield, momentum, term spread, VIX, TED spread, SP500, industrial production, USD — almost exactly the user's feature set (cross-asset, macro, COT, technicals). Essentially a principled, interpretable generalization of the user's Ridge/ARIMAX + ensemble stack.

key_papers.citation: Buncic, D. & Moretto, C. (2015), 'Forecasting copper prices with dynamic averaging and selection models', North American Journal of Economics and Finance 33, 1-38
key_papers.method: Forecast monthly LME copper returns with DMA/DMS over 18 predictors (fundamental: excess demand, inventories, convenience yield; financial: SP500, VIX, TED spread, yield/term spread, industrial production, momentum), OOS May 2002-June 2014; evaluate with Campbell-Thompson OOS R^2 and Clark-West MSFE-adjusted test.
key_papers.finding: DMA/DMS significantly beat the random walk for horizons up to 6 months; one-step-ahead OOS R^2 reached 18.5% (DMA) and 13.7% (DMS) with Clark-West p-values 0.002/0.013; even a simple expanding-window OLS on the full predictor set beat the random walk (~10% OOS R^2). Much of the gain was realised around the 2008 crisis, and the most relevant predictors (SP500, VIX, yield spread, TED spread, industrial production) changed importance substantially over time.

approaches.name: Structural fundamental supply-demand balance models (mine supply, scrap, China consumption, inventories) — IMF/World Bank/ICSG style
approaches.one_line: Build an explicit market-balance accounting and behavioural equations (demand as a function of activity/price, supply from mine + scrap, inventory change) and back out the equilibrium copper price from projected surplus/deficit and elasticities.
approaches.mechanism: Estimate structural equations: refined-copper demand driven by global/China industrial activity and price (with small long-run elasticities); primary supply from mine production plus secondary supply from scrap (price- and stock-responsive); the price clears the balance, with inventory changes absorbing surplus/deficit. Each elasticity and balance identity is economically named, so a forecast can be explained as 'X kt deficit -> Y% price support given demand elasticity e'. This is the IMF/World Bank/IEA/ICSG modelling tradition.
approaches.horizon_fit: Weak at WEEKLY and only fair at MONTHLY — its natural horizon is quarterly-to-multi-year. Mine supply, scrap, and consumption data are reported with long lags and low frequency, and copper's supply/demand elasticities are small in the short run, so the model says little about next-week/next-month moves but is valuable for the 3-month-and-beyond strategic view and for scenario analysis (e.g. China stimulus, mine disruption).
approaches.interpretability: Highest economic transparency of all — every input (mine output, scrap, China demand, inventories) and elasticity is an observable, debatable quantity; the forecast is a told-as-a-story balance.
approaches.strengths: Most defensible to a human/decision-maker; explicitly encodes the copper drivers analysts care about (Chilean/Peruvian mine supply, scrap, China ~60% of demand, exchange + bonded inventories); ideal for scenario/stress analysis and for anchoring long-horizon expectations and prediction-interval framing.
approaches.weaknesses: Estimated price elasticities of copper supply and demand are small but statistically significant (Shojaeini 2023), so the price is very sensitive to small balance errors; data are lagged, revised, and incomplete (off-exchange/Chinese bonded stocks, true scrap flows hard to measure); poor at short horizons where the user operates; full structural macro models (e.g. Oxford) shine only at long horizons in the World Bank suite; risk of large misses when expectations/financial flows, not fundamentals, drive copper.
approaches.copper_relevance: The model is entirely copper-specific: ICSG/IWSS-style balances, LME/COMEX/SHFE + bonded inventories, mine and scrap supply, China industrial production/consumption, USD. Best used in the user's stack as a slow-moving fundamental anchor / regime input and for the 3-month (66d) horizon and scenario commentary rather than weekly forecasting.

key_papers.citation: Shojaeini, S. (2023), 'Metal market analysis: an empirical model for copper supply and demand in US market', Mineral Economics 36(3), 509-517
key_papers.method: Estimate price elasticities of copper supply and demand from production, consumption, and price data, 1990-2020.
key_papers.finding: Both long-run supply and demand price elasticities for copper are small but statistically significant — implying that supply/demand imbalances translate into meaningful price changes (it is not a no-change market) but that precise price forecasts require accurate balance projections, which is the model's main vulnerability.

key_papers.citation: Arroyo-Marioli, F., Khadan, J., Ohnsorge, F. & Yamazaki, T. (2023), 'Forecasting Industrial Commodity Prices: a Model Suite', World Bank PRWP 10611
key_papers.method: Within the six-model suite, include a large-scale macro-structural model (Oxford Economics Model) and consensus forecasts, compared against futures/correlations/BVAR/ML for copper and other metals.
key_papers.finding: Consensus forecasts and the macro-structural model were preferred at LONG horizons, while futures/bivariate correlations won at SHORT horizons — confirming that fundamental/structural models add value at strategic horizons but are dominated by market-price and simple statistical models at the weekly/monthly horizons the user targets.

findings.evaluation_notes: The credible literature evaluates these models out-of-sample against a no-change random walk (and the futures curve), the two strong benchmarks the user already has. Standard tooling: relative MSE/RMSE ratios vs the random walk; Diebold-Mariano (1995) tests of equal predictive accuracy; the Clark-West (2007) MSFE-adjusted statistic and Campbell-Thompson (2008) out-of-sample R^2 for nested comparisons (essential because futures/ECM/DMA models nest the random walk); and Pesaran-Timmermann directional-accuracy tests for sign forecasts. Key methodological cautions evident across the sources: (1) in-sample fit (e.g. cointegration, high in-sample R^2) frequently fails to translate into OOS gains — Rubaszek et al. and the World Bank both stress this; (2) results are highly sample-dependent — copper futures beat the random walk pre-2000 but the random walk beat futures for copper during the late 2000s (Reeve-Vigfusson); (3) reported edges often concentrate in one volatile episode (2008 for Buncic-Moretto), so rolling/period-split evaluation matters; (4) for copper specifically, distinguish LEVEL forecasting (where beating the random walk is hard) from DIRECTIONAL and VOLATILITY forecasting and from SCENARIO/relative-value use (where storage, positioning, factor, and structural models add clear interpretable value). Best practice in this literature is forecast COMBINATION — averaging futures/random-walk/ECM/DMA forecasts — which the user already does via weighted + stacking ensembles.
key_takeaways: For COPPER at weekly/monthly horizons, the random walk (no-change) and the futures curve are very strong, fully interpretable benchmarks that most models fail to beat OOS for LEVEL forecasts. Reeve-Vigfusson (Fed 2011) find copper's 3-month futures-vs-RW relative MSE is ~1.00 (a tie) and 1.08-1.20 a year ahead in 2003-2010 (futures worse); keep both as the bar every other model must clear.

The single best-evidenced interpretable model that actually beats the copper random walk at the MONTHLY horizon is Buncic-Moretto (2015) dynamic model averaging/selection over fundamentals (excess demand, inventories, convenience yield) PLUS financial predictors (VIX, TED, SP500, yield spread, IP), with OOS R^2 up to 18.5% one-step-ahead. It is essentially a principled, regime-switching, interpretable generalization of the user's existing Ridge/ARIMAX + ensemble stack and is the highest-priority addition.

Theory of storage makes the futures-spot basis an interpretable inventory/scarcity state variable: backwardation (cash>3M on LME) signals low inventories and predicts higher spot volatility (Fama-French 1988; Geman-Smith 2012, who show adding CHINESE/SHFE inventories strengthens the relationship). Use the LME cash-3M spread and LME/COMEX/SHFE+bonded stocks as features and as a volatility/regime signal, not just a level predictor.

Hedging-pressure / normal-backwardation says the futures RISK PREMIUM is driven by net positioning. Basu-Miffre (2013) show positioning premia are real, rise with volatility, and are distinct from carry and momentum — so CFTC COT for COMEX copper (already ingested) is a legitimate interpretable monthly signal, but heed Kolb's caveat that 'normal backwardation is not normal' (backwardation alone does not guarantee positive returns).

Commodity factor signals — carry/basis (Koijen et al. 2018), momentum, and basis-momentum (Boons-Prado 2019, JF) — are interpretable and computable from the HG/LME curve, but they are CROSS-SECTIONAL relative-value premia; for a single-name copper forecast use them as features (copper's own basis, trend, curve slope-vs-curvature), not as standalone forecasters.

Cointegration/VECM against copper's macro drivers fits the user's existing Engle-Granger setup; the World Bank (2023) suite finds metal VECMs vs US industrial production forecast best at MONTHLY frequency and that bivariate correlations win at short horizons, while their reduced-form BVAR was significantly WORSE than every alternative. The world output gap and USD real effective exchange rate are statistically significant copper drivers — keep DXY/CNY and IP in the ECT.

Structural supply-demand balance models (mine supply, scrap, China ~60% of demand, inventories; IMF/World Bank/ICSG style) are the most economically transparent but are data-lagged and low-frequency; copper's short-run price elasticities are small (Shojaeini 2023), so they are best for the 3-month/strategic horizon and scenario analysis, NOT weekly forecasting. Use them as a slow fundamental anchor and prediction-interval framing rather than a short-horizon point forecaster.

Across the literature the winning practical recipe is interpretable forecast COMBINATION (futures + random walk + ECM + DMA/TVP), evaluated OOS with Diebold-Mariano and the Clark-West/Campbell-Thompson nested tests, and split by sub-period because copper's relative model performance flips across regimes (futures beat RW pre-2000; RW beat futures in the late 2000s). This validates the user's existing weighted/stacking ensemble and argues for adding TVP/DMA and basis/positioning features rather than a black box.
