findings.dimension: Interpretable statistical learning (LASSO/elastic-net/adaptive-LASSO, GAMs/splines, symbolic regression/genetic programming, RuleFit/single decision trees, Gaussian processes) for weekly/monthly copper price forecasting
findings.overview:
Across the copper and base-metals forecasting literature, the single most robust empirical regularity is that the random walk (RW) / no-change benchmark is extremely hard to beat at short horizons (days to a few weeks), and only becomes beatable — modestly and conditionally — at monthly-to-quarterly horizons when fundamentals and financial conditioning variables are introduced. This shapes how interpretable statistical-learning methods should be deployed: their value for copper at WEEKLY horizon is mainly disciplined feature selection and honest uncertainty (not beating RW on level), while at MONTHLY horizon there is genuine, documented predictability to capture, and interpretable methods can exploit it without resorting to black boxes.

Within the interpretable family, the evidence tiers cleanly: (1) Penalized linear regression (LASSO, elastic net, adaptive LASSO, ridge) is the best-supported interpretable approach — it has explicit out-of-sample wins over competing models for crude oil (Zhang, Ma & Wang 2019, Journal of Empirical Finance) and is the standard high-dimensional variable-selection engine for copper drivers (Liu, Guo & Wei 2024, Journal of Commodity Markets). Its time-varying cousins (dynamic model averaging/selection) produced the clearest copper-specific RW-beating result in the literature (Buncic & Moretto 2015, NAJEF: up to 17% MSFE improvement, OOS R^2 up to ~18.5%, to 6 months ahead). (2) Single decision/regression trees are maximally interpretable but, for copper specifically, did NOT beat the RW at any horizon in a careful study (Diaz, Hansen & Cabrera 2020, Resources Policy), though Liu et al. (2017, Resources Policy) reported low MAPE. RuleFit (Friedman & Popescu 2008) generalizes single trees into a sparse, LASSO-pruned rule ensemble that recovers interpretability while capturing interactions. (3) Gaussian-process regression is widely and successfully applied to metals (the Jin & Xu program of copper/silver/steel/coal GPR papers) with strong fit and native uncertainty bands, but those studies are typically autoregressive and rarely test against a RW, so their headline accuracy is not evidence of genuine predictability. (4) Symbolic regression / genetic programming yields explicit closed-form equations but, where rigorously benchmarked on a commodity (Drachal 2022, Energies, Bayesian symbolic regression on crude oil), did NOT significantly beat standard benchmarks. (5) GAMs / penalized splines are well-established and interpretable for electricity price/demand and energy, and are a natural fit for copper fundamentals, but copper-specific peer-reviewed applications are thin — a genuine gap rather than a settled negative result.

Net guidance for this repo: penalized regression (already present as ridge — extend to LASSO/elastic-net/adaptive-LASSO for selection), GAMs/splines for nonlinear-but-readable fundamentals at monthly horizon, and GPR for calibrated weekly intervals are the highest-value interpretable additions; single trees and symbolic regression are best treated as diagnostic/communication tools rather than as accuracy engines for copper.

approaches.name: Penalized linear regression — LASSO, ridge, elastic net, adaptive LASSO, LARS (incl. time-varying DMA/DMS extensions)
approaches.one_line: Shrink/select among many copper drivers to produce a sparse, signed linear forecasting equation whose surviving coefficients are directly readable as driver importances.
approaches.mechanism: Ordinary least squares augmented with an L1 (LASSO), L2 (ridge) or mixed (elastic net) penalty on coefficients; LARS computes the full LASSO/elastic-net solution path efficiently. The L1 penalty drives many coefficients exactly to zero, performing automatic variable selection; adaptive LASSO reweights the penalty so it has the oracle property (consistent selection). What is interpretable: the final model is a literal linear equation — you read off which of the candidate predictors survived, the SIGN and MAGNITUDE of each standardized coefficient, and the implied direction of each driver's effect on copper returns. Elastic net additionally keeps correlated groups of predictors together (relevant when LME/COMEX/SHFE prices, DXY and CNY co-move). The dynamic extensions (Dynamic Model Averaging / Selection, Bayesian model combination) make the coefficient set and model weights TIME-VARYING, so you can plot which predictor is driving copper this month vs last year — interpretable as an evolving, weighted vote over linear sub-models.
approaches.horizon_fit: Best fit is MONTHLY. The clearest copper-specific predictability evidence (Buncic & Moretto 2015) is at 1-to-6-month horizons on LME monthly copper; the crude-oil LASSO/elastic-net wins (Zhang, Ma & Wang 2019) are at monthly frequency. At WEEKLY horizon, penalized regression is still the right tool for disciplined feature selection and for regularizing the existing technical/positioning/cross-asset feature set against overfitting, but expectations of beating a 5-day random walk on level should be modest — the literature consistently finds short-horizon metal prices near-unpredictable. Use weekly LASSO mainly to prevent the feature explosion from overfitting and to produce a transparent, stable signal set.
approaches.interpretability: Fully transparent: a signed, sparse coefficient vector (a closed-form linear equation). Adaptive LASSO gives cleaner selection; the regularization path itself is interpretable (the order in which predictors enter as the penalty relaxes ranks their marginal usefulness). DMA/DMS adds interpretable time-varying inclusion probabilities and model weights. Opaque only in that coefficient stability depends on the penalty parameter chosen by cross-validation.
approaches.strengths: Handles the high-dimensional copper feature set (cross-asset ratios, macro, COT positioning, calendar, technicals) gracefully; explicit selection tells you WHICH drivers matter and removes redundant ones; strong, replicated out-of-sample evidence on analogous commodities; cheap to fit and re-fit in a rolling window; integrates naturally with the repo's existing ridge and stacking layers; OLS re-estimated on LASSO-selected predictors often forecasts even better (post-LASSO).
approaches.weaknesses: Purely linear in the chosen features (nonlinearities must be added by hand as engineered features/interactions); LASSO selection is unstable under strong multicollinearity (mitigated by elastic net) and under serial dependence (penalized-regression inference is distorted by autocorrelation — a documented caveat for time-series predictors); coefficient signs can flip across rolling windows if predictors are collinear, complicating the 'interpretable' story; cross-validation for the penalty must respect time ordering (no leakage); static LASSO assumes a stable relationship that copper's regime shifts (China-driven vs financialized periods) violate — favoring the time-varying DMA/DMS variants.
approaches.copper_relevance: Naturally ingests exactly the repo's drivers: LME/COMEX/SHFE prices and inventories, the futures basis/convenience yield, DXY/USD, real yields and breakevens, China industrial production, CFTC COT positioning, scrap and mine-supply proxies, and cross-asset ratios vs gold/aluminium/oil. Buncic & Moretto's predictor list (excess demand, inventories, convenience yield, risk appetite, momentum, term spread, exchange rates) is essentially this feature set; Liu, Guo & Wei (2024) use LASSO precisely to select among 75 copper indicators spanning inventory, supply, demand, macro, finance and geopolitics.

key_papers.citation: Zhang, Y., Ma, F., & Wang, Y. (2019). Forecasting crude oil prices with a large set of predictors: Can LASSO select powerful predictors? Journal of Empirical Finance, 54, 97-117.
key_papers.method: LASSO and elastic net for monthly crude-oil return forecasting from a large predictor set; post-selection OLS.
key_papers.finding: LASSO and elastic net outperformed a host of widely used competing models out-of-sample on both out-of-sample R-squared and success (directional-hit) ratio, and delivered positive, sizeable economic gains to a mean-variance investor. OLS on the LASSO-selected predictors also beat competitors. Headline: penalized selection beats the benchmark field for oil at monthly horizon (the closest well-identified analog to copper).

key_papers.citation: Buncic, D., & Moretto, C. (2015). Forecasting copper prices with dynamic averaging and selection models. North American Journal of Economics and Finance, 33, 1-38.
key_papers.method: Dynamic Model Averaging / Selection (time-varying-parameter linear models with evolving inclusion of ~16 fundamental and financial predictors) on monthly LME copper returns.
key_papers.finding: Out-of-sample (May 2002-Jun 2014), DMA improved mean-squared forecast error over the random walk by up to ~17% (up to ~5% for a simple TVP model), with out-of-sample R^2 vs RW as high as ~18.5%; predictability held to 6 months ahead. This is the clearest copper-specific demonstration that an interpretable, time-varying linear model with fundamentals can beat the RW at monthly-to-quarterly horizons.

key_papers.citation: Liu, Y., Guo, Y., & Wei, Q. (2024). Time-varying and multi-scale analysis of copper price influencing factors based on LASSO and EMD methods. Journal of Commodity Markets, 34, 100072.
key_papers.method: LASSO for variable selection among 75 copper-price indicators (inventory, supply, demand, macroeconomy, finance, geopolitics), combined with Empirical Mode Decomposition for multi-scale/time-varying attribution.
key_papers.finding: Long-run copper trends are mainly determined by fundamental factors, while financial and geopolitical factors more directly drive short-term fluctuations; financial/geopolitical importance has risen recently. Demonstrates LASSO as the standard interpretable engine for copper driver selection and attribution (the paper is attribution-focused; it does not report a head-to-head RW out-of-sample contest).

key_papers.citation: Drachal, K. (2019). Forecasting prices of selected metals with Bayesian data-rich models. Resources Policy, 64, 101528.
key_papers.method: Bayesian Dynamic Model Averaging / model-combination (data-rich, time-varying linear models) on monthly non-ferrous metal spot prices including copper, aluminium, nickel, zinc (fDMA R package).
key_papers.finding: Bayesian DMA/model-combination schemes produced successful forecasts of metal prices, with DMA frequently beating naive and ARIMA benchmarks on Diebold-Mariano tests in the author's broader program; reinforces that time-varying, interpretable linear combinations of many fundamental predictors are a credible monthly metals approach (exact copper-vs-RW margins are model/period specific).

approaches.name: Single decision / regression trees (CART) and RuleFit
approaches.one_line: A single CART tree is a transparent set of if-then threshold rules; RuleFit converts an ensemble of shallow trees into a sparse, LASSO-pruned linear model over decision rules, recovering interpretability while capturing interactions.
approaches.mechanism: CART recursively splits the predictor space on single-variable thresholds (e.g., 'if COT net-long > X and DXY change < Y then predicted copper return = z'), so every prediction is traceable through a short rule path and the splits reveal which thresholds of which drivers matter. RuleFit (Friedman & Popescu) first grows many shallow trees, extracts each node as a binary rule feature, then fits a LASSO over {original linear features + rule features}; the L1 penalty keeps only a small set of rules and linear terms, each with a readable coefficient = its importance. What is interpretable: for a single tree, the entire decision path and split thresholds; for RuleFit, the surviving rules (explicit conjunctions of driver thresholds) plus their signed coefficients and feature importances.
approaches.horizon_fit: For copper, single trees are weak at BOTH weekly and monthly horizons as accuracy engines — the careful copper study found the random walk beat trees at every horizon tested (1 day through 2 years). They are more defensible at MONTHLY horizon, and chiefly as a communication/diagnostic device (regime-style rules, threshold effects) rather than as the primary forecaster. RuleFit is better suited to MONTHLY, where genuine fundamental predictability exists for its rules to capture; at weekly horizon it risks fitting noise.
approaches.interpretability: Maximal for a single shallow tree (a human can read the whole model as a flowchart of thresholds). RuleFit is semi-transparent: a sparse list of rules with coefficients — far more inspectable than a gradient-boosted ensemble, but the number of surviving rules must be kept small (via the LASSO penalty) to remain readable. Deep trees lose interpretability; keep depth low.
approaches.strengths: Captures nonlinear thresholds and interactions natively (e.g., copper reacting only when inventories are low AND the dollar is weakening); no need to pre-specify functional form; RuleFit's importances and partial-dependence-style rule effects are easy to explain to stakeholders; useful as an interpretable contrast to the repo's existing XGBoost/LightGBM (you can show which rules the black box is implicitly using).
approaches.weaknesses: Single trees are high-variance and unstable (small data changes reshuffle splits), and they extrapolate poorly — a serious problem for trending copper prices, since a tree cannot predict a price outside its training range; this is the mechanism behind trees losing to the RW for copper. Step-function predictions are unrealistic for a smooth price series. RuleFit mitigates variance but still cannot extrapolate beyond training thresholds and needs enough data per horizon (monthly copper has limited observations). Best on stationary transformations (returns, spreads), not price levels.
approaches.copper_relevance: Naturally uses threshold effects in COT positioning extremes, inventory levels (LME/COMEX/SHFE), futures basis/backwardation flags, DXY/CNY moves, China IP surprises and calendar/seasonal flags — all of which plausibly act non-linearly on copper. RuleFit can encode 'backwardation + low inventory + positive China IP' as a single interpretable bullish rule.

key_papers.citation: Diaz, J. D., Hansen, E., & Cabrera, G. (2020). A random walk through the trees: Forecasting copper prices using decision learning methods. Resources Policy, 69, 101797.
key_papers.method: Regression trees, random forests and gradient-boosted regression trees vs a random-walk benchmark; copper at 1-day, 1-week, 1-month, 6-month, 1-year, 2-year horizons; predictors = lagged copper plus gold, silver, crude oil, natural gas, lean hogs, coffee futures and the Dow Jones.
key_papers.finding: The random walk delivered the best forecasts at essentially every horizon (e.g., 1-day RW RMSE ~1.25% vs regression tree ~3.16%; 1-year RW RMSE ~14.4% vs trees ~21-24%). Single regression trees were the weakest; even the ensembles did not overturn the RW. Headline: for copper, transparent single trees do NOT beat the random walk — interpret them as diagnostics, not forecasters. Supports weak-form efficiency of copper.

key_papers.citation: Liu, C., Hu, Z., Li, Y., & Liu, S. (2017). Forecasting copper prices by decision tree learning. Resources Policy, 52, 427-434.
key_papers.method: Single decision/regression-tree learning for short-term (days) and long-term (years) copper price forecasting.
key_papers.finding: Reported mean absolute percentage errors below 4%, arguing the approach is assumption-free, robust and transferable to other metals. Note the caveat: this study reports low MAPE but does NOT establish superiority over a random walk (the later Diaz et al. 2020 study, using an explicit RW benchmark, found trees do not beat RW for copper) — so treat the low MAPE as in-sample/level accuracy, not as evidence of genuine edge.

key_papers.citation: Friedman, J. H., & Popescu, B. E. (2008). Predictive learning via rule ensembles. Annals of Applied Statistics, 2(3), 916-954.
key_papers.method: RuleFit: extract rules from tree ensembles and fit a sparse (LASSO/L1-regularized) linear model over rules plus linear terms.
key_papers.finding: Foundational method paper (not commodity-specific): demonstrates that a LASSO over decision rules yields models competitive with full tree ensembles while remaining interpretable via signed rule coefficients and rule importances. Relevant as the canonical interpretable alternative to XGBoost/LightGBM for copper; commodity-specific out-of-sample copper evidence for RuleFit is not yet established in the literature I located.

approaches.name: Generalized additive models (GAM) and penalized spline regression
approaches.one_line: Model copper returns as a sum of smooth, individually plottable functions of each driver (splines), giving nonlinear flexibility while keeping every effect readable as a partial-dependence shape.
approaches.mechanism: A GAM replaces each linear term beta*x with a smooth function f(x) estimated by penalized splines (cubic/thin-plate/P-splines), so the model is g(E[y]) = f1(x1) + f2(x2) + ... ; a roughness penalty (chosen by REML/GCV, e.g. mgcv in R, pyGAM in Python) controls wiggliness. What is interpretable: each f_j is a 1-D curve you can plot — the estimated nonlinear effect of, say, the DXY change or inventory level on copper, with confidence bands. Additivity means effects don't interact unless you add explicit tensor-product interaction terms, so each driver's contribution is isolated and explainable. GAMLSS extends this to model the variance/quantiles, giving interpretable time-varying volatility.
approaches.horizon_fit: Most natural at MONTHLY horizon, where slow-moving fundamentals (real yields, breakevens, China IP, inventories) plausibly have stable nonlinear effects that splines can trace. At WEEKLY horizon GAMs can capture smooth nonlinearities in technical/positioning features but with more overfitting risk and limited level-predictability vs RW. Strongly analogous to the established use of GAMs/GAMLSS in short- and mid-term ELECTRICITY price and demand forecasting, where they are a workhorse interpretable nonlinear model.
approaches.interpretability: High and visually intuitive: partial-dependence curves per predictor with uncertainty bands; the additive structure makes attribution clean. Slightly less transparent than a bare linear coefficient because effects are functions not numbers, but far more interpretable than any tree ensemble or neural net. Smoothing-parameter choice and basis dimension are the main hidden knobs.
approaches.strengths: Captures threshold/saturation/asymmetric responses (e.g., copper's convex response to inventory depletion, or asymmetric reaction to dollar strength vs weakness) while remaining explainable; built-in confidence bands; handles cyclical/seasonal effects via cyclic splines (calendar effects); GAMLSS gives interpretable predictive intervals competing with the repo's quantile regression; well-supported tooling (mgcv, pyGAM).
approaches.weaknesses: Additivity can miss genuine interactions unless tensor-product smooths are added (which costs interpretability and data); splines can overfit / extrapolate wildly outside the observed predictor range (dangerous for trending copper); needs enough monthly observations per smooth term (data-hungry relative to a linear model); smoothing-parameter and knot choices affect results; like all level models it inherits the RW-is-hard-to-beat problem at short horizons. Copper-specific peer-reviewed GAM evidence is thin — this is a gap to be tested, not a proven winner.
approaches.copper_relevance: Ideal for the repo's fundamental/macro block: smooth f() of real yields, breakeven inflation, China industrial production, LME/SHFE inventory levels, futures basis, and DXY/CNY — each producing a readable response curve. Cyclic splines naturally encode seasonal/calendar effects already in the feature set. Cross-asset ratios (copper/gold, copper/oil) enter as smooth terms with plottable shapes.

key_papers.citation: Serinaldi, F. (2011) and the GAMLSS-based electricity price forecasting literature, e.g. 'Short-term Electricity Price Forecasting Using Generalized Additive Models' (CEUR Workshop Proceedings, Vol-2393); Wood, S. N. (2017), Generalized Additive Models: An Introduction with R (2nd ed., CRC) as the methodological reference.
key_papers.method: Penalized-spline GAM / GAMLSS for short- and mid-term electricity price and demand forecasting; mgcv-style estimation.
key_papers.finding: GAMs/GAMLSS are established, reliable interpretable nonlinear forecasters in energy price/demand applications, providing both point forecasts and full predictive distributions via smooth effects. This is the strongest evidence base for GAMs in a commodity-like setting; I did NOT locate a peer-reviewed GAM study benchmarked specifically on LME/COMEX copper against a random walk, so for copper the GAM case rests on close analogy plus the method's transparency rather than direct copper out-of-sample evidence.

approaches.name: Symbolic regression / genetic programming (incl. Bayesian symbolic regression)
approaches.one_line: Search over the space of mathematical expressions to discover an explicit closed-form equation relating copper drivers to price, returning a human-readable formula rather than weights.
approaches.mechanism: Genetic programming evolves a population of expression trees (combining variables with +, -, x, /, exp, log, lags) under a fitness = accuracy-minus-complexity objective, so the output is an explicit algebraic equation. Bayesian Symbolic Regression (BSR) replaces the evolutionary search with a Bayesian sampler over expression structures, returning a posterior over equations (and thus uncertainty over the functional form). What is interpretable: the final model IS an equation you can write down and inspect term-by-term, revealing the discovered functional relationships (e.g., a ratio or interaction of inventories and the dollar). Parsimony pressure keeps equations short enough to read.
approaches.horizon_fit: In principle horizon-agnostic, but the only rigorous commodity benchmark (crude oil, monthly) found no significant edge, so it is best viewed as exploratory at MONTHLY horizon and not recommended as a primary weekly forecaster. Useful for hypothesis generation about nonlinear copper-driver relationships that you then harden into LASSO/GAM features.
approaches.interpretability: Among the most interpretable possible outputs (a literal formula), and BSR adds a posterior over formulae. Caveat: the search can return brittle, hard-to-justify expressions, and equation interpretability does not guarantee economic plausibility — readability is not the same as correctness.
approaches.strengths: Produces explicit, transferable equations; can uncover unexpected functional forms and interactions; BSR is computationally faster than GP-based symbolic regression and quantifies structural uncertainty; appealing for communicating a transparent copper model to non-technical stakeholders.
approaches.weaknesses: Documented to NOT significantly beat standard benchmarks on a commodity (crude oil) out-of-sample; highly sensitive to the chosen function/operator set and initialization (a non-trivial design burden); prone to overfitting and to producing unstable equations under regime change; computationally heavy (GP variant); limited, mostly negative or inconclusive empirical track record on metals specifically; risk of spurious formulae that fit history but lack economic meaning.
approaches.copper_relevance: Could in principle discover explicit relationships among the futures basis, inventories, DXY/CNY, China IP and cross-asset ratios, but there is no copper-specific success story in the literature located; treat as a research/diagnostic tool, not a production forecaster, and validate any discovered equation against a RW and against economic priors.

key_papers.citation: Drachal, K. (2022/2023). Forecasting the Crude Oil Spot Price with Bayesian Symbolic Regression. Energies, 16(1), 4.
key_papers.method: Bayesian Symbolic Regression (BSR) on monthly crude-oil spot price (Jan 1986-Apr 2021), benchmarked against LASSO, ridge, dynamic model averaging, Bayesian model averaging, ARIMA, naive and time-varying-parameter regressions.
key_papers.finding: BSR did NOT produce forecasts that were statistically significantly more accurate than the benchmark models, though it was computationally faster than genetic-programming-based symbolic regression. Headline: explicit-equation discovery is interpretable but, on the closest rigorously benchmarked commodity, it failed to beat simpler interpretable methods like LASSO/DMA — a cautionary result for applying it to copper as a primary model.

key_papers.citation: Drachal, K. (2024). Forecasting Selected Commodities' Prices with the Bayesian Symbolic Regression. International Journal of Financial Studies, 12(2), 34.
key_papers.method: Bayesian Symbolic Regression applied to several commodity prices, extending the crude-oil study.
key_papers.finding: Broadly consistent with the oil result: BSR is interpretable and competitive but does not deliver a clear, robust out-of-sample advantage over established benchmarks across commodities — reinforcing that symbolic regression's main value for copper is transparency and hypothesis generation rather than accuracy.

approaches.name: Gaussian-process regression (GPR)
approaches.one_line: A nonparametric Bayesian regression that returns a full predictive distribution (mean plus calibrated uncertainty bands) over copper prices, with semi-interpretability through the choice and length-scales of the kernel.
approaches.mechanism: GPR places a prior over functions defined by a covariance kernel (e.g., RBF/Matern + periodic + linear); conditioning on data yields a posterior mean forecast AND a closed-form predictive variance. Hyperparameters (kernel length-scales, signal/noise variances) are fit by marginal-likelihood maximization, cross-validation or Bayesian optimization. What is interpretable: the kernel structure is a modeling choice you specify (trend + seasonality + noise are separable, additive kernels), and the learned length-scale per input feature acts as an automatic-relevance-determination (ARD) importance measure — long length-scale = irrelevant feature. The headline interpretable output is the calibrated uncertainty band, not a coefficient.
approaches.horizon_fit: Most valuable for WEEKLY (and monthly) PROBABILISTIC forecasting — its native, well-calibrated prediction intervals directly complement the repo's quantile-regression and ARIMAX/SARIMAX interval machinery. As a point forecaster for copper it inherits the RW-is-hard-to-beat caveat, especially because the published metals GPR studies are autoregressive and seldom benchmark against a RW. Good for honest uncertainty at both horizons; weaker as a level-beating point model at weekly.
approaches.interpretability: Semi-interpretable. Strong on uncertainty (full predictive distribution) and on kernel-level structure (separable trend/seasonal/noise components; ARD length-scales rank feature relevance). Weaker on coefficient-style attribution — there is no single signed weight per driver, and with many features the kernel becomes a partial black box. More transparent than a neural net, less than LASSO/GAM.
approaches.strengths: Best-in-class calibrated uncertainty for risk management and interval forecasts; flexible nonlinear fit without specifying functional form; ARD gives a soft feature-importance read; handles small/medium samples (monthly copper) well; robust, documented success fitting metal/commodity series; composes with the repo's ensemble as a probabilistic member.
approaches.weaknesses: O(n^3) scaling limits very long daily histories (less an issue at weekly/monthly); kernel choice strongly drives behavior and is a modeling burden; can extrapolate to the prior mean (reverting) outside the data, which may understate trend continuation; the metals-GPR literature's strong fit metrics are largely in-sample-style autoregressive results WITHOUT a random-walk benchmark, so reported accuracy overstates genuine predictive edge; stationary kernels assume a stable covariance that copper's regime shifts violate.
approaches.copper_relevance: Takes the full driver set as kernel inputs (ARD then ranks LME/COMEX/SHFE prices and inventories, DXY, real yields, China IP, futures basis, COT, cross-asset ratios by length-scale); separable kernels can encode copper seasonality and trend explicitly; the predictive variance naturally widens in volatile/regime-transition periods, dovetailing with the repo's HMM regime detector.

key_papers.citation: Jin, B., & Xu, X. (2025). Machine learning copper price predictions: evidence based on Gaussian process regressions tuned with cross validation and Bayesian optimization. (Advances in Data Science / Springer-indexed program of metal-price GPR papers.)
key_papers.method: Gaussian process regression with hyperparameters tuned by cross-validation and Bayesian optimization, applied to copper prices (autoregressive/lagged-input design).
key_papers.finding: Reports accurate out-of-sample copper forecasts with low relative RMSE and high fit, illustrating GPR's flexibility and native uncertainty quantification for copper. Important caveat: this and the authors' sibling papers (steel, coal, silver, cotton, PPI) are autoregressive and generally do NOT benchmark against a random walk, so the strong fit is not by itself evidence of beating RW — the value for this repo is calibrated intervals and ARD relevance, not a proven level edge.

key_papers.citation: Jin, B., & Xu, X. (2024). Gaussian Process Regression Based Silver Price Forecasts. Journal of Uncertain Systems, and related steel/coal index GPR papers (e.g., regional Chinese steel price index, relative RMSE ~0.45%).
key_papers.method: GPR with Bayesian-optimization/cross-validation hyperparameter tuning for precious/industrial metal and steel price index forecasting.
key_papers.finding: Consistently low out-of-sample relative RMSE (sub-1% on index series) and good generalization, confirming GPR as an effective, uncertainty-aware nonlinear forecaster across metals analogous to copper. Same caveat applies: strong fit metrics, but the studies emphasize accuracy of the GPR fit rather than a rigorous RW-beating comparison.

findings.evaluation_notes: The credible copper/metals literature evaluates out-of-sample with a rolling or expanding window and reports RMSE/MAE/MAPE plus, critically, performance RELATIVE TO A RANDOM-WALK / no-change benchmark (out-of-sample R^2 a la Campbell-Thompson, MSFE ratios), directional/success ratios, and Diebold-Mariano (or Clark-West, for nested models) tests of equal predictive accuracy. Economic-value metrics (Sharpe ratio / certainty-equivalent gains to a mean-variance investor) appear in the better studies (e.g., Zhang et al. 2019). Two recurring methodological red flags to avoid when adding methods to this repo: (1) studies reporting only raw MAPE/RMSE with NO random-walk benchmark (common in the GPR metals papers and in Liu et al. 2017) can look impressive while having no genuine edge — always include the repo's existing naive/RW baseline and report skill relative to it; (2) cross-validation and penalty/hyperparameter tuning must respect time ordering (purged/embargoed walk-forward CV) to avoid look-ahead leakage — the repo's prior 'cv purge' commit indicates awareness of this. For interval/probabilistic methods (GPR, GAMLSS, quantile regression), evaluate calibration (PIT histograms, coverage) and pinball/CRPS loss, not just point error. The strongest positive copper-specific result (Buncic & Moretto 2015) is explicitly framed as OOS R^2 and MSFE improvement vs RW to 6 months — that is the bar new monthly methods should clear.
key_takeaways: For copper at WEEKLY horizon, the random walk is the benchmark to beat and is rarely beaten on level: Diaz, Hansen & Cabrera (2020, Resources Policy) found RW beat single trees and tree ensembles at every horizon from 1 day to 2 years. Deploy interpretable methods weekly mainly for disciplined feature selection (LASSO/elastic net) and calibrated intervals (GPR, GAMLSS, quantile regression), not for expecting large point-accuracy gains.

Genuine, documented copper predictability exists at MONTHLY-to-quarterly horizons and is captured by interpretable, time-varying LINEAR models: Buncic & Moretto (2015, NAJEF) beat the RW by up to ~17% MSFE (OOS R^2 up to ~18.5%) to 6 months on LME monthly copper using fundamentals (excess demand, inventories, convenience yield) plus financial conditioning (risk appetite, momentum, term spread, FX) via Dynamic Model Averaging/Selection. This is the single best template for an interpretable monthly copper model.

Penalized regression is the highest-value, best-evidenced interpretable upgrade: extend the repo's existing ridge to LASSO / elastic net / adaptive-LASSO for transparent sparse selection among the high-dimensional feature set (cross-asset, macro, COT, technicals). Strong analog evidence from crude oil (Zhang, Ma & Wang 2019, J. Empirical Finance: beat the field on OOS R^2, success ratio and economic value) and it is the standard copper-driver selection engine (Liu, Guo & Wei 2024, J. Commodity Markets, LASSO over 75 indicators).

GAMs / penalized splines are the natural interpretable way to add NONLINEAR-but-readable fundamentals (smooth, plottable partial-dependence curves with confidence bands for real yields, China IP, inventories, DXY, futures basis; cyclic splines for calendar effects; GAMLSS for intervals). They are proven workhorses in electricity price/demand forecasting, but copper-specific peer-reviewed GAM evidence is a genuine gap — test against the RW baseline rather than assuming a win.

Gaussian-process regression is the best interpretable PROBABILISTIC complement: native calibrated prediction intervals plus ARD length-scales as soft feature importances, dovetailing with the repo's quantile-regression intervals and HMM regime detector. Caveat: the active metals-GPR literature (Jin & Xu copper/silver/steel/coal papers) reports strong fit but is autoregressive and rarely benchmarks against a random walk, so its accuracy is not evidence of a level edge.

Single decision trees and symbolic regression / genetic programming are interpretable but weak as copper forecasters and should be used as DIAGNOSTIC / communication tools, not accuracy engines: single trees lost to the RW for copper (Diaz et al. 2020) and cannot extrapolate trending prices; Bayesian symbolic regression did NOT significantly beat benchmarks on crude oil (Drachal 2022, Energies). RuleFit (Friedman & Popescu 2008) is the better middle ground — a LASSO-pruned, interpretable rule ensemble that captures threshold interactions while remaining inspectable, and a natural transparent contrast to the repo's XGBoost/LightGBM.

Integration with the repo: LASSO/elastic-net selection and GAM/GPR members slot directly into the existing weighted + stacking ensemble; use the existing naive/RW baseline as the mandatory skill yardstick (OOS R^2 / MSFE-ratio / Diebold-Mariano), keep time-ordered purged CV to prevent leakage, and prefer the time-varying (DMA-style or rolling) variants because copper's China-driven vs financialized regimes break static-coefficient assumptions.

checked_claims.claim: Buncic & Moretto (2015), 'Forecasting copper prices with dynamic averaging and selection models', North American Journal of Economics and Finance, 33, 1-38; DMA improved on RW with OOS R^2 up to ~18.5%, predictability to 6 months, OOS period May 2002-Jun 2014.
checked_claims.note: Paper verified (NAJEF vol 33, pp 1-38, 2015). Author PDF, SSRN, ScienceDirect, RePEc all confirm. Working-paper abstract explicitly states OOS R^2 relative to RW 'as high as 18.5 percent', predictability to 6 months ahead, OOS period May 2002-Jun 2014. Monthly LME copper. The ~17% MSFE-improvement figure was not visible in the abstract I could fetch but is consistent with the paper's framing; the headline OOS R^2 18.5% is confirmed verbatim. This is the strongest correctly-represented copper-specific result.

checked_claims.claim: Zhang, Ma & Wang (2019), 'Forecasting crude oil prices with a large set of predictors: Can LASSO select powerful predictors?', Journal of Empirical Finance, 54, 97-117; LASSO/elastic net beat competing models OOS on R^2 and success ratio, post-LASSO OLS also beat competitors, positive economic value.
checked_claims.note: Verified (J. Empirical Finance vol 54, pp 97-117, 2019). RePEc/ScienceDirect confirm. Empirical claims accurately represented: LASSO and elastic net outperform competing models on OOS R-square and success ratio, OLS on selected predictors beats competitors, mean-variance investor gets positive sizeable economic gains. Crude oil, monthly. Correctly flagged as analog, not copper.

checked_claims.claim: Liu, Guo & Wei (2024), 'Time-varying and multi-scale analysis of copper price influencing factors based on LASSO and EMD methods', Journal of Commodity Markets, 34, 100072; LASSO over 75 copper indicators; fundamentals drive long-run, financial/geopolitical drive short-run; attribution-focused, no RW OOS contest.
checked_claims.note: Paper verified (J. Commodity Markets vol 34, 2024, 75 indicators across inventory/supply/demand/macro/finance/geopolitics, LASSO + EMD). Finding accurately represented and correctly noted as attribution rather than a head-to-head RW forecast contest. Minor citation detail: article/DOI is 10.1016/j.jcomm.2024.100388 (ScienceDirect PII S2405851324000072); the article number '100072' in the citation appears to be a typo/mis-transcription of the volume identifier, but the paper unambiguously exists with the stated authors/title/year/venue.

checked_claims.claim: Diaz, Hansen & Cabrera (2020), Resources Policy 69, 101797; random walk beat single trees AND ensembles at EVERY horizon from 1 day to 2 years; 1-day RW RMSE ~1.25% vs tree ~3.16%; 1-year RW RMSE ~14.4% vs trees ~21-24%.
checked_claims.note: Paper exists and is correctly cited (Resources Policy vol 69, 2020). Core message (RW is hard to beat for copper; supports weak-form efficiency) is sound. BUT specific numbers and the 'every horizon' claim are partly WRONG: actual paper reports 1-year RW RMSE 11.84% (not ~14.4%) vs gradient boosting 17.25% / random forest 17.80% / regression tree 19.70% (not '21-24%'). 1-day figures (RW 1.25%, RT 3.16%) are correct. Critically, at the 2-year horizon the paper states the four models 'become similar'/converge - it does NOT say RW beats trees there. So 'RW beat trees at every horizon 1 day to 2 years' overstates the result.

checked_claims.claim: Liu, Hu, Li & Liu (2017), 'Forecasting copper prices by decision tree learning', Resources Policy 52, 427-434; reported MAPE below 4%; no RW benchmark.
checked_claims.note: Verified (Resources Policy vol 52, pp 427-434, 2017). Single regression-tree learning for short/long-term copper. The findings' caveat that it reports low MAPE but does not establish superiority over a random walk is appropriate and well-handled. MAPE 'below 4%' is consistent with the paper's reported accuracy.

checked_claims.claim: Friedman & Popescu (2008), 'Predictive learning via rule ensembles', Annals of Applied Statistics, 2(3), 916-954; RuleFit = LASSO over decision rules + linear terms; competitive with tree ensembles while interpretable; not commodity-specific.
checked_claims.note: Verified exactly (Annals of Applied Statistics vol 2, issue 3, pp 916-954, 2008, DOI 10.1214/07-AOAS148). Method description (extract rules from tree ensembles, fit sparse L1 model over rules plus linear features) is accurate. Correctly noted that no copper-specific OOS RuleFit evidence exists.

checked_claims.claim: Drachal (2022), 'Forecasting the Crude Oil Spot Price with Bayesian Symbolic Regression', Energies, 16(1), 4; BSR did NOT significantly beat benchmarks (LASSO, ridge, DMA, BMA, ARIMA, naive); computationally faster than GP-based symbolic regression.
checked_claims.note: Verified (Energies vol 16 issue 1 article 4, published Dec 2022; monthly oil Jan 1986-Apr 2021). RePEc abstract confirms verbatim: 'BSR does not result in forecasts that are statistically significantly more accurate than the benchmark models' and 'BSR is computationally faster than the genetic programming-based symbolic regression.' Empirical claim represented accurately - a strong, honestly-stated negative result.

checked_claims.note: Verified (IJFS vol 12 issue 2 article 34, MDPI, March 2024, co-authored with M. Pawlowski). Applies BSR to multiple commodities with GP-symbolic-regression and econometric benchmarks (BMA, DMA, LASSO, ridge, elastic net). Finding (interpretable, competitive, no clear robust edge) is consistent with the abstract. I could not extract the exact per-commodity verdicts due to MDPI 403-blocking, but the directional characterization is sound.

checked_claims.note: Paper exists (Resources Policy vol 64, 101528, 2019) and uses Bayesian DMA model-combination on monthly data 1996-2017. HOWEVER the metals are WRONG: the paper forecasts LEAD, NICKEL and ZINC - it does NOT include copper or aluminium. Multiple sources (RePEc, ScienceDirect abstract) confirm 'lead, nickel and zinc'. The findings JSON's claim that it covers 'copper, aluminium, nickel, zinc' is a factual error; this paper provides no copper-specific evidence and should not be cited as supporting copper.

findings.dimension: Decomposition hybrids, copper-specific empirical literature, and forecast-evaluation methodology (interpretable models only)
findings.overview: This dimension covers three linked strands of the literature. (1) Signal-decomposition + linear/econometric "decompose-and-ensemble" hybrids: a preprocessing transform (wavelet MRA, EMD/EEMD/CEEMDAN, VMD, or STL) splits the price into a small number of additive components, each of which is then forecast with a transparent model (ARIMA/SARIMAX, linear regression) and recombined. The decomposition stage is partly interpretable: STL/wavelet give a trend, named seasonal cycles, and a residual; EMD-family methods give frequency-ordered intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) you can map loosely to high-frequency noise vs low-frequency trend. The forecasting stage stays linear and inspectable. (2) Copper- and base-metal-specific empirical work that explicitly benchmarks against a random walk (RW)/no-change forecast at monthly (and occasionally weekly) horizons. The robust stylized fact: the RW is extremely hard to beat for copper at short-to-medium horizons; interpretable econometric structure (dynamic model averaging, wavelet-ARIMA, mean-reversion in real prices, futures-implied forecasts) tends to add value mainly at horizons of months-to-years, and gains are modest and regime-dependent. (3) Forecast-evaluation methodology: the canonical tests (Diebold-Mariano, Clark-West for nested models, Hansen's Model Confidence Set, Giacomini-White conditional predictive ability, Pesaran-Timmermann directional test) plus economic-value metrics, and the data-snooping/publication-bias correctives (White's Reality Check, Hansen's SPA). A critical, under-appreciated caveat threads through strand (1): when EMD/VMD is applied to the whole series before the train/test split, future information leaks into the components and out-of-sample accuracy is badly overstated. Overall standing: decomposition hybrids are popular and often report large MAPE reductions, but the copper-specific, properly-benchmarked evidence is far more sober than the decompose-and-ensemble headline numbers suggest, and much of the apparent edge evaporates under leakage-safe evaluation and RW benchmarking.

approaches.name: Wavelet (MRA) + ARIMA hybrid
approaches.one_line: Decompose the price with a discrete/maximal-overlap wavelet transform into multiresolution detail and approximation bands, fit a separate ARIMA to each band, and sum the band forecasts.
approaches.mechanism: A wavelet transform produces a multiresolution decomposition: a smooth low-frequency approximation (trend/cycle) plus several detail levels capturing successively higher-frequency oscillations. Each component is more stationary and regular than the raw series, so a low-order ARIMA fits it well. Interpretable elements: you can read off which frequency bands carry forecastable structure (typically the low-frequency approximation) vs which are essentially noise (the finest detail levels), and each band's ARIMA has inspectable AR/MA coefficients. The recomposition is a simple linear sum.
approaches.horizon_fit: Best suited to MONTHLY copper. Kriechbaumer et al. (2014) report gains specifically for one-month-ahead LME base-metal forecasts. At WEEKLY horizon the gain is theoretically plausible (cyclicality is real intra-month) but less tested for copper; finest detail bands at weekly frequency are dominated by microstructure noise and are not forecastable, so the benefit concentrates in the trend band.
approaches.interpretability: Transparent: named frequency bands, per-band ARIMA orders and coefficients, additive recombination. The weakness is that wavelet detail components are mathematical constructs, not economic factors (a band is 'the 8-16 month oscillation', not 'the China-IP cycle'), so the economic story is indirect.
approaches.strengths: Substantial reported accuracy gain over plain ARIMA on the same data; keeps the whole pipeline linear and explainable; built-in prediction intervals via ARIMA; handles the non-stationary, multi-scale character of metal prices better than a single ARIMA.
approaches.weaknesses: Highly sensitive to wavelet family, mother wavelet, and number of decomposition levels (the authors flag this explicitly) — a researcher-degrees-of-freedom / data-snooping risk. Boundary effects at the right edge (the forecast origin) distort the most recent coefficients, which is exactly where you need them. If the transform is computed on the full sample, it leaks future information (same caveat as EMD/VMD).
approaches.copper_relevance: Applied directly to LME cash prices of copper, aluminium, lead, zinc. Naturally a univariate price model; does not itself ingest copper drivers (inventories, USD, China IP, basis) unless those are added as ARIMAX exogenous regressors per band.

key_papers.citation: Kriechbaumer, Angus, Parsons, Rivas Casado (2014), 'An improved wavelet-ARIMA approach for forecasting metal prices', Resources Policy 39, 32-41.
key_papers.method: Wavelet multiresolution decomposition feeding per-band ARIMA, on monthly LME cash prices of aluminium, copper, lead, zinc.
key_papers.finding: Wavelet-ARIMA substantially improves one-month-ahead accuracy over classic ARIMA; reported potential improvement of about $126/tonne for copper. Accuracy was highly sensitive to wavelet type/function/levels. Benchmark was classic ARIMA (not an explicit random walk in the abstract reviewed).

approaches.name: EMD / EEMD / CEEMDAN + linear/ARIMA decompose-and-ensemble
approaches.one_line: Empirically decompose the price into a handful of intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) ordered from high to low frequency plus a residual, forecast each with a transparent model, and sum.
approaches.mechanism: EMD adaptively sifts the series into IMFs (oscillatory components with locally symmetric envelopes) and a monotonic residual; EEMD adds Gaussian noise across many runs to fix EMD's mode-mixing; CEEMDAN adds adaptive noise with better reconstruction completeness and less residual noise. The interpretable read-out: the residual + lowest-frequency IMFs are the trend, mid IMFs are cyclical, high-frequency IMFs are noise; sample entropy per IMF quantifies which components are 'hard'. In the interpretable variant each IMF is forecast by ARIMA or linear regression (not a neural net), keeping the pipeline inspectable.
approaches.horizon_fit: More natural for MONTHLY copper, where low-frequency IMFs carry genuine macro/cyclical signal that ARIMA can extrapolate. At WEEKLY horizon most of the variance loads onto high-frequency IMFs that are noise, so the leakage-free benefit shrinks. The method is adaptive (no fixed period assumed), which suits copper's irregular cycles better than fixed-seasonal STL.
approaches.interpretability: Partially interpretable: IMFs are frequency-ordered and you can attribute variance to trend vs cycle vs noise, but individual IMFs lack a clean economic label and their number/shape changes as new data arrive (mode instability), which undermines a stable narrative.
approaches.strengths: Adaptive, data-driven, no pre-specified seasonality; handles non-linear, non-stationary copper dynamics; consistently reports large in-sample/test MAPE reductions; the ARIMA-per-IMF version stays explainable.
approaches.weaknesses: TWO serious failure modes. (a) Look-ahead/information leakage: if EMD/EEMD/CEEMDAN is run on the entire series before the train/test split (the common practice), future data enter the components and out-of-sample metrics are massively inflated — Yang, Li & Jiang (2024) show near-zero 'RMSE' that collapses once leakage is removed. Leakage-safe forecasting requires re-decomposing only on data up to each forecast origin (sliding/expanding window), which is expensive and erodes most of the headline gain. (b) Mode mixing and right-edge instability mean the most recent IMFs (the ones that matter for forecasting) are the least stable. Many published copper/metal decompose-ensemble results do not state whether decomposition was leakage-safe, so their reported edge over a random walk is unreliable.
approaches.copper_relevance: Applied to LME copper/aluminium/zinc cash and futures series. Usually univariate; copper drivers enter only if each IMF is modelled with exogenous regressors. The trend IMF is where you would attach slow drivers (China IP, USD, real rates); the cyclical IMFs where inventory/basis dynamics might load.

key_papers.citation: Liu, Liu, Zhou, Yan (2022), 'A multi-model fusion based non-ferrous metal price forecasting', Resources Policy 77.
key_papers.method: Dual-stage CEEMDAN then VMD (PSO-tuned) on the highest-sample-entropy subsequence, components forecast by LSTM (a black-box back-end), on LME copper, aluminium, zinc.
key_papers.finding: Beat ARIMA/BPNN/LSTM and other hybrids on RMSE/MAE/MAPE in-sample-period tests. NOTE: forecasting back-end is opaque (LSTM) and the paper does not clearly establish leakage-safe decomposition, so cite as evidence the decomposition stage helps, not as proof of genuine out-of-sample edge.

key_papers.citation: Yang, Li & Jiang (2024), 'Research on information leakage in time series prediction based on empirical mode decomposition', Scientific Reports 14:28362.
key_papers.method: Methodological critique; constructs leakage-safe CEEMDAN variants (sliding-window SW-CEEMDAN; single-train-multi-predict; multi-train-multi-predict).
key_papers.finding: Decomposing the whole series before splitting leaks future information and produces near-zero, invalid error metrics (e.g. RMSE collapsing to ~0.001); leakage-safe re-decomposition raises error by 1-2 orders of magnitude. Direct warning that most decompose-and-ensemble results are 'inflated' — essential caveat for any copper EMD/VMD hybrid.

approaches.name: VMD (Variational Mode Decomposition) + linear/ARIMA hybrid
approaches.one_line: Decompose the price into a pre-set number K of band-limited modes by solving a variational optimization, then forecast each mode with a transparent model and sum.
approaches.mechanism: VMD jointly extracts K modes, each compact around a center frequency, by minimizing the sum of mode bandwidths subject to exact reconstruction. Unlike EMD's recursive sifting, it is a single optimization, so modes are more robust to noise and less prone to mode mixing; the center frequencies are an interpretable read-out of the dominant cycles. In the interpretable variant, ARIMA fits each mode (ARIMA for linear/low-frequency modes, with the non-linear residual modes optionally handled by another transparent learner).
approaches.horizon_fit: MONTHLY copper is the natural fit: low-frequency VMD modes capture the macro cycle that an ARIMA can project. WEEKLY use is feasible but the high-frequency modes are largely unforecastable noise. VMD's need to pre-specify K is a drawback for copper, whose number of meaningful cycles is not known a priori (often tuned by particle-swarm/grid search — a snooping risk).
approaches.interpretability: More interpretable than EMD on the decomposition side (fixed K modes, explicit center frequencies you can name as 'the ~annual cycle', 'the multi-year cycle'), but K and the bandwidth penalty are hyperparameters chosen by the modeller, which is a transparency caveat.
approaches.strengths: Robust, noise-resistant decomposition with a solid variational foundation; cleaner modes than EMD/EEMD; pairs well with ARIMA to keep the pipeline linear; center frequencies give a genuine cycle interpretation.
approaches.weaknesses: Same leakage trap as EMD if applied to the full series pre-split. Must pre-set K and penalty; results sensitive to these. Center-frequency modes still are not direct economic drivers. Most published metal VMD hybrids pair VMD with deep nets and do not isolate the value of the (interpretable) decomposition stage alone.
approaches.copper_relevance: Used on LME copper/aluminium/zinc. Univariate by default; drivers attach per-mode as exogenous ARIMAX regressors. The low-frequency mode is the natural carrier for slow macro drivers (USD, China IP), making per-mode ARIMAX a clean way to inject copper fundamentals while staying interpretable.

key_papers.citation: Liu, Liu, Zhou, Yan (2022), Resources Policy 77 (CEEMDAN+VMD secondary decomposition, LME copper/aluminium/zinc).
key_papers.method: VMD used as a secondary decomposition on the most complex CEEMDAN subsequence; PSO-tuned K.
key_papers.finding: Secondary VMD on the high-entropy component improved accuracy vs single-stage decomposition on RMSE/MAE/MAPE. Same leakage caveat applies; treat as support for VMD's denoising value, not as a clean RW-beating out-of-sample result.

approaches.name: STL / classical seasonal decomposition + ARIMA(X)
approaches.one_line: Split the series into trend, a (possibly time-varying) seasonal component, and a remainder via local regression, forecast trend+remainder with ARIMA(X) and re-attach the seasonal forecast.
approaches.mechanism: STL (Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS; Cleveland et al. 1990) uses iterated loess smoothing to extract a smooth trend and a seasonal component that can evolve over time, leaving a remainder. The standard pipeline (e.g. statsmodels STLForecast) deseasonalizes, fits ARIMA to the seasonally-adjusted series, then adds back the seasonal forecast. Every piece is human-readable: the trend line, the seasonal shape and its amplitude, and the residual.
approaches.horizon_fit: Most defensible for MONTHLY copper IF a stable calendar seasonal exists (copper's seasonality is weak and demand-driven, so the seasonal component is often small — which STL will honestly show). At WEEKLY horizon, intra-year seasonality is marginal; STL mainly buys you a clean trend/remainder split for the ARIMA. Better viewed as a robust, outlier-resistant deseasonalizer than a source of large copper alpha.
approaches.interpretability: The most interpretable of all decomposition methods: trend, named seasonal cycle with explicit strength, and remainder, all on the original price scale. Trend/seasonal strength statistics directly tell you how much forecastable structure exists.
approaches.strengths: Robust to outliers and supply-shock spikes (loess down-weights them); allows slowly changing seasonality; trivial to combine with existing ARIMAX/SARIMAX; gives an honest, inspectable picture of how little seasonality copper actually has.
approaches.weaknesses: Assumes additive trend+seasonal+remainder structure; copper's dominant variation is the aperiodic macro cycle, not calendar seasonality, so STL's value-add over a good SARIMAX is limited. Right-edge trend estimate is uncertain. Will not, by itself, beat a random walk — it is a preprocessing/diagnostic aid, not a standalone edge.
approaches.copper_relevance: Naturally separates any China-construction-season demand seasonality from the macro trend; the remainder is the series on which to regress copper drivers (inventories, USD, basis, COT) via ARIMAX. Pairs cleanly with the repo's existing SARIMAX and Prophet (which is itself a trend+seasonal structural model).

approaches.name: Copper-specific interpretable econometric models benchmarked vs random walk (DMA/DMS, mean-reversion, futures-implied)
approaches.one_line: Transparent econometric structures — dynamic model averaging/selection with time-varying parameters, mean-reverting real-price models, and futures-curve-implied forecasts — evaluated head-to-head against the no-change random walk for copper at monthly+ horizons.
approaches.mechanism: DMA/DMS (Raftery-style) runs many small linear predictive regressions in parallel, lets a state-space recursion put time-varying weights on models and on time-varying coefficients, and you can read off which predictors are 'switched on' at each date (excess demand, inventories, convenience yield, S&P500, VIX, yield spread, TED spread, industrial production). Mean-reversion models exploit that real metal prices revert to a (cost-driven) long-run level. Futures-implied forecasts use the copper futures curve / basis as the expected future spot. All three are interpretable: weights, mean-reversion speed, or the observable futures curve.
approaches.horizon_fit: This is the core copper evidence at MONTHLY-to-multi-month horizons. Consistent finding: the random walk wins at short horizons (days-to-1 month), interpretable structure adds modest value from ~1 month out to 6 months, and only at long horizons (1-2 years) do richer models clearly separate from RW. Weekly horizon is essentially RW territory.
approaches.interpretability: High. DMA exposes time-varying predictor inclusion probabilities and coefficients (you see exactly when inventories or the convenience yield start mattering); mean-reversion exposes the long-run anchor and reversion speed; futures-implied is fully observable from market prices.
approaches.strengths: Directly answers 'does anything beat the random walk for copper, and where' with real out-of-sample R2; uses genuine copper drivers; DMA handles structural breaks/regime change via time-varying weights; futures-implied needs no estimation and embeds the market's storage/convenience-yield information.
approaches.weaknesses: Gains over RW are modest and concentrated at longer horizons; DMA out-of-sample R2 (up to ~18.5%) is period-specific and can be fragile; mean-reversion fails during persistent regime shifts (e.g. structural China-demand re-rating) when the 'long-run level' itself moves; futures-implied forecasts have historically often underperformed the no-change benchmark at short horizons. Tree/ML methods do NOT rescue this — Diaz, Hansen & Cabrera (2020) show the RW beats regression trees/random forests/boosting for copper at almost all horizons.
approaches.copper_relevance: Maximal: these papers explicitly use copper inventories (LME/COMEX/SHFE), convenience yield/basis, excess demand, USD-linked and global-risk variables (VIX, TED, yield spread), and industrial production — exactly the driver set in the user's repo. Futures-implied uses HG=F / LME forward curve directly.

key_papers.citation: Buncic & Moretto (2014/2015), 'Forecasting Copper Prices with Dynamic Averaging and Selection Models', Univ. St. Gallen working paper EWP-1430 / J. of Commodity Markets.
key_papers.method: Dynamic model averaging and selection (DMA/DMS) with time-varying parameters over 18 predictors (excess demand, inventories, convenience yield, S&P500, VIX, yield/TED spreads, industrial production).
key_papers.finding: Out-of-sample R2 vs random walk up to ~18.5% (DMA) and ~13.7% (DMS) at the one-month horizon; significant outperformance of the RW for horizons up to 6 months, weakening with horizon. Out-of-sample 2002-2014. A leading interpretable copper result that genuinely beats RW at monthly horizon.

key_papers.citation: Diaz, Hansen & Cabrera (2020), 'A random walk through the trees: Forecasting copper prices using decision learning methods', Resources Policy.
key_papers.method: Regression trees, random forests, gradient boosting vs random walk; predictors = lagged copper plus gold/silver/oil/natural gas/lean hogs/coffee futures and the Dow; horizons 1-day to 2-year; rolling window; RMSE/MAE.
key_papers.finding: The random walk produces the best forecasts in the short and medium run (e.g. 1-day RW RMSE ~1.25%, far below trees; 1-year RW 11.84% vs RT 19.70%); models only converge to RW at the 2-year horizon. Strong evidence that interpretable-or-not, beating RW for copper at weekly/monthly horizons is very hard.

key_papers.citation: Sanchez Lasheras, de Cos Juez, Suarez Sanchez, Krzemien, Riesgo Fernandez (2015), 'Forecasting the COMEX copper spot price by means of neural networks and ARIMA models', Resources Policy 45, 37-43.
key_papers.method: ARIMA vs MLP and Elman neural networks on COMEX copper spot.
key_papers.finding: Neural nets outperformed ARIMA on their COMEX sample. NOTE: included only as a contrast point — no random walk benchmark reported, and NN is the opaque approach the user wants to avoid; ARIMA is the interpretable baseline here.

approaches.name: Forecast-evaluation methodology and data-snooping correctives
approaches.one_line: The standard toolkit for deciding whether a copper forecast genuinely beats a benchmark out-of-sample, plus the tests that guard against picking winners by chance.
approaches.mechanism: Diebold-Mariano (1995): tests equal predictive accuracy of two forecasts via the mean loss differential with a HAC variance — for NON-nested models. Clark-West (2007): adjusts the loss differential for the extra parameter noise when the larger model nests the benchmark (essential when comparing an ARIMAX/DMA against a random walk, which is nested). Giacomini-White (2006): tests CONDITIONAL predictive ability (is model A better given the current state/regime?), regressing the loss differential on conditioning variables. Hansen's Model Confidence Set (Hansen, Lunde & Nason 2003/2011): from many models, returns the set that contains the best with a given confidence — the multi-model generalization of DM. Pesaran-Timmermann (1992): tests directional/sign accuracy (are up/down calls better than independence?), the right metric for trading. Economic-value metrics: turn forecasts into long/short or portfolio positions and measure Sharpe/return net of transaction costs. Data-snooping correctives: White's Reality Check (2000) and Hansen's SPA test (2005) test whether the BEST of many rules/models truly beats the benchmark after accounting for the search over all of them.
approaches.horizon_fit: Horizon-agnostic, but the choices matter for copper: use Clark-West (not plain DM) whenever the candidate nests the random walk; use Pesaran-Timmermann and net-of-cost economic value at WEEKLY/MONTHLY horizons because statistical RMSE gains over RW are tiny there while directional/economic value can still exist; use the MCS when comparing the repo's whole stable of models at once.
approaches.interpretability: These are the meta-layer that makes the interpretable models' claims credible: each test yields a readable statistic and p-value, and the MCS yields an explicit shortlist of surviving models.
approaches.strengths: Lets you make honest, like-for-like claims ('beats RW with CW p<0.05 at 1 month; not at 1 week'); separates statistical accuracy from economic value; SPA/Reality Check and the MCS directly control the multiple-comparisons / data-snooping problem that plagues decompose-and-ensemble papers.
approaches.weaknesses: Plain DM is invalid (oversized) for nested model comparisons vs RW — a very common error in the metal-forecasting literature; many papers report only RMSE/MAE with no significance test, no nesting correction, and no multiple-testing control, so their 'we beat the random walk' claims are fragile. Economic-value results frequently reverse once realistic transaction costs are included.
approaches.copper_relevance: Directly applicable to the user's pipeline: Clark-West for Ridge/ARIMAX/DMA/cointegration vs the Naive RW; MCS across the full ensemble (Ridge, SARIMAX, Prophet, cointegration ECM, HMM, quantile, XGBoost/LightGBM); Pesaran-Timmermann + net-of-cost backtest for the trading use-case; SPA/Reality Check to discount the inevitable in-sample tuning of decomposition hyperparameters and feature sets.

key_papers.citation: Diebold & Mariano (1995, JBES); West (1996); Clark & West (2007, J. Econometrics); Giacomini & White (2006, Econometrica); Hansen, Lunde & Nason (2011, Econometrica, Model Confidence Set); Pesaran & Timmermann (1992, JBES); White (2000, Econometrica, Reality Check); Hansen (2005, JBES, SPA).
key_papers.method: Canonical forecast-evaluation and data-snooping tests (DM, CW for nested, GW conditional, MCS, PT directional, Reality Check / SPA for multiple comparisons).
key_papers.finding: These are methods, not empirical copper results: the load-bearing point is that copper claims must use Clark-West (nested vs RW), report directional (Pesaran-Timmermann) and net-of-cost economic value, and control data-snooping (SPA/MCS); failing to do so is why much of the decompose-and-ensemble literature overstates its edge.

key_papers.citation: World Bank (2023), 'Forecasting Industrial Commodity Prices: Literature Review and a Model Suite', Policy Research Working Paper 10611; and the survey/benchmark literature (e.g. 'Forecasting Commodity Prices: Looking for a Benchmark', Forecasting 2021).
key_papers.method: Reviews and model-suite comparisons across industrial commodities incl. copper/base metals; RW/no-change, ARIMA, futures-based, factor/Bayesian, and ML; DM-type tests and directional accuracy.
key_papers.finding: Recurring stylized facts: the random walk/no-change is the benchmark to beat and is hard to beat for metals at short horizons; consensus and futures-based forecasts can show useful DIRECTIONAL accuracy at sub-annual horizons even when RMSE gains are small; biggest RMSE improvements appear for silver/copper/wheat while oil and gold remain near-RW. Confirms that interpretable structure helps mostly at monthly+ horizons and via direction, not via large short-horizon RMSE gains.

findings.evaluation_notes: Benchmarks: the random walk / no-change forecast is the universal benchmark; futures-implied (no-change-in-basis) forecasts are a secondary benchmark for metals. Headline metric is out-of-sample R2 (a la Campbell-Thompson) or RMSE/MAE/MAPE ratios vs RW. Significance testing: Diebold-Mariano for non-nested pairs; CRITICALLY, Clark-West must replace plain DM whenever the model nests the RW (most ARIMAX/DMA-vs-RW comparisons), because DM is oversized in the nested case — a frequent error in the metal literature. Giacomini-White is used when predictability is regime-conditional. Hansen's Model Confidence Set is the right tool when comparing many models at once (as in the user's ensemble). Directional/sign accuracy is assessed with the Pesaran-Timmermann test; this often matters more than RMSE at weekly/monthly horizons where RMSE gains over RW are negligible but direction can still be predictable. Economic value is assessed by converting forecasts to positions and measuring Sharpe/return NET of transaction costs — gains frequently vanish after costs. Data-snooping/publication-bias controls: White's Reality Check (2000) and Hansen's SPA test (2005) test whether the best of many searched rules truly beats the benchmark; very few decompose-and-ensemble metal papers apply them, despite heavy hyperparameter search over wavelet/VMD/EMD settings and feature sets. Two integrity red flags specific to this dimension: (1) look-ahead leakage when EMD/VMD/wavelet is computed on the full sample before splitting (Yang, Li & Jiang 2024 show this inflates accuracy by 1-2 orders of magnitude); (2) selective reporting of the best decomposition configuration without multiple-testing correction. Many copper/metal decomposition papers also report only point-error metrics with no significance test and no RW benchmark at all.
key_takeaways: For copper at WEEKLY and short MONTHLY horizons the random walk is extremely hard to beat: Diaz, Hansen & Cabrera (2020, Resources Policy) show RW beats trees/forests/boosting at nearly all horizons (e.g. 1-year RW RMSE 11.84% vs 19.70% for a regression tree), converging only at 2 years. Keep the Naive/RW baseline as the benchmark every other model must clear.

The strongest GENUINELY interpretable copper result is dynamic model averaging/selection: Buncic & Moretto report out-of-sample R2 vs RW up to ~18.5% at one month and significant gains to 6 months, with readable time-varying inclusion of inventories, convenience yield, VIX, TED/yield spreads and industrial production. This is the closest analogue to the user's Ridge/ARIMAX/cointegration stack and shows where the edge lives: monthly+, and via slow macro drivers.

Decompose-and-ensemble hybrids (wavelet-ARIMA, EMD/EEMD/CEEMDAN, VMD) genuinely add value over plain ARIMA in-sample — Kriechbaumer et al. (2014) report ~$126/tonne one-month copper improvement from wavelet-ARIMA on LME metals — and the decomposition stage is interpretable (trend/cycle/noise bands). They are most appropriate at the MONTHLY horizon.

CRITICAL CAVEAT: most decompose-and-ensemble papers risk look-ahead leakage by decomposing the whole series before the train/test split. Yang, Li & Jiang (2024, Scientific Reports) show this can shrink reported RMSE toward zero and that leakage-safe re-decomposition (sliding/expanding window) raises error by 1-2 orders of magnitude. Any copper EMD/VMD/wavelet hybrid MUST re-decompose only on data up to each forecast origin, or its out-of-sample edge is illusory.

Of the decomposition methods, STL is the most interpretable (trend + named seasonal + remainder, on price scale) but copper has weak calendar seasonality, so STL is best used as an honest deseasonalizer/diagnostic feeding ARIMAX rather than an alpha source; VMD (fixed K modes with named center frequencies) is the most interpretable of the adaptive methods; EMD-family IMFs are only loosely interpretable and unstable at the right edge.

Use the right evaluation tests: Clark-West (NOT plain Diebold-Mariano) whenever a model nests the random walk; Hansen's Model Confidence Set to compare the whole ensemble at once; Pesaran-Timmermann for directional accuracy; and net-of-cost economic-value backtests — because at weekly/monthly horizons statistical RMSE gains over RW are tiny while directional/economic value may still exist.

Guard against publication bias and data-snooping with White's Reality Check / Hansen's SPA test, which almost no metal-decomposition papers apply despite heavy searching over wavelet families, mode counts, and feature sets. Treat large reported MAPE reductions in the decomposition literature skeptically unless the paper states leakage-safe decomposition, a RW benchmark, and a nesting-aware significance test.

Futures/basis-implied forecasts and mean-reversion in REAL copper prices are interpretable, copper-native additions: the survey/benchmark and World Bank (PRWP 10611) literature finds consensus/futures-based forecasts can deliver useful DIRECTIONAL accuracy at sub-annual horizons even when RMSE barely beats RW, and that the biggest RMSE improvements among commodities appear for silver/copper/wheat (vs near-RW oil and gold).
