verdict.dimension: Decomposition hybrids, copper-specific empirical literature, and forecast-evaluation methodology (interpretable models only)

checked_claims.claim: Kriechbaumer, Angus, Parsons, Rivas Casado (2014), 'An improved wavelet-ARIMA approach for forecasting metal prices', Resources Policy 39, 32-41 — wavelet-ARIMA improves one-month-ahead copper accuracy by ~$126/tonne vs classic ARIMA, highly sensitive to wavelet type/function/levels; benchmark was classic ARIMA (not RW).
checked_claims.note: Verified exactly. Resources Policy vol. 39(C), pp. 32-41, DOI 10.1016/j.resourpol.2013.10.005. Abstract confirms one-month-ahead improvement of $126/t for copper (and $53/$50/$51 for Al/Pb/Zn) relative to classic ARIMA, and that the method identifies the optimal wavelet transform/function/decomposition-level combination (i.e. results depend on these — the findings' data-snooping caveat is fair). Benchmark is classic ARIMA, not a random walk, exactly as the findings state.

checked_claims.claim: Buncic & Moretto, 'Forecasting Copper Prices with Dynamic Averaging and Selection Models' — DMA/DMS over ~18 predictors; out-of-sample R2 vs RW up to ~18.5% (DMA) and ~13.7% (DMS) at one month; significant gains to 6 months; OOS period 2002-2014.
checked_claims.note: Paper exists; DMA out-of-sample R2 up to 18.5% vs RW and OOS period May 2002-June 2014 confirmed; predictors (excess demand, inventories, convenience yield, S&P500, VIX, yield/TED spreads, industrial production) and time-varying predictor importance confirmed. CAVEAT ON VENUE: the citation lists 'Univ. St. Gallen working paper EWP-1430 / J. of Commodity Markets.' The working paper (St. Gallen EWP / SSRN 2482015) is real, but the published version appeared in The North American Journal of Economics and Finance, vol. 33 (2015), pp. 1-38 — NOT the Journal of Commodity Markets. The DMS ~13.7% figure was not independently confirmed in search but is plausible and consistent with the paper; the headline DMA 18.5% and the qualitative claims are solid.

checked_claims.claim: Diaz, Hansen & Cabrera (2020), 'A random walk through the trees: Forecasting copper prices using decision learning methods', Resources Policy — RW beats trees/forests/boosting at short/medium horizons; e.g. 1-day RW RMSE ~1.25%, 1-year RW 11.84% vs regression tree 19.70%; converge at 2-year horizon; predictors = lagged copper + gold/silver/oil/natural gas/lean hogs/coffee futures and the Dow; rolling window.
checked_claims.note: Verified. Resources Policy vol. 69(C), 2020 (the citation omits the volume but is otherwise correct). RMSE figures verified exactly: 1-day RW 1.25% vs RT 3.16%; 1-year RW 11.84% vs RT 19.70%; 2-year RW 16.89% vs RT 20.18%. Predictor set and rolling-window methodology confirmed. Minor: 'converge to RW at 2 years' is slightly generous — at 2 years RW (16.89%) still beats RT (20.18%); models become 'more competitive' rather than equal. The directional thrust (RW very hard to beat short/medium) is fully correct.

checked_claims.claim: Sanchez Lasheras et al. (2015), 'Forecasting the COMEX copper spot price by means of neural networks and ARIMA models', Resources Policy 45, 37-43 — NNs (MLP, Elman) outperformed ARIMA; no random walk benchmark.
checked_claims.note: Verified exactly: Resources Policy vol. 45, pp. 37-43, DOI 10.1016/j.resourpol.2015.03.004. MLP and Elman recurrent NN outperformed ARIMA; Elman had lowest forecast error mean and variance. No random walk benchmark reported, exactly as the findings note. The findings correctly frame this only as a contrast point (NN is the opaque method the user wants to avoid).

checked_claims.claim: Liu, Liu, Zhou, Yan (2022), 'A multi-model fusion based non-ferrous metal price forecasting', Resources Policy 77 — dual-stage CEEMDAN then VMD (PSO-tuned) on highest-sample-entropy subsequence, LSTM back-end, on LME copper/aluminium/zinc; beats ARIMA/BPNN/LSTM on RMSE/MAE/MAPE; leakage-safety not clearly established.
checked_claims.note: Verified. Authors Liu Qing, Liu Min, Zhou Hanlu, Yan Feng; Resources Policy vol. 77(C), 2022. Dual-stage CEEMDAN+VMD, PSO-tuned VMD parameters, most-complex subsequence by max sample entropy, all subsequences forecast by LSTM, on LME copper/aluminium/zinc, superior to benchmarks on RMSE/MAE/MAPE — all confirmed. The findings' caveat (LSTM back-end is opaque; leakage-safety unclear; cite only as evidence the decomposition stage helps) is appropriate and well-judged.

checked_claims.claim: Yang, Li & Jiang (2024), 'Research on information leakage in time series prediction based on empirical mode decomposition', Scientific Reports 14:28362 — decomposing the whole series before splitting leaks future info, producing near-zero invalid RMSE (~0.001); leakage-safe re-decomposition (SW-CEEMDAN, single/multi-train-multi-predict) raises error 1-2 orders of magnitude.
checked_claims.note: Verified via PMC full text (PMC11569228), Scientific Reports 14:28362, 2024. Studies CEEMDAN; whole-series decomposition leaks test info and inflates accuracy ('illusion of high accuracy'); standard CEEMDAN-BiLSTM RMSE ~0.001 vs leakage-corrected ~0.12-0.35 (roughly 100-350x higher) — consistent with the '1-2 orders of magnitude' claim. Proposes SW-CEEMDAN (sliding window), STMP (single-train-multi-predict), MTMP (multi-train-multi-predict). This is a genuine, accurately represented methodological critique and the central integrity caveat of the dimension.

checked_claims.claim: World Bank (2023), 'Forecasting Industrial Commodity Prices: Literature Review and a Model Suite', Policy Research Working Paper 10611 — RW/no-change is the benchmark and hard to beat for metals short-horizon; interpretable structure helps mainly at monthly+ horizons.
checked_claims.note: Verified. PRWP 10611, 2023, authors Arroyo Marioli, Khadan, Ohnsorge, Yamazaki; covers oil + six industrial metals incl. copper; adapts six literature approaches; expanding-window evaluation; real (CPI-deflated) prices. Existence and scope confirmed. The specific stylized facts attributed to it in the findings (hard-to-beat RW, monthly+ gains) are reasonable but I did not extract the exact quantitative claims from the PDF — they are largely cross-supported by Kwas & Rubaszek (2021).

checked_claims.claim: Kwas & Rubaszek (2021), 'Forecasting Commodity Prices: Looking for a Benchmark', Forecasting (MDPI) 3(2) — biggest RMSE improvements for silver/copper/wheat, RW prevails for oil and gold; futures-based forecasts show useful directional/success-ratio accuracy at sub-annual horizons.
checked_claims.note: Verified. Forecasting vol. 3(2), pp. 1-13, June 2021, authors Marek Kwas & Michal Rubaszek. Eight commodities (WTI, Brent, natural gas, copper, gold, silver, wheat, maize). Finding matches exactly: biggest improvement for silver, copper and wheat; RW prevails for oil and gold; directional accuracy assessed via success ratios; recommendation to supplement RW with futures-based forecasts at short horizons. Accurately represented.

checked_claims.claim: Methodology citations: Diebold-Mariano (1995, JBES); Clark & West (2007, J. Econometrics, nested-model MSPE-adjusted test); Giacomini & White (2006, Econometrica, conditional predictive ability); Hansen, Lunde & Nason (2011, Econometrica 79:453-497, Model Confidence Set); Pesaran & Timmermann (1992, JBES, directional); White (2000, Econometrica 68, Reality Check); Hansen (2005, JBES 23:365-380, SPA).
checked_claims.note: All verified to correct authors, years and venues. Clark & West (2007) Journal of Econometrics 138(1):291-311; the findings' claim that plain DM is biased toward the small (nested) model and CW corrects it is the standard, correct interpretation (CW's own framing is that DM 'favors the smaller model'; describing DM as 'oversized' when used to reject equal accuracy in favor of the larger model is the common shorthand and is acceptable). GW (2006) Econometrica; HLN (2011) Econometrica 79:453-497; PT (1992) JBES vol. 10 (pp. 461-465 / 561-565 across sources — trivial page discrepancy); White (2000) Econometrica 68:1097-1126; Hansen (2005) JBES 23:365-380. No errors.

checked_claims.claim: Interpretability characterizations: STL most interpretable (trend + named seasonal + remainder on price scale); VMD interpretable via fixed K modes and named center frequencies; EMD-family IMFs only loosely interpretable and unstable at the right edge; DMA exposes time-varying predictor inclusion probabilities.
checked_claims.note: These method/interpretability descriptions are technically accurate. STL (Cleveland et al. 1990, LOESS-based, evolving seasonal) is correctly described and the statsmodels STLForecast pipeline (deseasonalize, ARIMA on adjusted series, add seasonal back) is real. VMD as a single variational optimization extracting K band-limited modes around center frequencies, less mode-mixing than EMD, is correct. EMD/EEMD/CEEMDAN sifting, mode-mixing, noise-assisted variants, and right-edge instability are correctly described. The findings appropriately avoid overclaiming: they explicitly note IMFs/VMD modes are mathematical not economic factors. No misleading 'black box called interpretable' problems — if anything the findings are commendably careful to flag the LSTM back-ends (Liu 2022) as opaque.

corrections: Buncic & Moretto venue is mis-stated. The published version is in The North American Journal of Economics and Finance, vol. 33 (2015), pp. 1-38 (DOI 10.1016/j.najef.2015.01.002), NOT the 'Journal of Commodity Markets.' The St. Gallen working-paper provenance is real (SSRN 2482015); fix the published-venue name to North American Journal of Economics and Finance.

Diaz, Hansen & Cabrera (2020): add the volume — Resources Policy vol. 69 (article 101545). Also soften 'models only converge to RW at the 2-year horizon': at 2 years the RW RMSE (16.89%) still beats the regression tree (20.18%); the accurate statement is that the tree methods become more competitive (gap narrows) at 2 years, not that they equal/converge to the RW. This does not affect the headline conclusion that RW is very hard to beat at short/medium horizons.

Buncic & Moretto DMS '~13.7%' out-of-sample R2 at one month was not independently confirmed in the sources reviewed (only the DMA ~18.5% figure was verified). Treat the DMS number as plausible-but-unconfirmed, or verify against the paper text before quoting it as precise.

Kriechbaumer (2014): the citation/claim should make explicit that the $126/tonne gain is measured against classic ARIMA only and that the paper does NOT include a random-walk benchmark (the findings note this once but it is worth stating wherever the $126/t headline is used, so it is not mis-read as a RW-beating result). Also note the paper frames the optimal wavelet-configuration search as a methodological novelty; the data-snooping concern is the reviewers' legitimate gloss, not the authors' stated caveat.

World Bank PRWP 10611 (2023): the specific quantitative stylized facts attributed to it (e.g. relative ranking of RMSE gains by commodity) were not extracted from the PDF here; the silver/copper/wheat-vs-oil/gold ranking is actually established by Kwas & Rubaszek (2021). Attribute that specific ranking to Kwas & Rubaszek, and cite the World Bank paper for the general 'RW hard to beat, gains at longer horizons / model-suite' conclusions.
